Module 3

Information Systems Infrastructure and Cloud Services

Module 1 asked what an information system is. Module 2 asked which system a company should build and why. This module asks the question underneath both of those: what does all of it actually run on, and who pays for it. Every app you have ever used is a program on a machine, in a room, reachable over a wire. A manager who cannot name those parts cannot judge a proposal about them — and cannot tell the difference between a bill that is large because the work is large and a bill that is large because nobody was watching.

How to use this page

  1. Assume no background. Every part is explained in ordinary language before anything uses it. If you have never opened a computer or thought about where a website lives, this page was written for you and nothing here assumes otherwise.
  2. Answer as you go. The activities sit inside the reading, at the point where the reading has just earned them. When you answer a question, every option explains itself — including the three you did not pick, because knowing why a wrong answer is wrong is the part that transfers.
  3. Watch for the two supplements. The last two sections are labeled application supplements. They are not textbook objectives; they connect this chapter’s material to the database work the course does elsewhere and to the way businesses actually use the internet.
  4. Retry anything. Restart one activity, one section, or the whole page. Your best result stays in this browser until you clear it; answers reset on reload so every attempt is fresh.
  5. Finish with the final challenge. Situations rather than definitions, scored by objective, so a weak area shows up instead of being averaged away.

Parts

What it is made of

Machines, the software that drives them, somewhere to keep the data, and wires between them. Five components, and every system you use is some arrangement of them.

Reach

How it connects

A network is three things: something to say, a path, and an agreed way of saying it. The internet and the web are that idea at world scale.

Decay

Why it never stays finished

Hardware ages, software stops being supported, data piles up, demand spikes in December, and the electricity bill grows. Owning is a running cost, not a purchase.

Rent

Why so much of it is rented

Somebody else owns the building, the power and the cooling, and you pay for what you use. That changes the economics, the risks and the questions you have to ask.

One idea connects the whole module Infrastructure is the part of technology a business would rather not think about, and that is exactly why it decides so much. What you can build, how fast you can try it, what it costs you when nobody uses it and what it costs you when everybody does — all of that is settled by the plumbing long before anyone writes a strategy about it.
Section 3–2a

Why infrastructure is a management question

A city works because of things nobody looks at: pipes under the road, cables under the pavement, a power station somewhere outside town. You notice them the day one of them stops. Organizations have the same layer underneath them, built from machines and programs and wire, and this module is about that layer.

The part you only see when it breaks

You do not lay your own roads when you open a shop; you rely on the ones already there. An organization’s technology works the same way. The information systems infrastructure is the shared foundation of machines, programs, storage and connections that every application in the company runs on.

No department owns it, everyone depends on it, and nobody thinks about it until it stops. That is what makes it a management question: foundation decisions are expensive to reverse, and they quietly settle what the business is able to attempt later.

The companies you know for something else

The chapter opens with Apple, Microsoft, Facebook and Google, then points out how little the obvious product captures. Google also works on driverless cars, life sciences, investment capital and space exploration, so a holding company called Alphabet was created to place around a dozen businesses under one umbrella and show investors where money is earned and where it is being spent.

What unites a robotics company and a search engine is one thing: the need for a reliable and high-performing infrastructure. It creates value three ways — efficiency, effectiveness and agility — and some of these firms rent theirs out.

  • Rented out — Google, Microsoft with Azure and Amazon with Amazon Web Services each built a fast, reliable infrastructure for their own operations, then sold capacity on it to everybody else.
  • Kept in-house — Apple runs its data centers only for users of its own ecosystem, and the owner of the Facebook app uses its own only for that network and its generative artificial intelligence models.
  • The judgment underneath — renting your foundation out turns a cost into revenue, and it also turns you into a supplier with customers, outages and support obligations you did not have before.

Three questions about that case before the components arrive.

1. The chapter describes a group of businesses that runs from search to robotics to life sciences to autonomous driving. Beyond the holding company itself, what does the chapter say unites them?

  • A. A single shared product line, since each of the companies is ultimately a way of selling advertising against search results — Advertising revenue is real, but the chapter’s own list of driverless cars, life sciences, investment capital and space exploration is precisely the point that these ventures did not fall neatly under a search engine company.
  • B. The need for a reliable and high-performing information systems infrastructure, which every one of them depends on — correct. The chapter states that beyond the holding company, what unites the different companies under the umbrella is the need for a reliable and high-performing information systems infrastructure.
  • C. A common set of customers, because the same people encounter each of the group’s businesses in the course of a week — The customers barely overlap at all. A buyer of industrial robots, a health researcher and a person running a search are not one market, which is part of why a holding company was needed in the first place.
  • D. Nothing beyond common ownership, since the chapter presents the restructuring as a purely financial arrangement — The restructuring did change financial reporting, showing where revenue is generated and where investments in new ideas are made, but the chapter names the shared infrastructure specifically as the thing lying under all of them.

2. Every company named in the opening case operates large data centers. The chapter still draws a contrast between two groups of them. What is the contrast?

  • A. Some run facilities of their own while the others rent all of their capacity from a third party — Every company in the case operates infrastructure of its own. The case is about what each of them then does with that infrastructure, not about which of them bothered to build one.
  • B. Some build facilities in many countries while the others keep all of their equipment inside one country — The chapter does describe one company’s sites as spread across many countries, but it never sorts the companies by geography, and a single-country footprint is not the distinction being drawn.
  • C. Some rent capacity on their infrastructure to other organizations, while the others use theirs only to run their own services — correct. Google, Microsoft with Azure and Amazon with Amazon Web Services capitalize on the investment by selling capacity, while Apple hosts services only for users of its own ecosystem and the owner of the Facebook app powers only that social network and its generative artificial intelligence models.
  • D. Some use their facilities for artificial intelligence work while the others use theirs only to store records — Artificial intelligence appears on both sides of the contrast, among the services sold to other organizations and among the workloads a company runs on its own machines, so it cannot be what separates the two groups.

3. A manager at a hypothetical distribution company argues that because infrastructure produces nothing a customer ever buys, the right goal is always to spend as little on it as possible. Which reply does the chapter best support?

  • A. Agree, because the chapter treats infrastructure spending as overhead to be squeezed wherever a business can get away with it — The chapter opens this objective by saying that computing, storage and networking technologies create value, and it spends its entire opening case on companies for which the infrastructure is central rather than incidental.
  • B. Agree, but only for companies selling physical goods, since the chapter limits its argument to firms whose product is itself digital — The argument is not limited by industry. The chapter’s later examples run from a parcel carrier’s facilities to an electronics factory in which sensors and controllers automate three-quarters of the production process, and it says that almost any business today is an electronic business.
  • C. Disagree, because the chapter argues that an organization should aim to own the largest infrastructure it can afford, on the grounds that owned capacity is the only capacity that can be relied on — Nothing in the chapter recommends owning as much as possible. The objectives that follow are largely about why owning is difficult and expensive, and about when renting somebody else’s foundation is the better answer.
  • D. Disagree, because the infrastructure creates value through efficiency, effectiveness and increasingly agility, and some firms sell the foundation they had to build anyway — correct. The lead-in says these technologies create value by enabling efficiency and effectiveness and increasingly by enabling agility, and the case shows several firms turning the infrastructure they built for themselves into a service that other organizations pay to use.

The five parts, named once

This objective takes the infrastructure apart into five components. From here on, every unfamiliar thing in this module is one of these five, or a decision about one of them.

  • Hardware — the physical machines that run an organization’s applications and databases, from the phone in a pocket to racks of servers answering everybody at once.
  • System software — the programs that control the basic operations of those machines, so an application can save a file without knowing what kind of disk is fitted.
  • Storage — where data stays when the day ends and the power goes off, which is a different question from where it sits while somebody is working on it.
  • Networking — the sharing of data or services between machines, which is what turns separate pieces of equipment into something an organization can actually use.
  • Data centers — the dedicated space the equipment lives in, with the power, cooling and physical security that keep it running, all of which somebody has to buy.

Follow one ordinary request through all five. The diagram gives each component its single job, where it appears when you tap a button to place an order, and what you notice the day it is missing.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Hardware — The physical machines, from the phone in a pocket to the racks in a locked room

What it is (The machines that run the applications and databases) → Its one job (Doing the computing work itself) → In an ordinary order (Your phone, and the machine that answers it) → Missing (There is nothing for anything else to happen on)

  • Organizations carry out hundreds or thousands of different activities, so they need several different types of computer to support them. A machine sized for one designer is not the machine that serves ten thousand customers at the same moment.
  • Hardware is where the spending is most visible, which is also why it is where the arguments start. It wears out, it is bought in whole units, and it has to be paid for whether or not it is busy.
  • A good deal of the hardware in a modern organization is not a computer in any form an ordinary person would recognise — the small controllers that start and stop a production line, or the sensors reporting a temperature every few seconds.
  • Section 3–2b takes this apart properly, from the classes of computer up through the specialised processors that explain why an artificial intelligence project carries a different budget line from an ordinary one.

System software — The layer sitting between an application and the machine it happens to be running on

What it is (Programs controlling the basic operations of the hardware) → Its one job (Letting software be written once, not per machine) → In an ordinary order (The operating system handing the app the screen) → Missing (Every program needs rewriting for every model of machine)

  • Application software does not talk to hardware directly. It asks the system software, and the system software talks to the machine, which is why one version of a program can run on equipment built by different manufacturers.
  • The operating system is the most prominent kind of system software, coordinating the hardware components, the attached devices, the application software and the users all at once.
  • This is the first appearance of an idea the whole module keeps reusing: put a common layer in the middle, and the things above it stop having to know anything about the things below it.
  • Section 3–2c covers it, together with the reason a company’s software eventually stops working on hardware that still switches on perfectly well.

Storage — Where data stays once the power is off and the working day is over

What it is (The place records are kept rather than used) → Its one job (Keeping data available for as long as it is needed) → In an ordinary order (The record of the order, still there tomorrow) → Missing (The organization forgets everything overnight)

  • Memory inside a running machine holds whatever is in use at this instant; storage is what survives the machine being switched off, and an organization needs far more of the second than of the first.
  • Not all stored data has the same job. Today’s live records, a nightly copy taken in case something fails, and records kept for years differ in how fast they must be reachable, how searchable they need to be, and how long they must last.
  • Storage is the component that grows without anybody deciding to grow it. Nobody chooses to have more data; it accumulates as a by-product of operating, and the cost follows it.
  • Section 3–2c covers storage alongside system software, because the choice of medium follows directly from what a given pile of data is actually for.

Networking — The path from one machine to another, whether across a room or across the world

What it is (The sharing of data or services between machines) → Its one job (Making the other four components reachable) → In an ordinary order (Everything between your tap and the answer) → Missing (Each machine becomes an island with a screen)

  • Taken alone, each individual piece of technology has little value; it is through connecting the different pieces that business value is realized. The best-performing database ever built is useless if the people who need it cannot reach it.
  • A network needs three things and no fewer: two parties with something to share, a pathway between them, and rules that both sides follow. Remove any one of the three and nothing has been communicated.
  • This is the component the internet and the World Wide Web belong to, which is why it needs two full sections rather than one, and why more of this module’s vocabulary lives here than anywhere else.
  • Sections 3–2d and 3–2e cover it, from what a network is at all up to how an address typed into a browser turns into a page in front of you.

Data centers — The room or the building around all of the above, with its power and its cooling

What it is (Dedicated space set aside for the infrastructure) → Its one job (Keeping the equipment running, cool and secure) → In an ordinary order (The building the answering machine stands in) → Missing (Equipment that overheats, loses power or walks away)

  • Equipment gathered in one place is easier to manage, repair, upgrade, power, cool and physically secure than the same equipment scattered through the cupboards of a dozen offices.
  • The range of sizes is enormous, from a single room with one server in it to a purpose-built facility the size of a warehouse with its own generators and its own cooling plant.
  • This is the component people forget, and it is the one that decides whether the other four are actually available at eight in the morning on the busiest day of the year.
  • Section 3–2f covers it, along with the two arrangements — a private area for employees and a shared one for business partners — that put the finished foundation to work.

Three kinds of value, one of them new

Two of the three came up in the previous module, so each gets a clause.

  • Efficiency — goals accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort, which is the value most people assume technology is for.
  • Effectiveness — goals and tasks accomplished well, which is a different question, since a process can be fast and still produce the wrong result.
  • Agility — the ability to change what the organization does, and to change it quickly, which computing, storage and networking increasingly deliver.

Agility is why so much of this module is about renting rather than owning. The chapter credits its rising importance to increasing digital density — more of the world, and more of every business process in it, now existing as data that something can act on.

Efficiency is doing today’s work faster, effectiveness is doing it well, and agility is being able to do tomorrow’s work at all. An infrastructure decision trades one against another, which is why it belongs to a manager and not only to a technician.

Why this is your problem even if you never touch a server

The chapter aims a box at students who do not intend to work in technology, and its argument runs in four beats. Each one names something specific that goes wrong when a manager lacks this vocabulary.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The foundation · It sits under nearly everything the organization does

  • The claim, in one line: The information systems infrastructure forms the foundation of almost all organizational activities, from managing customer relationships and supply chains through to supporting decision-making and innovation.
  • What it looks like in an ordinary week: Every ordinary thing you do at work rests on it: a customer record that loads, a report that runs, a file a colleague in another building can open, a payment that clears while somebody is still standing at the counter.
  • What skipping it costs you: Without a grasp of hardware, software, networks and data management, the chapter says, a future business leader risks missing critical opportunities or making uninformed decisions — and that sentence is aimed at business students rather than at technologists.
  • What it lets you do: It lets you treat an infrastructure proposal as a business proposal: what does this let us do, what does it stop us doing, and what happens to the business on the day it is not working.

The shared language · You will have to talk to technical people, and they to you

  • The claim, in one line: Whether you are working on a marketing campaign, developing a new product or improving an internal process, you will have to collaborate with the people who run the technology.
  • What it looks like in an ordinary week: Somebody tells you the delay is a network issue, or that the request needs another server, or that the data is in the cloud. Each of those sentences means something specific, and each one has a cost and a timescale attached to it.
  • What skipping it costs you: Not being able to speak the language of infrastructure produces misunderstandings in both directions. You cannot state what you actually need, and you cannot tell a genuine constraint from a convenient one.
  • What it lets you do: The chapter’s claim is that understanding terms such as servers, cloud computing, cybersecurity and databases enables clear communication, reduces misunderstandings and achieves better outcomes. It is also the cheapest of the four to act on.

The opportunities · Where this chapter reaches back into strategy

  • The claim, in one line: Businesses able to make use of cloud services, the Internet of Things and artificial intelligence infrastructure are better positioned to innovate and to respond to changes in their market.
  • What it looks like in an ordinary week: A competitor tries four ideas in the time it takes you to buy the equipment for one, because it rented its foundation instead of buying it and simply stopped paying for the three experiments that did not work.
  • What skipping it costs you: Without foundational knowledge of information systems, the chapter warns, you might overlook how technology can be used strategically to drive efficiency, customer satisfaction and growth. Nobody recommends a move they cannot picture.
  • What it lets you do: This is the hinge back to Module 2. Competitive advantage was the question there; here you learn what the answers are physically made of, and which parts of them a company would have to own rather than rent.

The personal skill · The same knowledge, turned on your own life

  • The claim, in one line: Individuals manage personal data across several devices, rely on storage they do not own, and face security threats such as phishing and identity theft.
  • What it looks like in an ordinary week: Your photographs sit on somebody else’s machines under an agreement you did not read, and your bank sends you a message that may or may not have come from your bank.
  • What skipping it costs you: Not knowing how data is stored, transmitted and protected leaves you unable to tell which of those situations is safe, which is merely irritating, and which is the one that will take a year to undo.
  • What it lets you do: The chapter’s conclusion is that this is not just a technical skill but a core life and business competency, one that supports smarter leadership, innovation and resilience in an increasingly digital world.

The third beat reaches back into strategy. Firms able to use cloud services, connected devices and artificial intelligence infrastructure respond faster when their market moves; without the vocabulary you may overlook how technology could be used strategically at all.

1. A hypothetical accounting firm lists its technology as the laptops and servers it owns, the operating systems running on them, the disks its records sit on, and the wiring and wireless equipment connecting them all. Which of the chapter’s five components has been left off the list?

  • A. Nothing has been left off, because those four descriptions cover all five components between them — Four of the five are indeed present — hardware, system software, storage and networking — but the chapter names a fifth component, and it is the one that is a place rather than a thing.
  • B. Data centers, meaning the dedicated space that houses the equipment and supplies its power, cooling and physical security — correct. The five components are hardware, system software, storage, networking and data centers, and the space itself counts because power, cooling and physical security are decisions somebody has to make and pay for.
  • C. Storage, because disks belong to hardware and the chapter means something different by storage — The disks are on the list and storage is exactly what they are for. Storage is a separate component because what the data is for decides which medium it belongs on, not because disks somehow stop being physical.
  • D. Networking, because cables and wireless equipment are hardware rather than a network — Cables and wireless equipment are physical, but the chapter counts networking as its own component because the value lies in the connection rather than in the parts, and this inventory does mention them.

2. The chapter says computing, storage and networking create value by enabling efficiency and effectiveness, and increasingly by enabling agility. What does the third of those add that the first two do not?

  • A. The ability to carry out the current work at a lower cost for each unit than competitors manage — Accomplishing goals faster, at lower cost or with relatively little time and effort is efficiency, which is the first of the two the chapter already had and which Module 2 defined.
  • B. The ability to carry out the current work to a higher standard, so that fewer results have to be corrected — Accomplishing goals and tasks well is effectiveness, the second of the two the chapter already had. Agility is not a measure of how good the output is.
  • C. The ability to change what the organization does, and to change it quickly — correct. Efficiency is about doing the current work faster and more cheaply and effectiveness about doing it well, whereas agility is about being able to change course quickly, which is why the chapter ties its rising importance to increasing digital density.
  • D. The ability to keep the current work running without interruption through an unusually busy period — Staying available under load is a genuine requirement and the module returns to it more than once, but that describes reliability rather than the capacity to do something different.

3. The chapter gives four reasons a business student should understand the infrastructure. Which one is the reason that connects this chapter back to competitive strategy?

  • A. That people who can make use of cloud services, connected devices and AI infrastructure are better placed to innovate — correct. The chapter says businesses able to leverage cloud services, the Internet of Things and artificial intelligence infrastructure are better positioned to innovate and respond to market changes, and that without this knowledge you might overlook how technology can be used strategically.
  • B. That the infrastructure is the foundation of almost all organizational activity — This is the chapter’s first reason and it is perfectly true, but it argues that the subject is unavoidable rather than that it is a source of advantage over anybody else.
  • C. That understanding the vocabulary makes conversations with technical colleagues clearer, so that a manager is not obliged to accept a recommendation simply because it was explained in words nobody else in the room understood — This is the second reason, about communicating with technical teams and reducing misunderstandings. It makes you better at working with a plan somebody else has proposed rather than better at seeing one.
  • D. That the same knowledge protects your own privacy, devices and personal data — This is the fourth reason, the personal one, about managing your own data and recognising threats such as phishing. Valuable, but it concerns you rather than the organization’s position in its market.
The habit worth forming now

When this module introduces something new, ask which of the five components it belongs to and which of the three values it should deliver. Those are the questions a manager asks when somebody arrives with a proposal and a price.

Section 3–2b

Hardware: the machines and the things that are not computers

Everything a business does with technology finally happens on a physical object somebody bought and plugged in. That object is the first component of an infrastructure, and the one people underestimate, because half of it looks nothing like a computer.

What hardware is, and why one kind is never enough

Hardware is the physical machinery of an information system: the computers running the applications and databases an organization needs to process transactions and analyze business data.

Business activities make different demands, so a company deliberately buys several kinds of machine. The chapter names six classes — its own sentence announces six and lists five, adding mobile devices afterwards.

  • Personal computer — used for personal and small-business computing, serving one person, and the reference point other classes get described against.
  • Workstation — a single-user machine for medical, engineering or animation work, with the processor and video hardware that rendering three-dimensional models needs.
  • Server — any computer on a network making files, printing and other services available to that network’s users, optimized for a thousand or more at once.
  • Mainframe — the central computing system of a major organization, serving ten thousand simultaneous users, built for availability and mission-critical transaction processing.
  • Supercomputer — the most powerful and expensive class, up to twenty times a mainframe, bought for massive scientific problems and typically not used by businesses.
  • Mobile device — tablets and smartphones, no longer a convenience beside the infrastructure but part of it, because real work now happens on them.

Pair each class with what it was optimized for; that outlasts any price figure.

Match

Six classes, six things they are optimized for

Pair each class of computer with what the chapter says it is built to be good at; the explanations say what each pairing rules out as well as what it rules in.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Personal computer
Personal computing and small business computing, for one person at a time This is the chapter’s reference machine, and the whole comparison table is really a description of how the other five differ from it. Its defining limit is the single user, not its speed.
Workstation
Visualizing and rendering three-dimensional models for a single demanding user Medical, engineering, architectural, animation and graphics work all need a fast processor, large memory and advanced video hardware. The user count stays at one, which is why it is not a server however expensive it gets.
Server
Access by many concurrent users, with high reliability and fast network connectivity The chapter defines a server by what it does for a network rather than by its size, and by the fact that many people reach it at once. That is what buys it more processing power, memory and storage than a single-user machine.
Mainframe
High availability, heavy shared use and security for mission-critical transaction processing This is the main, central computing system of a major organization, the machine the chapter reaches for when ten thousand or more users depend on the same records and the work cannot stop.
Supercomputer
Massive scientific problems that no ordinary machine could finish in a useful time It is the most expensive and most powerful class, and the chapter says plainly that business organizations typically do not use one. It is bought for a problem, not for a workload.
Mobile device
One person’s work, done on a handheld machine that travels with them Tablets and smartphones are in the table because they became part of the infrastructure rather than an accessory beside it, supporting today’s working arrangements as well as personal use.

Servers, because almost everything you use is one

What makes a server a server is not its shape. Many people reach it at once, so it carries more processing, memory and disk than a single-user machine, and is built for reliability and fast network connectivity.

Servers differ in what one request costs them. An informational website hands every visitor content it prepared once. A social network builds a different page for each visitor. Email, print and file servers serve no pages at all.

Two identical-looking sites can cost wildly different sums to run: one hands out something prepared earlier, the other builds something new for everyone who asks.

1. The chapter’s sentence introducing the classes of computer says there are six and then names five. Which class does that sentence leave out, and how can you tell it belongs?

  • A. The mobile device, which the sentence adds afterwards and which the chapter’s own comparison table carries as a sixth row — correct. The sentence names personal computer, workstation, server, mainframe and supercomputer, then adds mobile devices as an afterthought; the table settles it by listing six rows, mobile devices among them.
  • B. The embedded system, which is a computer built into another product and so ought to be counted among the general classes — Embedded systems are real and important, but the chapter deliberately places them outside the six general classes, under hardware that is not a general-purpose computer at all.
  • C. The workstation, which is easily mistaken for a personal computer and is the class most often dropped from such lists — The workstation is named explicitly in that sentence and has its own row in the table, with its own definition about rendering three-dimensional models for a single user.
  • D. Nothing is left out, because the chapter counts the personal computer and the notebook computer as two separate classes — The chapter treats personal computers and notebook computers together in one class, both used for personal and small business computing, so splitting them does not produce the missing sixth.

2. A hypothetical national parcel carrier keeps its billing and consignment records on one central system that ten thousand staff use simultaneously and that is not permitted to stop. A consultant suggests buying a supercomputer instead. What does the chapter’s comparison say?

  • A. A supercomputer fits, because it is the most powerful class available and this is the carrier’s most demanding system — Power is not the axis here. The chapter says supercomputers are used primarily for massive scientific problems and typically not by business organizations; buying one would spend a fortune on the wrong strength.
  • B. A mainframe fits, because it is optimized for high availability, heavy shared use and security, and is the chapter’s machine for mission-critical transaction processing — correct. Ten thousand simultaneous users on records that cannot go down is precisely the mainframe description: the main central computing system of a major organization, optimized for availability, shared use and security.
  • C. Several servers fit better than either, since the chapter describes servers as the class that handles more than a thousand simultaneous users — The figure is right and the conclusion is not. Servers do serve a thousand or more users, but the chapter reserves enterprise-wide transaction processing at this scale and this availability requirement for the mainframe.
  • D. The two classes are interchangeable at this scale, since the table describes both as serving anywhere from one user to many — The table gives supercomputers one to many users and mainframes ten thousand and more, and it gives them entirely different typical uses, so they are not interchangeable in either direction.

3. Two hypothetical sites look the same to a visitor. One is a public library’s opening-hours page, identical for everyone. The other is a member portal that assembles a different page for each person out of that person’s own records. Why does the chapter treat these as different requirements?

  • A. Because the second must be a mainframe, since building a page for each person counts as mission-critical transaction processing — Nothing in the situation says the records cannot go down or that ten thousand people use them at once. The chapter’s dynamic-page example is an ordinary web server, not a mainframe.
  • B. Because the first is an output device and the second is a general-purpose computer, which is the distinction the chapter draws whenever a machine hands something out rather than working something out — Output devices are monitors, printers and speakers. Neither of these machines is one, and the difference the chapter is drawing is between two kinds of server rather than between hardware families.
  • C. Because the first hands out content prepared once, while the second does fresh work for every request, so the two differ in processing power, network connectivity and software — correct. The chapter contrasts servers that display the same static pages for every visitor with servers that create pages dynamically from each user’s request, and says these have different requirements in processing power, network connectivity and software.
  • D. Because the second is a server and the first is not, since a machine handing out an unchanged file provides no service to the network — Both are servers. The chapter’s definition is any computer on a network making access to files, printing, communications or other services available to users, and handing out a page is exactly that.

The computers nobody calls computers

Everything so far has a screen and a user. Most computing in a modern economy has neither.

  • Embedded system — a computer built to do one set of tasks well, inside something nobody calls a computer: a media player, a traffic light.
  • Programmable logic controller — a specialized device automating machines and processes, in settings as different as a factory and a ski lift.
  • Sensor — an input technology measuring the physical world, reporting temperature, pressure, vibration or proximity in real time rather than waiting to be told.
  • Input and output devices — an input device gets data in, such as a mouse or a dock scanner; an output device presents results, such as a monitor.

Sensors are why this category exploded. The Internet of Things is a vast network of interconnected physical devices collecting and sharing data, often in enormous volumes.

Wire that reporting tightly enough to control something and it earns a name. A cyber-physical system integrates computing with physical processes, coordinating software, sensors and machinery closely enough to run on its own.

Why these are harder to protect. They are densely interconnected, that interconnection creates vulnerabilities, and failures land in the physical world. A failed web page is an inconvenience; a failed controller opens a valve.

Sort these devices into three families before the vocabulary blurs.

Sort

General-purpose computer, special-purpose device, or input and output

Place each piece of hardware in the family the chapter puts it in. Every situation described here is a hypothetical practice situation, and each one states the conditions you need.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

General-purpose computer — one of the six classes: it runs whatever software is installed on it, and the classes differ mainly in scale and in how many people it serves

  • A machine in the back room of a hypothetical online shop that holds the product catalogue and answers a thousand shoppers at once — This is the chapter’s server: a computer on a network making access to files and services available to many concurrent users, which is what buys it the extra processing power, memory and reliability.
  • The central system of a hypothetical insurer, used simultaneously by ten thousand staff for transaction processing and never permitted to stop — Ten thousand simultaneous users on mission-critical transaction processing is the chapter’s description of a mainframe, optimized for high availability, heavy shared use and security.
  • The machine a hypothetical animation studio buys so one artist can render three-dimensional scenes — A workstation is still a general-purpose computer serving one user; what separates it from an ordinary desktop is the processor, memory and video hardware needed for visualization and rendering.
  • The handheld a hypothetical delivery driver uses to receive the day’s jobs, record what was delivered and take payment — Mobile devices are the sixth class in the chapter’s table, and this one is doing organizational work rather than personal work, which is exactly why the chapter counts them as infrastructure.

Special-purpose device — built into something else to do one job for years, usually with no screen, no keyboard and nobody sitting at it

  • The computer inside a media player that will only ever play discs and that nobody will ever install other software on — This is the chapter’s definition of an embedded system: designed to perform one specific set of tasks effectively, inside a product nobody thinks of as a computer.
  • A small unit at a hypothetical resort that starts, stops and speeds up a ski lift according to a fixed control program — The chapter names ski lifts alongside manufacturing plants when it defines a programmable logic controller, a specialized device used to automate machines and processes.
  • The unit built into a car that manages engine performance and is never used for anything else — Controlling engine performance is one of the chapter’s own examples of an embedded system. The giveaway is that the task set is fixed at manufacture rather than chosen later by a user.

Input or output device — it does not do the deciding; its job is getting data into a system, or getting a result out to a person

  • A touch screen on a self-service ordering kiosk in a hypothetical cafe — The chapter lists touch screens with mice and cameras as input devices. It gathers what a person wants and passes it on; the machine behind it does the processing and the deciding.
  • A printer in a hypothetical warehouse producing the list of items a picker must collect — Printers are one of the chapter’s output devices, and this is the moment a system’s decision becomes something a person can act on. Nothing is being computed by the printer itself.
  • A small unit clamped to a motor in a hypothetical plant that measures vibration and reports it continuously to a maintenance system — This is a sensor, which the chapter treats as an input technology: it measures vibration in the physical environment and supplies that information in real time to something else that decides.
  • A reader mounted in a doorway at a hypothetical depot that picks up identifiers from tags on passing cartons and hands them to the stock system — The reader’s entire job is getting data into a system without anyone typing or aiming a scanner, which is what an input device does. The Internet of Things widened this category rather than creating a new one.

Tags, and the chip a budget turns on

Radio frequency identification, or RFID, moves data by electromagnetic field between a reader and a small RFID tag on an object. Against a bar code it needs no line of sight, holds more data, and reads at a distance.

  • Passive tags — a few cents each, no battery, readable from several feet, which suits anything shipped in bulk.
  • Active tags — several dollars each, carrying a battery, readable from hundreds of feet, which suits containers worth the cost.

Inside the box, the processor is where one proposal stops being interchangeable with another. A central processing unit is versatile and handles instructions in sequence, each result feeding the next — right for a formula waiting on the cell above.

A graphics processing unit runs thousands of small cores on many pieces of data at once, because every pixel can be worked out without knowing its neighbours. Training a model has that same parallel shape.

  • Tensor processing units — built by large providers to speed the matrix calculations that dominate deep learning, beating general graphics hardware.
  • Field-programmable gate arrays — processors reconfigurable after manufacture, so an unusual calculation reshapes the hardware rather than waiting for a chip.
  • Neuromorphic chips — designs modelled on the human brain, aimed at energy efficiency and speed for artificial-intelligence work rather than general throughput.

Training models is not a proposal to buy more of the machines you already own.

Explore

Four kinds of processor, and what choosing one commits you to

Open each card and read all four panels; the last card sets the families against each other, which is where the reason for all this specialization becomes visible.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Central processing unit · The general-purpose processor

  • What it is: The processor that performs a computer’s calculations, built for versatility across a very wide range of operations, which is why it sat at the heart of server architecture for decades.
  • The kind of work it suits: Sequential work, where instructions and results depend on one another, which the chapter says describes most traditional software.
  • The example that makes it click: Recalculating a spreadsheet, where a formula may need the answer from the cell above it before it can run at all, so nothing is gained by having a thousand helpers standing idle.
  • What it means for a budget: It is the default line in almost every hardware budget, and for transaction processing, reporting and ordinary business applications it is also the correct one. Nothing here needs a special case.

Graphics processing unit · Thousands of small cores working at once

  • What it is: A processor optimized for parallel processing, performing the same operation on very many pieces of data simultaneously using thousands of small cores.
  • The kind of work it suits: Work that splits into many identical, independent pieces, where no piece has to wait for another piece’s answer before it can start.
  • The example that makes it click: Rendering an image, where determining the colour value and intensity of one pixel needs nothing from the surrounding pixels, so every pixel can be handled at the same moment.
  • What it means for a budget: Faster training times made these a staple of machine-learning infrastructure, which means a modelling project buys different hardware than a database project and should be costed separately from the start.

Tensor processing unit · Custom-built for one shape of calculation

  • What it is: A processor developed by large providers and custom-designed to optimize the tensor computations that dominate deep learning, using a matrix-based architecture.
  • The kind of work it suits: The narrow band of work it was designed around, where the chapter reports it outperforming general graphics hardware on specific tasks.
  • The example that makes it click: The provider’s own language models, processed in batches on hardware the same provider designed, and then rented out to customers doing work of a similar shape.
  • What it means for a budget: You are unlikely to buy one; you rent time on it. That is the first place in this module where owning and renting stop being equivalent choices, and the cloud sections pick the thread up.

Reconfigurable and experimental silicon · Gate arrays, brain-inspired chips, whole wafers

  • What it is: Three further steps along the same road: field-programmable gate arrays offering customizable hardware acceleration, neuromorphic chips inspired by the brain’s architecture, and wafer-scale engines integrating vast numbers of cores.
  • The kind of work it suits: Work specialized enough that no general processor fits it well, or constrained enough by electricity that ordinary hardware is uneconomic to run.
  • The example that makes it click: A team with one unusual calculation reshaping a gate array around that calculation, rather than waiting for a chip that no manufacturer has any reason to build.
  • What it means for a budget: These are research and niche lines rather than standing budget items, but they are the reason to ask what a proposal actually runs on instead of assuming every machine is priced alike.

The four compared · Why specialization keeps increasing

  • What it is: A progression from general-purpose processors toward increasingly specialized hardware, which the chapter presents as the industry’s response to the escalating demands of machine learning and generative artificial intelligence.
  • The kind of work it suits: Every step trades flexibility for performance on a narrower band of work, which is a bargain worth making only when the work is both demanding and predictable.
  • The example that makes it click: The same chip family that renders video games became standard for training models, because the underlying calculation had the same independent, repeated shape in both cases.
  • What it means for a budget: The manager’s version of this whole box is one question: does this project run on the machines we already buy, or on a different kind of machine at a different price? The answer changes the number before anyone negotiates.

Application software never talks to this hardware directly. It talks to the system software, which talks to the machine.

Name the machine and you have named the constraint: how many people it serves at once, whether it does one job or any job, and whether it works in sequence or in parallel.

Check yourself

Devices, tags, and processors

Three questions on the hardware that is not a general-purpose computer; each explanation says what the wrong option genuinely describes.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical dairy installs small units that start and stop its bottling conveyors according to a fixed control program. None of them has a screen or a keyboard, and no one will install anything else on them. What does the chapter call these, and what separates them from the computers in the office?

  • A. Servers, because they make a service available to the other machines on the plant network and are reached by many devices at once — A server provides files, printing, communications and other services to users of a network. These units are controlling machinery, and nobody is requesting anything from them.
  • B. Input devices, because they take signals from the line and act on them, which is what the chapter says an input device does — An input device supplies data to a computer and stops there. These units decide and act, which is the difference between reading a sensor and running a conveyor.
  • C. Embedded systems, because any computer without a screen is by definition embedded inside the product it controls — The absence of a screen is not the test. Embedded systems sit inside a consumer product such as a media player or a traffic light; the chapter gives control of machines and processes, including ski lifts, its own name.
  • D. Programmable logic controllers, which are specialized devices used to automate machines and processes rather than to run whatever software someone installs — correct. The chapter defines programmable logic controllers as specialized computing devices used to automate machines and processes, in environments from manufacturing plants to ski lifts, and that fixed job is what separates them.

2. A hypothetical equipment yard wants to locate trailers parked across a site several hundred feet wide, and separately wants to identify low-value cartons as they pass through a doorway. What does the chapter’s account of tags suggest?

  • A. Active tags for the trailers, because they carry a battery and can be read from hundreds of feet, and passive tags for the cartons, because they cost a few cents and need only a few feet — correct. The chapter gives passive tags a range of up to several feet at a cost starting from a few cents, and active tags a battery, a cost upward of several dollars and a range of hundreds of feet, which matches the two requirements exactly.
  • B. Passive tags throughout, because they cost a fraction of the alternative and the real difference between the two kinds is how long they survive being knocked about rather than how far away they can be read — Durability is not the distinction the chapter draws. Passive tags simply cannot be read from hundreds of feet, so the trailers across the yard would go unlocated however many tags were bought.
  • C. Active tags throughout, because using a single kind of tag simplifies the readers and the extra cost per tag is trivial at any volume — Cost is not trivial when the tagged item is a low-value carton. Several dollars a tag against a few cents is the whole reason the chapter describes two kinds instead of one.
  • D. Bar codes for both, because the chapter presents tags as a replacement that has not actually arrived in practice — The chapter actually claims tags are rapidly replacing bar codes, and this module softens that rather than reversing it. The doorway requirement alone rules bar codes out, since they need line of sight and hand scanning.

3. Why, according to the chapter, did hardware built for rendering images turn out to suit the training of machine-learning models?

  • A. Because graphics hardware runs instructions one after another faster than a general-purpose processor does, and training a model is mostly one long chain of steps each of which waits for the one before it — This reverses the chapter’s argument. Sequential processing is what the central processing unit is designed for, and the point about training is precisely that it does not have to happen in sequence.
  • B. Because models are stored as images, so the hardware that displays pictures is also the hardware that can read them — Models are not stored as images, and nothing in the chapter suggests they are. The resemblance is in the shape of the calculation, not in the shape of the data.
  • C. Because graphics hardware carries far more memory than a general processor, and memory is the binding constraint when training a model — Memory matters, but it is not the explanation the chapter gives. Its account rests on parallelism: thousands of cores each doing an independent piece of the same work.
  • D. Because both jobs consist largely of the same calculation repeated over many pieces of data that do not depend on one another, so thousands of small cores can work at the same time — correct. Determining the colour value and intensity of a pixel is independent of the surrounding pixels, and the matrix and vector calculations underneath deep learning are independent in the same way, which is why parallel hardware suits both.

Section 3–2c

System software and storage

A machine full of hardware does nothing on its own. Something must tell the drive to save the file, and it cannot be the spreadsheet, which has no idea what machine it is running on.

The software that runs the machine, not the work

Sort every program into two piles. One holds the software the computer was bought for: the word processor, the browser. The other makes that pile possible. System software is the collection of programs controlling the basic operations of computer hardware.

Its most prominent kind is the operating system — Windows 11, macOS and Ubuntu Linux on computers, Android and iOS on phones. Its job is coordination, and it has four things to coordinate.

  • Hardware components — the parts inside the machine, such as processor and monitor, which cannot be aware of each other on their own.
  • Peripherals — devices attached to the computer, such as a printer, which is why any application can print without knowing every printer made.
  • Application software — the programs a person opens, which ask the operating system for what they need instead of reaching for hardware.
  • Users — the people giving instructions, whose clicks and keystrokes must become something the electronics can act on.

That order is the shape of the machine: user, application, operating system, hardware. The diagram redraws the relationship three ways.

Interactive diagram

What the operating system sits between

Pick a view to see the same relationship from a different angle: who talks to whom, why one layer covers many machines, and what a single drag of the mouse actually starts.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The operating system as coordinator — The centre of the machine, where every request from a person eventually arrives

Users (Clicks, keystrokes and gestures) → Application software (The word processor or accounting package the work is done in) → Operating system (Coordinates all four of the things around it) → Hardware and peripherals (Processor, monitor, drives, printers)

  • The chapter’s figure draws the operating system as a circle encompassing everything else, with arrows flowing between it and users, application software, hardware components and peripherals.
  • Nothing in the outer ring communicates with anything else in the outer ring. An application does not talk to a printer; it asks the operating system, which knows how to reach the printer.
  • That is why a peripheral only has to be understood once. Add a printer and every application on the machine can print, because printing was never the application’s job.
  • It also explains a familiar frustration: when one program cannot see a device, the fault is usually in the coordinating layer or its device driver rather than in the program complaining about it.

One common layer, many machines — The join between software that is written once and hardware that comes in hundreds of shapes

Applications (Written for an operating system, not for a model of computer) → Operating system (The common layer, plus a driver for each device) → Many different machines (Desktops, laptops and everything else running that system)

  • The chapter’s second figure stacks applications on top of the operating system with a double-headed arrow between them, then three arrows down to three different machines.
  • The sentence to remember: the operating system provides a common layer for different underlying devices so that applications only have to be developed for different operating systems rather than for each different computer model.
  • The arrow between applications and the operating system points both ways because the traffic runs both ways: the application asks, and the system reports back what happened.
  • Device drivers are what make the bottom arrows possible. Each one teaches the common layer to communicate with one particular device, so hardware variety is absorbed in one place instead of in every program.

One gesture, a long sequence underneath — The chapter’s own example: copying a file from a flash drive to a hard disk

You drag an icon (Point, click, drop it on the hard disk) → The graphical interface (Turns the gesture into an instruction) → The operating system (Issues the complex set of coded instructions) → The hardware (Bits and bytes move from one device to the other)

  • A graphical user interface lets you send instructions by selecting or manipulating pictures, icons and menus, which is the only part of this sequence you ever see.
  • Underlying the icons and the simple dragging is a complex set of coded instructions telling the electronic components that a set of bits and bytes is being transferred from the flash drive to a location on the internal hard disk.
  • The chapter’s challenge is a good one: imagine typing that whole set of instructions every time you wanted to copy a file. The interface is not decoration; it is the reason the machine is usable without training.
  • The same hiding happens one level down, where the system is often written in assembly language and is designed to insulate you from it — the layer exists so that nobody above it has to learn the language below it.

One layer, many machines

The operating system provides a common layer over different devices, so applications are built for each operating system rather than each computer model. A firm whose customers own hundreds of laptop models writes a handful of versions.

Underneath, the differences still have to be handled. Device drivers let a computer communicate with particular hardware: a small program for one make and model. A printer released years after your operating system works because a driver arrived.

Operating systems are often written in assembly language, a very low-level language that lets a computer operate quickly and efficiently, and which the system exists to keep out of sight. What you see instead is a graphical user interface, taking instructions through pictures, icons and menus rather than typed commands.

Code somebody else already wrote

A solid infrastructure also includes frameworks and libraries: collections of prewritten code such as NodeJS, JQuery, React and TensorFlow. They buy an organization three things.

  • Development time — work already solved by somebody else is reused, which is how a small team ships something substantial in weeks.
  • Reach across platforms — some frameworks build applications that run on several platforms, so a firm does not pay twice to reach two audiences.
  • Specialized capability — libraries for work such as machine learning put techniques within reach of teams that could not write them.

Choosing a framework is also choosing a dependency: it shortens the build and ties you to somebody else’s decisions about what to keep supporting.

Check yourself

System software, drivers, and the common layer

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A colleague says the accounting package on her laptop “talks to the hard drive when it saves.” What does the chapter’s account of system software say is actually happening?

  • A. She is right, because application software reaches the hardware directly and the operating system is only there to manage the screen, the keyboard and the mouse while the application gets on with the work — The operating system does manage the screen and the mouse, but it does far more than that. Reading from and writing to a storage device is one of the tasks the chapter lists as performed by the operating system itself.
  • B. The accounting package asks the operating system, which is the system software controlling the basic operations of the hardware, and the operating system reaches the drive — correct. System software is the collection of programs that control the basic operations of computer hardware, and the operating system coordinates the interaction between hardware components, peripherals, application software and users, so the save request travels through it.
  • C. The accounting package writes to the drive itself, and the operating system checks afterwards that the file arrived intact — If applications wrote to hardware themselves, every application would need to understand every make of drive. Verifying afterwards is not the arrangement; the operating system does the writing, not the inspecting.
  • D. The hard drive requests work from whichever application is open, so the package responds rather than instructs — Hardware does not request work from applications. A drive is a device the operating system reaches on behalf of whatever asked, which is why one program cannot seize a device from another.

2. A hypothetical print shop buys a printer model released long after the operating systems on its computers were written, and the printer works. Which piece of the chapter’s account explains that, and what is assembly language doing in the same story?

  • A. A device driver lets the computer communicate with that particular piece of hardware, and the operating system is written in assembly language so that nobody else has to be — correct. Device drivers allow the computer to communicate with various different hardware devices, and the chapter says operating systems are often written in assembly language, a very low-level language, with the system designed to insulate you from it and make operations unobtrusive.
  • B. The graphical user interface recognizes the printer visually, and assembly language is the language users type instructions in when the interface cannot help — A graphical user interface enables you to send instructions by selecting or manipulating pictures, icons and menus. It is how a person addresses the machine, not how the machine identifies an unfamiliar device.
  • C. The printer contains its own operating system that replaces the computer’s for the duration of the job, and assembly language is what applications are written in — Nothing in the chapter puts a replacement operating system inside a peripheral, and assembly language is described as the language operating systems are often written in rather than the language of applications.
  • D. Frameworks and libraries supply the printing code to each application, and assembly language is a kind of storage medium used while a document waits — Frameworks and libraries are collections of prewritten code that reduce development time and help applications run on different platforms; they are not a substitute for a driver, and assembly language is a programming language rather than a medium.

3. A development team proposes building its new application on a widely used framework instead of writing everything itself. What does the chapter say frameworks and libraries provide, and what should the manager also notice?

  • A. They provide finished applications the firm can rebrand, so the manager should notice that the product will look like competitors’ products — A framework is a set of building blocks rather than a finished product, and the chapter describes it as supporting the development and operation of applications rather than as something to rebrand.
  • B. They provide the operating system functions the application needs, so the manager should notice that the firm no longer needs to license an operating system — Frameworks sit above the operating system rather than replacing it. An application built on a framework still runs on an operating system, and the licensing question is untouched by the choice.
  • C. They provide collections of prewritten code that cut development time and help an application run on different platforms, so the manager should notice the firm is taking on a dependency — correct. The chapter says frameworks and libraries offer collections of prewritten code, helping to reduce development time, enable building applications that run on different platforms, or develop machine learning models — and reusing somebody else’s code means depending on their future decisions.
  • D. They provide faster access to the hardware by going round the operating system, so the manager should notice that the application will need a device driver of its own for every machine it is installed on — Nothing bypasses the operating system in this account; applications reach hardware through it. Drivers belong to devices rather than to applications, so a framework choice does not create one.

Storage, and the three kinds of data

Storing and retrieving data is the other half of the job, and the amount held grows every year. Some industries must keep records — email included — long after anyone needed them.

  • Operational data — data used for managing business processes and for analysis; what the business is running on right now.
  • Backup data — short-term copies used to recover from a system-related disaster, frequently overwritten as newer backups are taken.
  • Archival data — long-term copies kept for compliance and reporting rather than for any current operational use.

Four requirements separate them: timeliness, access speed, searchability and life span. Operational data must be current, immediate and searchable. Backups must be recent and restorable. Archives are read rarely and must simply last.

The medium follows. Operational data sits on fast disk, or on flash where speed is critical, as in machine learning. Backups go somewhere secure but quick to restore. Archives go to magnetic tape.

Tape is chosen for its weaknesses. Data is written sequentially, so access is slow and contents are not quickly searchable. In exchange it lasts up to 30 years, costs very little, and is removable.

A caution the chapter leaves out. Archives are lost far more often because nothing can still read them — the format abandoned, the last drive dead — than because the tape decayed.

Sort a set of situations by which type of data is in front of you.

Sort

Which kind of data is this, and where does it belong?

Place each situation with the type of data it describes, then read why the requirements push it onto that medium. Every organization here is a hypothetical practice situation.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Operational data — used for managing business processes or for analysis; needed now, fast, and searchable

  • The stock figure a shopping site reads the instant a customer adds an item to a basket — This is data used for managing a business process as it happens, and response time is of the essence, so it belongs on hard drives or on flash-based storage such as solid-state drives.
  • Customer records and transaction data that staff query all day from a database — The chapter puts transaction-processing data and customer data in databases on disk-based storage media, because hard drives offer high access speeds for data that is frequently accessed.
  • Business documents, images and company brochures that employees open during the working day — Not all operational data sits in a database. The chapter names business documents, images and brochures as operational content stored as files, still on fast disk because people are waiting for them.
  • The large volume of varied data a machine learning project reads over and over while training a model — The chapter says AI and machine learning require fast storage to analyze vast quantities of different data, which is exactly the case flash-based storage exists for.

Backup data — short-term copies for recovering from a disaster, frequently overwritten by newer ones

  • Last night’s complete copy of the order system, written to a secure location in case this morning’s server fails — This is a short-term copy made to recover from a system-related disaster. Keeping it on hard drives enables quick recovery without slowing the company’s operations.
  • A completely redundant second set of systems, held ready so that business continues seamlessly if the primary systems fail — The chapter describes redundant systems as the strongest form of the same idea: the copy exists so operations continue, so its whole value is in being recent and fast to bring up.
  • A copy that tomorrow’s copy will overwrite, because what matters about it is that it is recent — Backups are frequently overwritten with newer backups, which is what separates them from archives; their life span requirement is short by design rather than by neglect.

Archival data — long-term copies kept for compliance and reporting, rarely read but required to last

  • Internal email from several years ago that nobody expects to open, but that the organization must be able to produce if it is ever asked — The chapter’s own example of archival data is old internal email, kept for compliance and reporting and stored long-term on magnetic tape rather than on working systems.
  • Records written sequentially to low-cost removable media and taken to a secure site some distance away — Sequential writing, very low cost and removability are the properties the chapter gives magnetic tape, and removability is what lets the archive be both expandable and stored remotely.
  • A store of finished records that is slow to read and cannot be searched quickly, and where nobody minds — Slow access and poor searchability would be disqualifying for operational data. For an archive they are an acceptable trade for a life span measured in years at a very low cost.

Files, folders, and a hierarchy that is not really there

Within most computers, digital information is organized using files and folders. Three terms carry that structure.

  • File — a block of data storing specific content, such as a document, image or spreadsheet, and the unit people name and move.
  • Folder — a grouping of related files, also called a directory, though strictly the folder is the graphical element representing it.
  • Root directory — the top of the tree, typically the drive itself, from which subdirectories branch, each holding files and further directories.

But this is a logical arrangement only. One file may be scattered across many places on the drive, and two files in the same folder on screen may sit nowhere near each other.

Almost everything here is one idea in different clothes: put a layer in between, and the thing above it stops having to know how the thing below it works.

Four questions on storage requirements and on how data is arranged.

Check yourself

Storage requirements, media, and the shape of a file system

Four options each, with an explanation for every one, including the options you rejected.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical charity is told to “buy faster storage” for everything it keeps. Which four requirements does the chapter use to separate the three types of data, and why does the instruction fail?

  • A. Cost, security, ownership and location, and the instruction fails because faster storage is harder to secure — Cost and security are real concerns and cost is precisely why tape is used for archives, but these are not the four requirements the chapter names for distinguishing the three types of data.
  • B. Timeliness, access speed, searchability and life span, and the instruction fails because archives need life span rather than speed — correct. The chapter distinguishes operational, backup and archival data by their requirements in terms of timeliness, access speed, searchability and life span, and archival data is defined by a long life span at low cost rather than by speed.
  • C. Volume, format, department and vendor, and the instruction fails because different departments buy different equipment — These describe how equipment gets purchased rather than what the data needs. The chapter’s categories are about purpose, and purpose is what decides the medium.
  • D. Accuracy, completeness, timeliness and relevance, and the instruction fails because speed cannot improve data quality — Accuracy, completeness and relevance are qualities of information rather than the storage requirements this section names, although the closing observation about speed and quality is sound.

2. Which arrangement matches what the chapter says about matching each type of data to a physical medium?

  • A. Operational data on magnetic tape because it is written continuously, backups on flash storage, and archives on hard drives so they stay searchable — This reverses the media. Data is stored sequentially on tape, so access can be very slow and the contents are not quickly searchable, which is why the chapter reserves tape for archives.
  • B. Everything on flash-based storage, because a slow read is a business risk wherever it happens — Buying the fastest medium for data nobody reads is the waste the three categories exist to prevent, and the chapter reserves flash for situations where access speed is of crucial importance.
  • C. Operational data in databases or files on hard drives or flash storage, backups on hard drives for quick recovery, and archives on magnetic tape — correct. The chapter stores operational data in databases or files on disk-based or flash storage, notes that storing backup data on hard drives enables quick recovery without slowing operations, and archives data no longer used operationally on magnetic tape.
  • D. Operational data on hard drives, backups written to the same drives to keep recovery simple, and archives deleted once they stop being read — A backup on the same drive as the live data disappears with it in the failure it was meant to survive, and archives are kept precisely because they may still be required for compliance and reporting.

3. A manager assumes that because two documents sit in the same folder on screen, they are stored next to each other on the disk. What is the chapter’s correction, and why does it matter?

  • A. The folder structure is a logical organization; the data is not physically organized the same way on the drive, which is another case of a layer hiding the machine — correct. The chapter is explicit that although you can access data using files and folders, the data is not physically organized the same way on the drive, and that gap is the same abstraction the operating system performs everywhere else.
  • B. The folder structure is physical, and moving a file between folders therefore moves it across the disk surface — This is the belief being corrected. Dragging a file between folders changes where it appears in the hierarchy, and says nothing about where its contents physically sit.
  • C. Folders exist only in the operating system’s memory and vanish when the machine is switched off, so nothing about them is stored at all — The hierarchy persists across restarts, since a drive that forgot its own structure would lose access to everything on it. What is logical is the arrangement, not its permanence.
  • D. Folders are the same thing as directories in every respect, so the question has no answer worth giving — The two words are close but not identical: the chapter says a folder is strictly a graphical element representing a directory, and in any case the physical question still has a definite answer.

4. What does the chapter mean by the root directory, and what follows from a hierarchy shaped that way?

  • A. The folder that holds the operating system itself, which is why deleting anything inside it stops the machine from starting and why ordinary users are kept out of it — System files usually do live somewhere below the root, but that is not what the word names. The root is the starting position of the whole tree, whatever happens to be stored in it.
  • B. The oldest folder on the drive, from which every later folder inherits its settings and permissions — Age has nothing to do with it, and the chapter does not describe folders as inheriting settings from one another. The root is defined by position in the hierarchy, not by history.
  • C. The top of the tree, typically the drive itself, from which subdirectories branch out and each directory can hold both files and other directories — correct. The chapter says that akin to a tree, the root directory, typically the hard drive, is at the top and subdirectories branch out, with each directory able to contain files as well as other directories.
  • D. A hidden folder used by the archive process, which is why ordinary users never encounter it — The root is the most visible location on a drive rather than a hidden one, and archiving is about moving data to different media rather than about a special folder.

Section 3–2d

Networks: how machines share

Taken alone, the chapter says, each piece of technology has little value; it is by connecting the pieces that business value is realized. Many innovative business models would not exist without the internet.

A network is a conversation, with equipment instead of people
