When you speak, you code a message into sounds, send it through the air, and the listener decodes it. Computer networking is the sharing of data or services, and it makes the same three moves — so it has the same three requirements.

  • Something to share — a source and a destination with a message between them; with nothing to share, there is nothing for equipment to do.
  • A pathway — the transmission media, the physical route data travels: a cable through a wall, or a radio signal across a room.
  • Rules both sides follow — protocols, which define the procedures computers follow when transmitting and receiving, so whatever arrives can be interpreted.

The chapter makes the third concrete. You write to employers in France; one replies in full. There is information to share and the internet carried it — but the reply is in French. Nothing failed; nothing was communicated.

Arrival is not communication. Two systems can be wired together perfectly and share nothing, because agreeing on a wire is not agreeing on a language.

Most network failures are one of the three requirements going missing.

Complete it

The three requirements, in the chapter’s own words

Choose the wording the chapter uses in each sentence; the explanation appears once you pick, and it says what the other choices would actually have described.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

  • Computer networking is the sharing of data or services, which is why a connection carrying nothing anybody wants is not doing any work. The chapter defines computer networking as the sharing of data or services, which keeps the definition about purpose rather than equipment. Cabling is only the second requirement, the pathway, and a network can use radio instead of any cable at all. Speed is bandwidth, which describes how well the sharing goes rather than what the sharing is.
  • The first requirement is a sender and a receiver — a source and a destination — that have something to share. A message has to exist before anything can carry it, which is why the chapter states this requirement first. Machines of entirely different makes exchange data constantly, because that is what the third requirement, an agreed protocol, exists to make possible. Being in the same building describes a local area network, which is one type of network rather than a condition every network has to meet.
  • The second requirement is a pathway or transmission medium, such as a cable, to send the message along. The transmission media are the physical pathway, cable or wireless, used to transmit data, and the chapter lists them second because a message with nowhere to go is going nowhere. A protocol is the third requirement, and it governs interpretation rather than travel. A server is a role a machine can play, not a requirement of a network: two peers with no server between them are still a network.
  • The third requirement is rules or protocols governing communication between senders and receivers. Protocols define the procedures that different computers follow when they transmit and receive data, which is what makes an arriving message interpretable. Bandwidth decides how long a transfer takes and never decides whether it can be understood. A shared physical medium restates the second requirement, and the chapter is careful to keep the pathway and the rules apart precisely because a message can have the first without the second.
  • In the chapter’s example the reply arrives intact but in a language the reader cannot decode, which shows that if the message is not understood by the receiver, there is no communication. This is the chapter’s own sentence, and it is the whole reason protocols are named as a separate requirement rather than assumed. The pathway plainly worked, because the email arrived complete and on time, so blaming the route misreads a delivery success as a delivery failure. The sender did encode the message, and encoded it perfectly well in French; the encoding and the decoding simply did not match.

What is sent, and how much of it

Computer communication is made of bits, the smallest unit of data a computer uses, and the only difference the network sees is how many: thousands of bytes for a customer address, fourteen thousand for a page of text, two hundred million for a photograph, billions for a design file.

Bandwidth is the transmission capacity of a channel, in bits per second. A network inside a building carries a hundred million to a thousand million of them per second — far more than the connection leaving that building.

Why one file takes eight seconds and the same file takes a day

The chapter sends one gigabyte — a forty-five-minute video — over six connections. Dial-up needs a day and a half; ordinary cable two hours; fifth-generation mobile twenty-seven seconds; gigabit fiber eight.

One sentence explains all six and outlives every figure: time equals size divided by rate. Only the path changed, and a path a thousand times wider finishes in a thousandth of the time.

One conversion first: storage is counted in bytes, networks in bits. A byte is eight bits, so a gigabyte is eight thousand megabits. Divide by megabits per second for seconds, twice by sixty for hours.

Write one formula for the first row below; it fills down the column.

Spreadsheet

How long does one gigabyte take?

Type one formula for row 2 in each column and run it; it is applied to every row the way a filled-down formula behaves in a real sheet.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Columns: Connection · Capacity in megabits per second · Seconds for one gigabyte · Minutes for one gigabyte · Times faster than the modem

1. Column C: how many seconds does one gigabyte take on each connection? One gigabyte is 8000 megabits and column B holds megabits per second. Round to the nearest whole second.

=ROUND(8000/B2, 0)

That is the whole table in one formula: time equals size divided by rate. Notice the first row runs to more than a hundred thousand seconds, which is where the chapter’s day and a half comes from.

2. Column D: the same answer expressed in minutes, rounded to one decimal place.

=ROUND(8000/B2/60, 1)

Rounding at the end rather than partway through keeps the small rows honest: the fiber row is a fraction of a minute, and rounding it to whole minutes would have reported zero and hidden the answer.

3. Column E: how many times faster than the dial-up modem in row 2 is each connection? Round to the nearest whole number.

=ROUND(B2/$B$2, 0)

This column is the two before it read backwards. A connection roughly eighteen thousand times faster finishes in roughly an eighteen-thousandth of the time, and that relationship holds no matter what a typical connection happens to cost this year.

No judgment entered anywhere: the same three symbols produced a day and a half and eight seconds. The same arithmetic explains an expensive mistake — a business that moves large files overnight on a connection sized for office traffic has bought a network that cannot finish by morning.

Check yourself

Requirements, bits, and the arithmetic

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for the options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. The chapter says business value comes from connecting the pieces rather than from the pieces themselves. Which statement is the chapter’s own reason for that claim?

  • A. A network costs more than the machines it joins together, so it deserves the larger share of management attention — Relative cost is not the chapter’s argument, and it would be a weak one, since a network is usually a small fraction of what an organization spends on its machines and its software.
  • B. Taken alone each piece of technology has little value: the best database in the world is useless if the people who depend on it cannot reach it — correct. The chapter states that taken alone each individual piece of technology has little value, and its own illustration is that the best-performing database would be useless if it could not be accessed by the people or applications throughout the organization that depend on the data.
  • C. A network is the one part of an infrastructure that keeps working when an individual machine fails, so it is what the organization actually depends on — Some networks are built to survive the loss of a machine, but plenty are not, and a network is quite capable of failing on its own. Resilience is a design choice rather than a property of being connected.
  • D. A network removes the need to keep data in any one place, because anything wanted can be requested from wherever it happens to be — Connecting machines does not remove the need to store anything. The data still has to sit somewhere, on somebody’s storage, and the network only changes who can reach it from where.

2. A hypothetical architecture practice and a hypothetical insurance office both report that transfers to a second site are slow. The practice is sending design files; the office is sending pages of text and customer records. What does the chapter’s comparison of content sizes suggest about the two complaints?

  • A. The two complaints describe the same problem, because bandwidth affects every kind of content in exactly the same way once it has been reduced to bits travelling over the same wire — Bandwidth does apply to every kind of content, which is exactly why the amount of content decides the outcome. Two workloads that differ by a factor of a million on the same connection are not the same problem.
  • B. The office should be affected more, because a large number of small items takes longer than one large item regardless of the total quantity involved — The chapter’s comparison is about total quantity, not about how it is packaged. A few thousand bytes remain a few thousand bytes whether they arrive as one item or several.
  • C. The practice is moving files of several billion bytes while the office is moving items of a few thousand, so the same connection is doing work that differs by orders of magnitude — correct. The chapter puts a customer’s address at a few thousand bytes and a computer-aided design file at several gigabytes, and since time equals size divided by rate, the same rate produces wildly different waits.
  • D. Neither complaint can be about the network, because all content is reduced to bits and bits travel at the same speed on any medium — Reducing everything to bits is what makes the sizes comparable rather than what makes them equal. The medium also matters, which is the entire content of the connection-speed table.

3. A hypothetical training centre is told that upgrading from a one megabit per second connection to gigabit fiber will help “a little” with a one gigabyte video. Using the chapter’s own comparison, what should it actually expect?

  • A. A change of roughly a thousandfold, turning a transfer of more than two hours into a matter of seconds — correct. Time equals size divided by rate, so multiplying the rate by a thousand divides the time by a thousand: the chapter’s own table takes the same one gigabyte from about two hours and thirteen minutes down to about eight seconds.
  • B. A modest improvement, because the size of the file is the main thing determining how long a transfer takes — Size is only half of the calculation. Holding the file constant and changing the rate is precisely the comparison the chapter’s table makes, and it changes the answer by orders of magnitude.
  • C. Almost no improvement, because bandwidth describes capacity rather than speed and the two are unrelated — Bandwidth is defined as how much data can reliably be transmitted over the medium in one second, which is what makes an estimate of the time possible in the first place.
  • D. No change worth having, because a video takes as long to transfer as it takes to watch, its length being fixed — Transfer time and playing time have nothing to do with each other. The forty-five minute video in the chapter’s example arrives in eight seconds over fiber and takes more than a day over a modem.

Three roles: server, client, and peer

Machines on a network are not equals. Three roles separate them, and the difference is which way requests travel.

  • A server — any computer making files, printing and other services available to a network’s users. Servers only provide.
  • A client — any computer or application, such as a mail program, that uses those services. Clients only request, and serve one user.
  • A peer — any computer that both requests and provides, so one machine is a client one moment and a server the next.

Once the work happens elsewhere, the desk machine can shrink. Thin clients are microcomputers with minimal memory, storage and processing, using desktop virtualization to give a worker a desktop running on a server. A terminal holding no data cannot lose any.

  • Client-server networks — servers and clients have defined roles; this is the typical business arrangement, and almost everyone at work is inside one.
  • Peer-to-peer networks — any device can provide as well as request, which is what homes and small offices run, with nothing set aside to serve.

Networks come in sizes, and the size is really a distance

Networks are classified by the distance they cover, which is easier to remember than the abbreviations suggest.

  • Personal area network — wireless communication between one person’s own devices, over technologies such as Bluetooth, under ten meters.
  • Local area network — sharing data, applications and other resources among several users, usually within one building.
  • Wide area network — connecting multiple local area networks, from several buildings to worldwide, with ownership often spread across parties.

The wide area network is elastic: across buildings on one site it is a campus area network, across a city a metropolitan area network. Once it leaves your buildings, part of the path is somebody else’s.

The pathway can be radio. A wireless local area network, almost always called a Wi-Fi network, runs on high-frequency radio waves, installed for mobile devices and wherever cable is impractical. Fifth-generation mobile suits large numbers of connected devices because its latency is very low.

Ask whether a machine answers requests, makes them, or does both, and how far the wire must reach. Those two questions name the role, the arrangement and the network at once.

Pair each type with its use and its reach.

Match

Which network, over what distance

Pair each kind of network with what the chapter says it is for and how far it reaches; the explanation names what makes each one distinct.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Personal area network
Wireless communication between one person’s own devices, using technologies such as Bluetooth, over a range under ten meters This is the smallest of the types and the one most people use without ever calling it a network: a phone and a set of headphones, or a laptop and a wireless keyboard on the same desk.
Local area network
Sharing data, software applications and other resources between several users, typically within a single building This is the ordinary office or home network. Its capacity is usually far higher than the connection leaving the building, which is why moving a large file to a colleague upstairs feels instant and sending it to another site does not.
Wide area network
Connecting multiple local area networks over a large physical distance, often with ownership and management distributed among several parties The distributed ownership is the part that matters managerially: once the path leaves your buildings, some of it belongs to other organizations, so availability is partly somebody else’s decision.
Campus area network
A wide area network spanning several buildings belonging to one organization on a single site It is the middle case between one building and a city. A hospital group whose clinic, laboratory and administration buildings share one site is the ordinary example.
Metropolitan area network
A wide area network covering the area of a city Larger than a site and smaller than a country, this is the scale of a transit authority connecting stations, depots and a control room across one urban area.
Wireless local area network
A local area network built on high-frequency radio-wave technology instead of cable, also called a Wi-Fi network The reach is the same as a wired local network; only the pathway changed. Organizations install them for mobile devices and wherever running a cable is impractical, and the ease of installation is why public ones are now almost everywhere.
Fifth-generation mobile network
A mobile network offering extremely low latency and high transmission speed, which the chapter flags as promising for large numbers of connected devices Latency is the delay before a response begins, which is a different measure from capacity. It is the one that matters when a machine has to wait for an answer before it acts on something physical.

One last pass over roles and sizes.

Check yourself

Roles, arrangements, and distances

Three situations rather than definitions; every option is explained, including the ones that describe something real but different.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. In a hypothetical two-person design studio each computer can open files kept on the other, and neither machine is set aside to serve. In a hypothetical accounting firm, thirty desks open files kept on one machine that answers all of them and asks nothing of anybody. How does the chapter classify the two?

  • A. Both are client-server networks, because in each case a machine is answering requests for files — Answering a request is not enough to make a machine a server in the chapter’s sense. A server provides services and does not request them, whereas each studio machine does both, which is the definition of a peer.
  • B. The studio is a peer-to-peer network and the firm is a client-server network, because a peer both requests and provides while servers and clients have defined roles — correct. The chapter defines a peer as any computer that may both request and provide services, and puts peer-to-peer arrangements in small offices and homes; client-server networks are those in which servers and clients have defined roles, and they are the typical business arrangement.
  • C. The studio is a client-server network with two servers, and the firm is peer-to-peer because thirty machines are sharing one resource between them — This reverses both cases. Two machines that each provide and request are peers, not servers, and thirty clients depending on one provider is the textbook picture of a client-server network.
  • D. Neither can be classified until it is known whether the connections are wired or wireless — The medium is a separate question from the roles. A wired network and a wireless one can each be arranged as client-server or as peer-to-peer, because the two decisions are independent.

2. A hypothetical call centre is choosing between three hundred ordinary desktop computers and three hundred thin clients running desktop virtualization. Which statement matches the chapter?

  • A. Thin clients cost less because they are smaller and simpler, but each one still needs its own installed copy of every application the centre uses, so the whole saving is confined to the purchase price of the hardware — The licensing and maintenance saving is the chapter’s stated reason for the arrangement, precisely because the software is not installed three hundred times. Confining the benefit to hardware misses the larger half of it.
  • B. Thin clients remove the need for a network, because a stripped-down machine runs its software locally without asking anything of a server — The opposite is true. A thin client is almost entirely dependent on the network, because the environment the worker sees is running on a server somewhere else and reaching it is the only thing the terminal does.
  • C. Thin clients are a kind of peer, because the desktop each one displays is assembled from the other terminals on the floor — A peer both requests and provides services. These terminals only request, and they request from a server rather than from each other, which makes the arrangement client-server.
  • D. Thin clients have minimal memory, storage and processing of their own, and desktop virtualization runs each worker’s desktop on a server instead, which cuts licensing and maintenance cost and keeps the data off the desk — correct. Thin clients are microcomputers with minimal memory, storage and processing capabilities, and the chapter says they use desktop virtualization to provide workers with a virtual desktop environment, helping reduce costs for software licensing or maintenance and comply with stringent privacy and data protection requirements.

3. A hypothetical hospital group has a network inside each of its three buildings on one site, a further network joining those three buildings together, and a wireless link between a nurse’s tablet and the scanner clipped to her belt. Which three types has it just described?

  • A. A wide area network in each building, a metropolitan area network joining them, and a wireless local area network between the tablet and the scanner — A wide area network covers a large physical distance and connects local networks, so it cannot be what sits inside a single building, and a metropolitan area network is specifically one covering the area of a city rather than one site.
  • B. A personal area network in each building, a local area network joining them, and a wide area network between the tablet and the scanner — This inverts the distances. A personal area network reaches under ten meters, which is nowhere near a building, and a wide area network spans far more than the gap between a nurse and her own belt.
  • C. A local area network in each building, a campus area network joining them, and a personal area network between the tablet and the scanner — correct. A network typically within a building is a local area network; a wide area network spanning several buildings on one site is what the chapter calls a campus area network; and wireless communication between one person’s devices under ten meters is a personal area network.
  • D. Three local area networks and nothing else, because everything described sits inside one organization on one site — Ownership is not what classifies a network. The chapter classifies by size, distance covered and structure, and on those measures the link to the belt scanner and the link between buildings are plainly different from the network inside one building.

Section 3–2e

How the internet and the web actually work

Everything before this becomes useful only when something far away can reach it. So this section pulls apart the most ordinary act in working life: opening a page.

One network made out of many networks

The internet is a large worldwide collection of networks using a common protocol to communicate with each other. Notice what that omits: not one network, and no owner. Internetworking means joining host computers and their networks into larger ones.

The web is not the internet

The World Wide Web is a system of interlinked documents on the internet — a graphical user interface to it, the chapter says. The web runs on the internet as an application runs on an operating system.

  • Hypertext — documents carrying links to other documents, so a reader moves between them in any order; the chapter calls this the web’s key feature.
  • A web page — a hypertext document, holding content and the links leading away from it, which makes it a page and not a file.
  • A hyperlink — a reference from one document to another that a reader can follow, turning separate documents into a web.
  • A web browser — the application used to locate and display web pages and their text, graphics and multimedia. It asks for documents, then decides how they look.
  • A website — a collection of interlinked web pages owned by one organization or person, usually hosted on a web server.

Email and file transfers cross the internet without being the web, so the two words name different arrangements and risks.

Check yourself

Two words that are not the same word

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical charity’s new volunteer says the internet and the World Wide Web are two names for the same thing. Which correction matches the chapter?

  • A. There is no real difference worth making; the chapter uses the two words interchangeably, and so may anyone else — The chapter defines the two separately, in different subsections, and the distinction does real work: a video call and a file transfer use the internet without touching the web at all.
  • B. The web is the collection of separately owned networks, and the internet is the set of documents that travels across it — This has a sound pair of definitions attached to the wrong words. The network of networks is the internet; the interlinked documents are the web, which the chapter calls one of the most powerful uses of the internet.
  • C. The internet is a worldwide collection of networks using a common protocol, and the web is a system of interlinked documents running on top of it — correct. The chapter defines the internet as a large worldwide collection of networks that use a common protocol to communicate with each other, and the World Wide Web as a system of interlinked documents on the internet.
  • D. The internet is the part of the web that ordinary members of the public can reach, and the web also takes in private company systems — Private company systems appear later in this objective as intranets, and they are not a further layer of the web. Who may reach something is a question of authorization, not of which of these two words applies.

2. What makes a document a web page rather than simply a file of text somebody stored on a machine?

  • A. It sits on a server rather than on a personal computer, which is what the word page is recording — Where a file sits does not decide what kind of thing it is. The chapter defines a web page by what it contains, and such a page can be written and read on one machine long before it is put on a server.
  • B. It is a hypertext document, so it carries both content and links to other documents, which is what lets a reader move between pages in any order — correct. The chapter defines a web page as a hypertext document containing not only content but also hyperlinks, and calls hypertext the key feature of the web.
  • C. It has been indexed by a search engine, since a document nobody can find is not yet part of the web — Indexing is something a search engine does afterwards, and the material on the deep web makes the opposite case: most of the web has never been indexed and is still the web.
  • D. It is written in a language browsers understand, which is the whole requirement, and links are an optional extra on top — Being readable by a browser is necessary but is not the defining feature. Without links the result would be a library of unconnected documents rather than a web, which is precisely the distinction the word carries.

3. The same page looks slightly different on two machines, although both asked the same server for the same address. Which division of labour explains that?

  • A. The server sends a finished picture of the page, so a difference has to be a fault in one of the two connections — A server sends a document, not a picture. If it sent finished images, the web could not adapt to a phone, a laptop and a projector without the site being rebuilt separately for each of them.
  • B. The server sends the document and its markup, and the browser interprets that markup and decides how the result is drawn on that particular screen — correct. In the chapter’s walkthrough the browser translates the markup, formats its visual appearance and displays the result, so the final drawing is the browser’s decision rather than the server’s.
  • C. The browser keeps pages permanently, so the second machine is showing an older copy that the server has since replaced — Browsers do keep copies to save time, but the chapter’s account of a request ends with the browser rendering what it has just received, and an older copy would not by itself explain a difference in appearance.
  • D. The difference comes from the address, since a small variation in an address returns a different version of the page — Both machines used the same address, which is what the situation states. Different addresses can certainly return different pages, but that is not what happened here.

What a page is actually made of

A page is written in Hypertext Markup Language, or HTML, the standard method of specifying the structure and content of web pages, using codes called HTML tags — in angle brackets, usually paired — that tell the browser how to present it.

HTML5 is the chapter’s name for the current version, which added multimedia without extra software. Cascading style sheets, or CSS, specify formatting and layout: HTML says what a document’s parts are, CSS says how they look, so one change restyles a thousand pages.

Match the chapter’s eight tags to what each one does.

Match

The chapter’s eight HTML tags

Pair each tag with what it does. All eight come from the chapter’s own table, and the addresses inside them are placeholders printed as inert text rather than working links.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

<html> ... </html>
Delineates the whole document, so every other element sits inside this one pair This is the outermost pair. A browser reading a file knows the markup starts here and ends at the closing tag, which is why it is the only tag that never sits inside another.
<head> ... </head>
Holds the title, scripts, styles and metadata that are not displayed on the page itself Everything in here is about the document rather than in the document. The title shows in the browser tab, the styles decide how things look, and none of it appears as text a reader can see.
<body> ... </body>
Holds the visible portion of the document, which is everything the reader actually sees The split between this and the head is the first structural decision in any page: information about the page in one place, the page itself in the other.
<b> ... </b>
Creates bold text, turning bolding on at the opening tag and off again at the closing one The chapter uses this to explain paired tags in general: one marks the beginning of an effect and the other marks its end, which is why leaving out a closing tag bolds the rest of the page.
<p> ... </p>
Creates a new paragraph, which is how the browser knows where to break the running text Pressing return in the source file does nothing at all. A browser only breaks the text where the markup tells it to, which is the first surprise for everyone who views the source of a page.
<table> ... </table>
Creates a table, so the enclosed content is laid out in rows and columns rather than as prose This tag changes the shape of the layout rather than the appearance of a few words, which is why it encloses a whole block of content instead of a phrase inside a sentence.
<a href="second-page.html"> ... </a>
Creates a hyperlink, so the enclosed words carry the reader to another document This is hypertext made concrete. The setting inside the opening tag names the destination, and the words between the two tags are what the reader sees and clicks.
<a href="mailto:name@example.org"> ... </a>
Creates a link that opens a new email message rather than opening a page The same tag with a different kind of destination. It is a useful reminder that a link names a resource in general, and a web page is only the most common kind of resource to name.

Where pages live, and how one is asked for

Pages sit on web servers, which handle requests using the Hypertext Transfer Protocol, or HTTP: rules letting one company’s browser read another’s page. Servers often build pages from databases on request, so the product page you opened did not exist until you asked.

Data between server and user is easily intercepted, so organizations use HTTPS, the secure form of that protocol. The padlock reports it in use; without it a card number crosses unknown networks readable.

How a request finds one machine out of billions

Every device carries an IP address, the destination the network routes to, in the older form four numbers under 256. Numbers being hard to remember, people type a uniform resource locator instead. Read mail.example-museum.org from the right.

  • The top-level domain — the suffix, here org, naming the family the address was registered under.
  • The domain name — here example-museum, the part identifying the organization, and the piece somebody registers and pays for.
  • The host name — here mail, naming which web server answers; www normally means the default site with the home page.

One registered domain can therefore carry mail, photos and the public site on separate machines. Suffixes fall into three families: organization kinds, country codes, and generic ones.

A QR code is a two-dimensional bar code holding an address, or an action such as a payment. Write the reading rule as code, which forces exactness.

Write the code

Read an address the way a machine has to

Write each function so every test passes; a failing test prints what your code returned beside what was expected.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. The chapter splits an address into a host name, a domain and a top-level domain. Implement addressParts(address): return those three parts as an array, in that order. The domain and the top-level domain are the last two labels; anything before them is the host name, and an address with fewer than two labels names no domain at all.

Signature: addressParts(address) -> [host, domain, topLevelDomain]

function addressParts(address) {
  var labels = String(address).split('.').filter(function (l) { return l.length > 0; });
  if (labels.length < 2) return ['', '', ''];
  var n = labels.length;
  return [labels.slice(0, n - 2).join('.'), labels[n - 2], labels[n - 1]];
}

Counting from the right is the whole trick, and it is the reason this is worth writing down. Reading a name from the left tells you what somebody wants you to notice; reading it from the right tells you which name was actually registered.

2. Two addresses belong to the same site when they share a domain and a top-level domain, whatever host names sit in front. Implement sameSite(a, b), returning true or false. An address that names no domain matches nothing, including another address that names no domain.

Signature: sameSite(a, b) -> boolean

function sameSite(a, b) {
  function registered(s) {
    var l = String(s).split('.').filter(function (x) { return x.length > 0; });
    return l.length < 2 ? '' : l[l.length - 2] + '.' + l[l.length - 1];
  }
  var ra = registered(a);
  return ra !== '' && ra === registered(b);
}

The fourth test is the one to remember. A convincing name in the host position proves nothing, because the host part is chosen freely by whoever owns the domain — and the domain is the last two labels, not the first two words you happen to recognize.

What actually travels

The internet moves everything using TCP/IP, the transmission control protocol and internet protocol together. It never sends a request whole: it breaks it into chunks called packets, sends those separately, and reassembles them.

  • Pieces travel independently — packets from one file take different routes, so no congested link decides how fast it all arrives.
  • A failure costs a fragment — a missing packet is resent alone, instead of restarting the whole transfer.
  • Many conversations share a path — all traffic is in small pieces, so one download cannot occupy a link while everybody waits.

Put the eight steps of one round trip in order.

Sequence

One request, from keystroke to page

Put the eight steps into the order the chapter describes, then read why each one has to sit where it does.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

This is the chapter’s own walkthrough of what happens between typing an address and seeing a page. It is worth getting the order exactly right, because almost every complaint you will ever hear about a slow or broken system is really a complaint about one of these eight steps.

  1. The user enters the address of a web page into the browser’s address bar, and the browser turns it into a request for the page at that address. — Nothing can begin until something has been asked for. Note that the person supplies a name, not a machine: everything that follows is the work of turning that name into a specific destination.
  2. TCP/IP breaks the request into small chunks called packets and routes them across the internet toward the web server where the requested page is stored. — This is where the request stops being one thing. Breaking it up is what lets the pieces travel efficiently over networks that are carrying millions of other people’s pieces at the same time.
  3. When the packets reach their destination, TCP/IP reassembles them into the original request and passes that request to the web server. — Reassembly has to happen before the server sees anything, because a web server answers requests and knows nothing about packets. Each layer hides its own mess from the layer above it.
  4. The web server recognises that a web page is being requested, because the transfer protocol is named at the front of the address, and it retrieves the page. — The protocol named in the address is what tells the server which kind of conversation this is. The same machine can answer several kinds, and it needs to know which set of rules applies before it can respond at all.
  5. The page is broken into packets by TCP/IP in turn and transmitted back across the internet toward the computer that asked for it. — The journey home works exactly like the journey out, which is why a connection can be fast in one direction and slow in the other. Nothing about the reply is privileged; it is traffic like any other traffic.
  6. TCP/IP reassembles the packets at the destination and delivers the finished page to the web browser. — The second reassembly restores the document the server sent. Only now does anything on your machine hold something that looks like a page rather than a pile of numbered fragments.
  7. The browser translates the HTML code, formats its visual appearance, and displays the results on the screen. — This is the step people mistake for the whole process. The server sent structure and content; the decision about what it looks like on this screen was made here, at the last possible moment.
  8. If the page contains a hyperlink and the user follows it, the whole process repeats from the beginning. — Hypertext is what makes the cycle a loop rather than a line, and it means the browser is not holding a session with one machine but starting a fresh conversation, often with a different organization entirely.

Calls, and programs talking to each other

Voice over IP uses internet infrastructure to place telephone or video calls — WhatsApp, FaceTime, Zoom, Teams — because once everything is packets, telephone and computer networks stop differing.

The same protocols let applications call each other. An application programming interface lets a consumer pass pre-specified parameters to a provider and get a result without knowing how it works: a ride-hailing app sends two points to a mapping service and gets a route.

Look at the last value. A request such as directions?origin=A&destination=B&key=YOUR_KEY ends in a credential naming the account that gets billed — and it lands in logs, screenshots and pasted examples.

The part of the web you cannot search

Search engines walk from link to link, so what they cannot reach never becomes findable. The deep web is what they cannot index: pages behind authentication, pages generated from a database on request, and pages nothing links to.

The dark web only shares a syllable: areas used for nefarious purposes — drugs, stolen card details, illegal material — reachable only through browsers that anonymize the user.

Sort

Surface, deep, or dark

Place each item in the layer it belongs to. Situations described as hypothetical are practice situations, and each one states the condition you need in order to decide.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Surface web — public pages that other pages link to, so a search engine can walk to them and put them in its index

  • A news agency’s front page, which dozens of other sites link to and any search engine can reach — Public and linked from elsewhere, which is the whole requirement. A program that navigates by following links has an obvious route to it and will index what it finds.
  • An encyclopedia article that anyone can open and that thousands of other pages point at — The chapter names this kind of site among its examples of the common or surface web. Public plus heavily linked is the most indexable combination there is.

Deep web — ordinary content a conventional search engine cannot index: behind a login, generated from a database on request, or linked from nowhere

  • The pages of a course system that open only after a student signs in with an account — This is the chapter’s first category of deep-web content: private areas requiring authentication. A learning management system is its own example, and nothing about it is hidden or improper.
  • An online store’s product page, assembled from a database at the moment somebody asks for that particular product — The chapter’s second category: dynamic pages created from connected databases. There is no stored page for an indexing program to walk to, because the page is made in response to a question.
  • A document on a public server that no page anywhere links to — The chapter’s third category: static pages that are not connected to other pages by hyperlinks. The document is public in the sense that anyone with the exact address can open it, and unfindable to anyone who does not have it.
  • A hypothetical hospital’s patient records, held behind its own firewall on its own network — Internal content behind a corporate or institutional firewall is not accessible to search engines. It is a variation on the authentication category, and it is why an organization has to build its own way of searching what it holds.
  • A scientific journal archive that charges institutions for access and admits no indexing program — The chapter names subscription archives directly. Because the publisher charges for access, the contents are not made freely available for indexing, so they sit outside the searchable surface.
  • A government agency’s weather records, which appear only once somebody runs a query against its database — The chapter names public agency databases among deep-web content for exactly this reason: their contents are dynamically generated from databases and displayed on demand, so there is nothing standing there to be indexed.

Dark web — a deliberately hidden area used for criminal purposes, reachable only with software that anonymizes the user and hides their traces

  • A marketplace trading stolen payment card details, reachable only through software that conceals who is visiting — Both halves of the chapter’s definition are present: a nefarious purpose, and access only through specialized browsers that anonymize the user. This is the part that is deliberately hidden rather than merely unindexed.
Check yourself

Protocols, addresses, packets and keys

Five situations drawn from this section; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical cooperative’s membership page asks for a bank account number, and the browser shows no padlock beside the address. What does the chapter’s account of the two web protocols say is at stake?

  • A. Nothing much, since the padlock reports whether the organization behind the site is trustworthy rather than anything about the connection — The padlock reports on the protocol in use, not on the character of the organization. A dishonest site can be reached over a protected connection and an honest one over an unprotected connection.
  • B. The page will load more slowly, because the secure form of the protocol is the one browsers are optimized for — Speed is not what separates them. The chapter’s reason for the secure protocol is interception in transit, together with growing concern about both legitimate and illegitimate monitoring of web traffic.
  • C. Data travelling between the server and the member’s computer can easily be intercepted, and the secure protocol is what stops the account number crossing in readable form — correct. The chapter says data traveling between a server and a user’s computer can easily be intercepted, which is why organizations now routinely use the secure protocol for anything sensitive, and the padlock is the browser reporting that it is in use.
  • D. The account number is safe the moment it reaches the server, so the protocol matters for what the server does with it afterwards rather than for the journey — What the server does later is a separate question with separate safeguards. The exposure described here happens on the way, across several networks belonging to companies neither party has any relationship with.

2. A hypothetical garden centre sells forty thousand products and its site shows a page for every one of them, yet its web server stores only a few dozen files. How does the chapter explain that?

  • A. The remaining pages are held on each visitor’s own computer and assembled there by the browser out of files it has kept from earlier visits — A browser draws what it is sent; it does not hold a company’s product data. Nothing on the visitor’s machine knows what is in stock this morning or what it now costs.
  • B. Web servers often employ scripting to assemble pages on the fly, retrieving data from a database and inserting it into the page when somebody asks for a particular product — correct. The chapter says web servers often employ scripting languages to assemble pages on the fly or retrieve data from databases and insert it into the page presented to the user, which is why the page did not exist until it was asked for.
  • C. The site must be using compression, which is what allows forty thousand separate pages to be squeezed into the space that a few dozen ordinary files would otherwise occupy on the server — Compression makes stored files smaller; it does not conjure a page that was never written. The gap here is between stored files and reachable pages, not between large files and small ones.
  • D. Forty thousand pages do exist as stored files, but a search engine reaches only the few dozen that other pages link to — This confuses storage with indexing. It is a true statement about why such pages sit in the deep web, but it assumes the pages were written and stored in advance, which is exactly what did not happen.

3. A hypothetical museum is told it can run its public site, its ticketing system and its staff mail under one registered name without any of the three interfering with the others. Which reading of an address explains how?

  • A. Each service needs its own registered domain, and the three would merely be made to look similar to visitors — Registering three names is possible but is not what was described, and it throws away the shared identity that made the arrangement attractive. One registration can carry as many host names as an organization needs.
  • B. The path written after the address is what separates one service from another, so all three would answer on the same single server out of three different folders sitting side by side on its disk — A path does name a particular resource inside a site, and it is a real part of many addresses, but it is not one of the three parts of the address itself and it cannot send a request to a different machine.
  • C. An address names a host, a domain and a top-level domain, so different host names in front of one registered domain can reach different servers or groups of servers — correct. The chapter dissects an address into the host name, the domain and the top-level domain, and gives an organization’s mail, photo and mapping services each answering on a different host name in front of the same domain.
  • D. The top-level domain selects the service, so the museum would register the same name under three different suffixes — Suffixes indicate the family a name was registered in and something about the registrant. Using three of them would create three separate registrations rather than three services under one name.

4. Why does the internet break a file into packets and send the pieces separately, rather than sending it as one continuous stream?

  • A. Because a network carries one message at a time and no more, so a long file has to be interrupted at intervals to let everybody else’s traffic through before it is allowed to continue — Networks carry traffic from many senders at the same time, which is what they exist to do. Packets are what makes that sharing orderly rather than a workaround for a network that could otherwise manage one thing.
  • B. Because breaking requests and files into small chunks lets them be routed and transferred efficiently, with pieces able to take different paths and a lost piece resent on its own — correct. The chapter’s justification is that breaking requests and files into small packets allows for efficiently routing and transferring data across a network, and reassembly at the destination puts the pieces back before anyone sees a result.
  • C. Because the receiving machine cannot hold a whole file at once and has to be given it in instalments — Storage is not the constraint. A machine with ample room for the entire file still receives it in packets, because the reason lies in the network between the two ends rather than at either end.
  • D. Because encryption operates on small blocks, so a file has to be divided before a secure protocol is able to carry it — Secure transport and packet transport are separate matters. Traffic carrying nothing sensitive at all is packetized in exactly the same way, and the chapter gives efficiency as the reason.

5. In the interface request shown in this section, the final value passed across is a key identifying the account that will be billed for the work. Which conclusion follows?

  • A. It is safe where it is, because values inside an address are discarded as soon as a page has finished loading — Addresses are among the most copied strings in computing. They turn up in server logs, browser history, screenshots, chat messages and pasted examples, any of which can outlive the page by years.
  • B. It is a credential travelling in a place that is routinely logged, copied and shared, so treating it exactly like a password is the least that is required — correct. The key names the account that pays, and it is sitting in the part of a request most likely to be recorded and passed on, which is why this section flags it before the cloud material returns to a case built on exactly this failure.
  • C. It identifies the provider rather than the consumer, so losing it would inconvenience the mapping service rather than the caller — The key is issued to the consumer so that the provider knows whose account to charge. Whoever holds it can spend against that account, which is why the consumer is the party exposed.
  • D. It cannot be misused on its own, because a request is accepted only when the other agreed values are supplied alongside it — Those other values are supplied by whoever makes the request, so they are no obstacle whatever. Anyone holding the key can supply their own and have the work billed to somebody else.

Section 3–2f

Intranets, extranets, and where the machines live

The last two sections built the web out of parts, all of them indifferent to who is asking. This section adds the two decisions that turn that machinery into a business: who is let in, and where the machines sit.

The same website, with a lock on the door

A company publishes pages anybody can read. Now picture a second set only staff can open: this month’s announcements, Friday’s training, the health-cover form. What changed is who is let in.

An intranet looks and acts like a public website and uses the same software, hardware and networking, but adds authentication, firewalls or both, so proprietary data is viewable only by authorized users. Five common uses:

  • Disseminating corporate information — announcements and policies published once, so nobody works from a copy emailed round last spring.
  • Employee training — courses staff work through on their own schedule, reachable from every desk but not publicly.
  • Project management — plans, schedules and status, where every member sees the same version at the same moment.
  • Collaboration — shared documents and discussions letting different departments work on one thing rather than separately.
  • Employee self-service — portals where staff handle their own benefits and retirement plans rather than asking an office.

An intranet reachable only from a desk fails the staff who are elsewhere, so companies let employees use a virtual private network, or VPN, to connect securely while travelling. The internet is a road anyone may drive on; the VPN is an armoured van.

Check yourself

Intranets and the private tunnel into them

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for the options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A company’s public site and its internal staff site look almost identical and were built by the same team with the same tools. What, according to the chapter, actually makes the second one an intranet?

  • A. It runs on proprietary software written for internal use, rather than on the ordinary web technologies the public site uses — The chapter says the opposite in as many words: an intranet uses the same software, hardware and networking technologies as a publicly accessible website. Nothing has to be rewritten to make a site internal.
  • B. It uses authentication techniques, firewalls, or both, so that proprietary data inside the corporate network can be viewed only by authorized users — correct. An intranet looks and acts just like a publicly accessible website and uses the same technologies to transmit and display data, but it adds authentication techniques and/or firewalls so that the data can be viewed only by authorized users.
  • C. It is stored on a separate machine, and keeping the two sets of pages on different servers is what makes one of them internal — Separate machines are common and often sensible, but a second server with no access control on it is simply a second public site. Where the pages sit is not what restricts who may read them.
  • D. It contains information about employees rather than about products, and the subject matter of the content is what decides the category — Subject matter is a good clue and a poor rule. A public site can carry a staff directory quite legitimately, and the chapter’s summary table separates the three arrangements by users and access rather than by topic.

2. An organization puts benefit elections, retirement-plan changes and other human-resources tasks on its intranet so that staff complete them themselves. What is the chapter’s name for this use, and what is the point of it?

  • A. Collaboration, because several people in different departments now work on the same record at the same time — Collaboration is a separate use the chapter lists, and it means shared work on a common document or discussion. Here each person is completing their own record, and nobody else is meant to touch it.
  • B. Disseminating corporate information, because publishing the current benefit rules in one place is the substance of what has been built — The rules almost certainly are published alongside the forms, which makes this tempting. Dissemination is one-way publication, though, and the distinctive thing here is that the employee changes something rather than reads something.
  • C. Employee self-service through employee portals, which lets staff administer benefits and similar human-resources applications for themselves — correct. The chapter lists enabling employee self-service for administering benefits, managing retirement plans, or other human-resources-based applications through employee portals as one of the standard uses of an intranet.
  • D. Project management, because enrolment runs to a deadline and the intranet is tracking progress towards it — Project management is another of the chapter’s listed uses, and it covers plans, schedules and the status of work in progress. An annual deadline does not turn a form into a project.

3. Employees increasingly work from home and while travelling, and they need the intranet. Why does the chapter say companies use a virtual private network rather than simply publishing the intranet on the open web behind a password?

  • A. Because a VPN lets employees connect securely to the company’s intranet from the road or from home, keeping the traffic protected while it crosses public infrastructure — correct. The chapter says increases in employee mobility mean the intranet must be accessible from anywhere, so most companies allow employees to use VPNs to connect securely to the intranet while on the road or working from home.
  • B. Because a VPN makes the intranet faster, and the speed of the connection is what stops remote staff from using the site — A tunnel adds work at both ends rather than removing it, so speed is not the argument. The problem being solved is that the path between the employee and the office is public, not that it is slow.
  • C. Because an intranet cannot technically be reached from outside the building, so a VPN is what makes the pages exist for a remote worker at all — The site is perfectly reachable in a technical sense, which is exactly the danger. The VPN is chosen so that reachable does not mean reachable by everyone, not because remote access is otherwise impossible.
  • D. Because publishing on the open web would require rewriting the intranet in different software, which a VPN avoids having to do — No rewriting is involved either way. An intranet already uses the same software, hardware and networking technologies as a public site; what a VPN changes is who can get to it and how the traffic travels.

Extranets: letting a partner in, deliberately

An intranet does nothing for the companies a business depends on — the supplier who must know what to ship, the distributor who needs prices. Not employees, so the intranet excludes them; not the public, so the public site is useless.

An extranet is a private part of the internet cordoned off from ordinary users, letting two or more firms do business together. Only authorized users reach it, after logging on with an ordinary browser. Crossing public infrastructure, it often uses VPNs to secure the transmission.

Work through the diagram one arrangement at a time.

Interactive diagram

Three arrangements, drawn one at a time

Step through the public site, the intranet and the extranet, and watch where the boundary moves in each one.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Public website — The baseline: one server, one browser, and no question about who is asking

Who asks (Anyone with an internet connection) → The path (The public internet, unrestricted) → The check (None — the content is meant for everyone) → What is reached (A web server holding general, public content)

  • This is the arrangement the previous section described, and the chapter’s summary table puts it first: external communications, general public content, anyone with an internet connection, public and not restricted.
  • There is no authentication step because there is nothing to protect. Everything published here has already been decided to be public, which is what makes the arrangement simple.
  • It is the right design for products, opening hours, job openings and anything else the organization wants a stranger, and a search engine, to find.
  • The other two arrangements are this one plus a decision about who is authorized. Nothing else about the technology changes, which is the point the whole section rests on.

Intranet, reached over a VPN — One organization’s own network, used from a desk inside it and from a laptop anywhere else

Who asks (A corporate client outside the local network) → The path (The public internet, crossed inside a VPN tunnel) → The check (A firewall at the edge of the corporate network) → What is reached (The server holding the internal site and its data)

  • Inside the building the picture is simpler still: a client on the local network reaches the same server directly, with no tunnel and no crossing of the internet at all.
  • That simplest form is worth remembering on its own. Communications take place only within the confines of organizational boundaries and do not travel across the internet, so nothing is exposed to be intercepted.
  • The VPN exists only because people move. It carries the outside client’s traffic across public infrastructure to the firewall, so that working from home reaches the same server as working from a desk.
  • The firewall is where the organization’s boundary is drawn. Everything inside it is corporate and proprietary content for authorized employees; everything outside it has to be let through deliberately.

Extranet, between two firms — Two separate corporate networks, joined across the public internet for as long as the business relationship lasts

Who asks (A client on the supplier’s own network) → First boundary (The supplier’s own firewall) → The path (The public internet, crossed inside a VPN tunnel) → What is reached (The partner’s firewall, and behind it the server and data)

  • Two firewalls appear here rather than one, because there are now two organizations and each defends its own boundary. Neither company is inside the other.
  • The partner logs on to the company’s extranet website using an ordinary web browser. Nothing unusual is installed on the partner’s machine, which is a large part of why extranets are practical between firms that share no technology.
  • Because the arrangement uses the public and normally insecure internet infrastructure to connect two or more business partners, it often uses a VPN to secure the transmission of proprietary information between them.
  • The content is genuinely on the web, and it is still private. Only authorized users reach it after logging on, which is how the chapter’s table can call an extranet external communication and private, restricted access at the same time.

What an extranet is actually worth

The chapter gives seven reasons a company builds one. Four carry most of the weight.

  • Timeliness and accuracy — communications improve sharply, cutting misunderstandings inside the firm and with partners.
  • Current information, centrally managed — little business information is static, and one managed copy cuts out-of-date versions stored elsewhere.
  • Automated transactions — moving orders, confirmations and invoices through a system rather than people cuts cost and cycle time.
  • Real-time data for management — transactions arrive as they happen, so activity is tracked without awaiting a monthly summary.

A fifth is a single point of data entry. Most errors between two companies come from one fact typed twice: two chances to be wrong, and no way to tell which is right.

The chapter’s summary table never mentions technology. The three differ by focus, content, users and access: unrestricted for anyone connected, restricted to authorized employees, restricted to authorized partners.

The question is always answered by naming the reader, never by comparing products.

Sort

Internet, intranet, or extranet?

Place each item using the chapter’s four dimensions: focus, type of content, users, and access. Situations that are not the chapter’s own are hypothetical practice situations, and each states the conditions you need.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Internet — external communications, general and public content, anyone with an internet connection, public and not restricted

  • External communications carrying general, public content, open to anyone with an internet connection — This is the chapter’s own summary row. All four dimensions point outward, and no authorization step exists because nothing here was meant to be withheld.
  • A page describing the company’s products and where its offices are, which the company wants search engines to find — Wanting to be found is the giveaway. This is general, public content aimed at anyone with a connection, and adding a login to it would defeat its only purpose.
  • A careers page inviting applications from people who do not work for the organization yet — The intended reader is by definition not an employee, so restricting it to authorized employees would make it useless. It is public content with an external focus.
  • In a hypothetical practice situation, a public help article the company deliberately publishes so that customers can solve a common problem without telephoning — The whole value depends on customers finding it unaided, which means anyone with an internet connection has to be able to read it. That is public, unrestricted access.

Intranet — internal communications, specific corporate and proprietary content, authorized employees, private and restricted

  • Internal communications carrying specific, corporate and proprietary content for authorized employees — The chapter’s intranet row. The content is proprietary and the users are on the payroll, so access is private and restricted even though the technology is ordinary web technology.
  • The required safety training every member of staff must complete, published where the public cannot reach it — Employee training is one of the five intranet uses the chapter lists, and the audience is authorized employees, which is what makes the access private and restricted.
  • A form on which employees change their own benefit elections and retirement-plan choices — This is employee self-service through an employee portal, the intranet use the chapter singles out, and only people on the payroll may have an election to change.
  • In a hypothetical practice situation, a hospital’s directory of which clinicians are on call tonight, visible only after signing in with a work account — Internal communication, proprietary content, authorized employees only. The sign-in is the authentication technique the chapter names as one of the two ways an intranet is secured.

Extranet — external communications between business partners, authorized business partners, private and restricted

  • External communications between business partners, restricted to authorized business partners — The chapter’s extranet row, and the one that catches people out: the focus is external, like the public internet, but the access is private and restricted, like an intranet.
  • In a hypothetical practice situation, a live order-status screen a component supplier logs in to see, so it knows what to ship next week — The supplier is neither an employee nor the general public. This is two firms using the internet to do business together, with the partner logging on through an ordinary browser.
  • In a hypothetical practice situation, a shared price list that two firms maintain together so that neither has to email a spreadsheet to the other — A single shared copy between two companies is the extranet benefit of central document management and a single point of data entry, avoiding the versions problem entirely.
  • In a hypothetical practice situation, a manufacturer gives an outside haulage firm a login so that the haulier can update delivery dates directly in the manufacturer’s system — The haulier is an authorized business partner rather than an employee, and letting it enter the data once, at source, is exactly the single point of data entry the chapter describes.

Where the machines actually live

Large organizations need thousands of servers — a parcel carrier routing packages, a store tracking orders, a game developer logging every player action, a company training artificial-intelligence models — so they set aside dedicated space.

That space is a data center, covering everything from one server room behind an office to a warehouse-sized building. Processing that much data takes great power, plus air-conditioning to hold equipment at its optimal temperature, so one upgrade buys two bills.

Concentrating everything in one place helps with managing, repairing, upgrading and securing it. Choosing the place is a trade-off: firms balance protection from earthquakes and hurricanes against proximity to users, which reduces latency. The safest ground is rarely the nearest.

Availability, and what five-nines means in minutes

Almost any business today is an e-business, so reaching data reliably is a key concern. Data-intensive organizations aim for five-nines availability: 99.999 percent, or five minutes of downtime a year — not per outage, but the whole budget for twelve months.

That reaches into the building: components swappable while the service runs, and a facility with connectivity, floor space, energy, cooling and security. Data centers are modular so they can expand.

One facility, described

The chapter describes a parcel carrier’s facilities in Atlanta and Mahwah as a shopping list.

  • Its own electricity — each site is self-sufficient and runs two days on power it generates itself if outside supply fails.
  • Cooling on the scale of a neighbourhood — each needs air-conditioning capacity equalling 2,000 homes.
  • Water, and backup water — cooling falls back on 600,000 gallons of chilled water, with backup wells if the mains fail.
  • A building designed against weather — walls rated for 200-mile-per-hour winds, and raised floors against flooding.

All of it is bought before a single request is served, and all of it prevents something rather than producing anything. Most organizations instead rent space for their servers in a collocation facility, a data center run by a third party for several customers. The tenant owns its machines but stops buying the building, power and cooling.

Work the siting and running decisions in order.

Decide

Siting and running a facility

Work the four decisions in order, and compare every outcome before moving on, including the outcomes of the options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

A hypothetical practice situation; no real organization is being described. You advise a growing logistics cooperative that has outgrown the server room behind its dispatch office. It now needs somewhere proper to put its machines, and four decisions have to be made before anything is built or rented.

Decision 1. Two candidate sites cost the same. One sits inland on stable ground, far from any concentration of the cooperative’s customers. The other sits close to the largest group of customers but on an exposed coast. The board wants a rule for choosing.

  • Treat it as a genuine trade-off between protection from the elements and proximity to users for lower latency, and decide it alongside power, cooling, connectivity, security and room to expand — the stronger call. Right. The chapter says organizations go to great lengths selecting locations that strike the optimal balance between protection from the elements, such as earthquakes or hurricanes, and proximity to the customers or users in order to reduce latency. Neither consideration outranks the other in advance, which is why the facility requirements have to be weighed in the same conversation.
  • Choose the inland site automatically, because once a connection is fast enough distance no longer affects anything the user notices — Distance still costs time. That is precisely why the chapter names proximity to customers and users as a siting consideration in its own right, and it is the same physical fact that later justifies putting copies of content nearer to the people requesting it.
  • Choose the coastal site automatically, because reducing delay for users is the only difference a customer will ever perceive — Latency is real, but a flooded facility is not slow, it is unavailable, and the chapter treats availability as the key concern for a data-intensive organization. A site that is fast on most days and absent on the worst day has not solved the problem.
  • Decide it on land price alone, since the two sites are equally priced today and the cost of the building will dominate everything else — The two sites are already equally priced, so this rule does not even separate them. It also ignores the running costs the chapter emphasises — power, cooling and the consequences of downtime — which continue for as long as the facility does.

Decision 2. The design brief doubles the number of servers. The facilities manager proposes keeping the existing air-conditioning, arguing that the machines have their own fans and that cooling is a comfort item rather than an operating requirement.

  • Reject it: processing that volume of data requires lots of power and also requires air-conditioning to hold the equipment within its optimal temperature range, which helps increase the life span of the equipment — the stronger call. Right. The chapter ties the two together explicitly. Heat is not a side effect to be tolerated; running outside the optimal range shortens the life of the hardware, so an upgrade that doubles the machines has quietly doubled a cooling requirement as well.
  • Accept it, because cooling capacity only has to be increased once the equipment actually begins to fail in service — By the time components fail, the damage is already paid for. The chapter presents cooling as what keeps equipment inside its optimal range and therefore extends its life, which makes it a preventive cost rather than a repair triggered by a failure.
  • Accept it, but move the servers further apart inside the room so the existing air-conditioning has less work to do — Spreading equipment out uses more floor space, which the chapter lists among the facility’s own requirements, and it does not remove any heat from the room. The total energy going in still has to come out as heat somewhere.
  • Defer it, on the grounds that electricity is a running cost and running costs are decided after the facility is built — Provision of energy and cooling is one of the demands the chapter places on the data center overall, alongside connectivity, floor space and security. Treating it as an afterthought is how a facility ends up unable to power the equipment it was built to hold.

Decision 3. The cooperative’s dispatch system now runs continuously, and the board asks what a five-nines availability target would actually commit it to.

  • Just over five minutes of unavailability in an entire year, covering every failure, upgrade and mistake, which constrains both the components and the building around them — the stronger call. Right. Five-nines means 99.999 percent availability, which the chapter translates into just over five minutes of downtime per year. That budget forces the specific demands it lists: parts such as hard drives that can be swapped quickly, and a facility with the connectivity, floor space, energy, cooling and security to keep running while that happens.
  • Five minutes of unavailability per incident, after which the service is expected to be restored — This is the most common misreading and it makes the target sound comfortable. The chapter’s figure is annual, so the whole year’s worth of interruptions has to fit inside the same five minutes.
  • A promise that no individual component will fail during the year, which is what the additional nines are counting — Availability is not the absence of failure. The chapter’s own requirement is being able to swap a failed hard drive or other part quickly, which assumes components will fail and asks that the service survive it.
  • A target about the speed of the service rather than its availability, since users judge a system by how quickly it responds — Response time matters and the chapter discusses it under latency, but availability answers a different question: whether the system can be reached at all. A fast system nobody can open is unavailable.

Decision 4. Finally, the board compares building a facility of its own against renting space for its servers in a data center run by a third party that also rents to other organizations.

  • Recognize the second option as a collocation facility: the cooperative still owns and manages its own servers, but stops paying for the building, the power, the cooling and the physical security — the stronger call. Right. The chapter defines a collocation facility as a data center managed by a third party that rents out space to multiple organizational customers. It is a change in what you own around the machines, not in who owns the machines, and that distinction is what makes it a different decision from renting computing itself.
  • Treat the two as identical in substance, since the servers are the same machines running the same software in both cases — The machines are indeed the same, which is what makes this tempting. Everything around them differs, though, and the chapter’s facility example is a list of exactly those surroundings: generated power, chilled water, engineered walls and raised floors.
  • Reject renting on the grounds that high availability can only be reached in a facility the organization has built and controls itself — The chapter presents collocation as a straightforward alternative rather than a compromise, and a shared facility built for many tenants may well exceed what a single small organization could justify building alone.
  • Choose renting on the grounds that it removes the cooperative’s responsibility for its servers and for the data on them — Renting space is not renting responsibility. In a collocation facility the tenant still owns, manages, patches and repairs its own servers; what the third party manages is the room they stand in.
Where this is heading Almost none of that spending was computing. Every item is something a cloud customer stops buying.
Check yourself

Facilities, availability, and the alternative
