  • Rapid elasticity — resources scale up or down almost instantly, often automatically, in step with what users do.
  • Broad network access — services are reached over the internet, from almost anywhere and almost any web-enabled device.
  • Resource pooling — the provider assigns distributed resources dynamically to many customers, so you rent capacity without knowing which machine supplied it.
  • Measured service — usage is monitored and you pay for what you used, turning fixed costs into variable, trackable ones.

Every one reads as an advantage, and every one has a failure mode. Read all four panels of each card, especially the last.

Explore

The five characteristics, benefit and failure mode together

Open each card and read all four panels; the fourth panel is what the same characteristic looks like when nobody is managing it, which is the half most descriptions leave out.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

On-demand self-service · Getting resources without asking a person

  • The chapter’s definition: Users can access cloud resources in a buffet-style fashion on an as-needed basis without lengthy negotiations with the service provider, and in many cases with no human interaction with the provider at all.
  • What it looks like in practice: The chapter’s example is a customer who needs only a payment card for billing and can then set up server instances or expand storage through a web-based control panel, which is what makes an experiment possible this afternoon.
  • Why owning could not do this: Obtaining equipment used to begin with a supplier, a quotation and a contract, so the earliest an idea could be tested was measured in weeks. The negotiation, not the technology, was usually the slow part.
  • What it looks like when nobody is watching: The same door is open to everybody who holds an account. Resources can be created that nobody approved, forgotten by the person who created them, and billed every month afterwards to a company that no longer knows what they are for.

Rapid elasticity · Capacity that follows the work

  • The chapter’s definition: In a cloud environment, computing resources can be scaled up or down almost instantaneously and often automatically, based on what users need at that moment.
  • What it looks like in practice: The chapter’s case is the pre-holiday surge: there is no need to purchase expensive equipment in advance for a spike that may never materialize, and if it does materialize the resources can be obtained instantly in almost any quantity.
  • Why owning could not do this: Servers typically take several weeks to be delivered and days or weeks to be configured, because system software, databases and application software all have to be installed and set up before anything runs on them.
  • What it looks like when nobody is watching: Capacity that grows automatically will also grow automatically for work that should not be happening. The mechanism does not ask whether the demand is legitimate, only whether there is more of it than there was a minute ago.

Broad network access · Reachable from wherever the work is

  • The chapter’s definition: Because cloud services are accessed over the internet, they are accessible from almost anywhere and from almost any web-enabled device.
  • What it looks like in practice: The chapter describes real-time management of business processes: an application can be reached whenever it is needed and from any location, so a knowledge worker can respond to something urgent without first travelling back to an office.
  • Why owning could not do this: An application on a machine inside one building is reachable inside that building. Everything else — the private tunnel, the remote desktop, the laptop carried home — was an arrangement bolted on to work around that limit.
  • What it looks like when nobody is watching: A service reachable from anywhere is reachable by anyone holding a credential for it. The question of who may come in moves from the door of a building, which the organization controls, to an account, which it can only manage.

Resource pooling · Somebody else’s machines, assigned as needed

  • The chapter’s definition: Rather than renting space or time on one specific physical machine, providers manage multiple distributed resources that are dynamically assigned to many customers according to their needs, so the customer rents a resource with no knowledge or control of how it is provided or where it is located.
  • What it looks like in practice: The chapter notes that providers often do allow a geographic area to be specified: a company may want its resources near its customers to reduce response latency, or its storage held in a particular region to satisfy data protection duties.
  • Why owning could not do this: An organization sizing its own equipment has to size it for its own busiest hour, and every other organization does the same, which leaves a great deal of machinery standing mostly idle across all of them at once.
  • What it looks like when nobody is watching: You cannot say exactly where the data physically sits, which is uncomfortable when a duty about where records may be held applies to your industry or your region. The default is convenient; the exception has to be asked for.

Measured service · Paying for what actually ran

  • The chapter’s definition: Providers monitor usage and customers pay only for what they use, with different resources metered differently — server instances charged by the hour according to their computing power, memory and operating system, or storage charged by the volume held and moved.
  • What it looks like in practice: For the customer, the fixed costs associated with an infrastructure become variable costs that are easy to track and monitor, which is the same transformation the chapter describes as moving from a capital to an operational expenditure.
  • Why owning could not do this: An owned machine costs the same on its busiest day and its quietest one. There is no meter to read, so there is also no way to discover from the bill that half the capacity has not been touched since it was installed.
  • What it looks like when nobody is watching: The meter runs whether or not anybody is reading it. An invoice is the first place an unnoticed mistake becomes visible, and by the time it is visible the resources have already been consumed and charged for.

Read the list again and it stops being a brochure: each characteristic answers a pressure from the sections before this.

Match

Each characteristic and the problem it answers

Pair each of the five characteristics with the infrastructure problem from the previous objective that it is answering; the explanation names where that problem was raised.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

On-demand self-service
Equipment that took weeks to arrive, with locating facilities and negotiating contracts happening before that, so an idea sat a quarter away from being tested The chapter lists significant time for locating the right facilities, contract negotiations and setting up hardware and software among the reasons growth hurts. Self-service removes the negotiation entirely, which is why an experiment can start the same day.
Rapid elasticity
Demand that spikes before the holidays and falls away afterwards, against capacity that can only be purchased in fixed chunks This is the demand-fluctuation problem in its clearest form: firms supporting consumer electronic commerce face large spikes in the pre-holiday season, and equipment bought for the spike is idle for the rest of the year.
Broad network access
Work that no longer happens at one desk, because people travel, work away from the office, and bring their own devices into the organization Mobility and the consumerization of information technology were raised as drivers of infrastructure change. A service reachable from any web-enabled device answers them without the organization owning the device in question.
Resource pooling
Machines standing mostly idle, because every organization sized its own equipment for its own busiest hour and then waited for that hour The chapter reports an estimate that as many as seven infrastructures in ten run at only about a fifth of their capacity. Pooling is what allows one provider’s machines to be busy for somebody at almost any moment, which is where the saving comes from.
Measured service
A large sum committed up front for capacity, plus the power and the cooling to run it, incurred whether or not the work ever arrived Rising energy costs and the capital cost of equipment were both named as pressures on the infrastructure. Metering is what converts those fixed costs into variable ones that follow the work, and it is what makes the spending visible at all.

What renting does not do

Two things survive the move. Choosing, integrating and managing services stays with the customer, so the technology function changes shape rather than disappearing; and the meter keeps running whether or not anybody reads it.

Owning means paying in advance for a guess about capacity. Renting means paying afterwards for what happened — better arithmetic and a worse habit, because a cost nobody approved in advance is a cost nobody is watching.

Check yourself

Characteristics, chunks, and the two gaps

Three questions on the mechanics of renting capacity; every organization described is a hypothetical practice situation, and each option explains itself whether or not you chose it.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical seed supplier needs about four times its usual computing capacity for six weeks each spring and its ordinary capacity for the rest of the year. Which characteristic addresses that most directly, and why?

  • A. On-demand self-service, because the extra capacity can be obtained through a control panel without negotiating with anybody at the provider — Self-service describes how the resources are obtained rather than how they grow and shrink. It genuinely helps here, but the question is about capacity following a seasonal curve, which is a different characteristic.
  • B. Resource pooling, because the provider holds distributed resources that many customers draw on as their needs change — Pooling is the precondition that makes spare capacity available to be assigned, and it is present. It does not describe the speed of the change or the fact that the capacity is given back in June.
  • C. Rapid elasticity, because resources scale up and down almost instantaneously and often automatically, where purchased equipment takes weeks to arrive and days to configure — correct. The chapter contrasts equipment that takes several weeks to deliver and days or weeks to configure with a cloud environment where resources scale up or down almost instantaneously and often automatically, and it uses a seasonal surge to make the point.
  • D. Broad network access, because the supplier’s staff can reach the extra capacity from anywhere and from any web-enabled device, which is what makes the spring arrangement workable at all — Broad network access explains who can reach a service and from where. The supplier’s problem is the size of the capacity in March compared with October, not the location of the people using it.

2. The chapter presents measured service as a benefit. What is the same characteristic’s cost?

  • A. The meter runs whether or not anybody is reading it, so a cost that nobody is monitoring can grow until the invoice makes it visible — correct. Measured service transforms fixed costs into variable ones that are easy to track and monitor, but tracking has to be done by somebody; the chapter’s own cautionary case is what happens when nobody does it.
  • B. Metering obliges the customer to commit to a minimum level of usage for the length of the contract — This is the opposite of what the chapter describes. A cloud customer can typically obtain resources without committing to minimum usage, which is exactly what it credits for the travel platform’s expansion.
  • C. Metering means the provider decides which physical machine the work runs on and where that machine is located — That is resource pooling, not measured service. It is a genuine consequence of renting, but it concerns where the work runs rather than how the customer is charged for it.
  • D. Metering prevents capacity from being reduced again once it has been increased, because the meter is set at the higher level — Releasing resources and having the charge fall is the point of the model. Metering records what was used in each period, so a reduction in usage appears in the next bill rather than being locked out.

3. The chapter draws a stepped in-house capacity line beside a cloud capacity line that follows demand. What are the two gaps in the in-house picture, and why does each one cost money?

  • A. Capacity above demand and capacity above budget, which are both forms of overspending, one on equipment and one on the staff to run it — Only one of these is a gap in the figure. Staffing is a real cost of ownership, and the chapter names it, but the two shaded areas in the diagram are both about the distance between capacity and demand.
  • B. Capacity above demand and demand above capacity: one is equipment being paid for while idle, the other is business the system cannot serve — correct. With a traditional in-house infrastructure an organization ends up either holding unused resources or being unable to satisfy its users, and the two shaded areas in the chapter’s figure are those two situations.
  • C. Demand above capacity and demand above forecast, which are both planning failures rather than problems with the infrastructure itself — A better forecast narrows the gaps but cannot close them, because capacity that arrives in whole machines cannot trace a demand curve however good the forecast is. The problem is the shape of the supply, not the quality of the guess.
  • D. Capacity above demand and demand above capacity, though only the first has a cost, because unserved demand usually returns later — The second gap has the larger and less visible cost. Nothing on an invoice records an order that was never placed by a customer who gave up waiting, and the chapter treats unsatisfied demand as a real loss rather than a delay.

Section 3–4b

Service models and kinds of cloud

“We moved to the cloud” describes two decisions. The first is how much of the machinery you hand over. The second is whose building it sits in, and who else is renting beside you.

Renting covers three very different deals

You could rent a bare plot and build on it, rent an empty flat where the wiring is somebody else’s problem, or take a hotel room.

All three are renting. What separates them is how much work is already done and how much you may still change. Cloud computing divides on that line, into three service models.

  • Infrastructure as a service — you manage the operating system and everything above it, licences included; the provider stops at hardware.
  • Platform as a service — you manage your application and nothing beneath; the operating system, web server and database engine arrive running.
  • Software as a service — you manage settings and data, because even the application is maintained by somebody else.

Infrastructure as a service

In infrastructure as a service, or IaaS, only processing, storage and networking are provided. You choose the operating system, configure it, and track your own licences. It gives the most control and leaves the most work, so setup costs are high.

The chapter’s example is Amazon Web Services, where a customer picks computing power, memory, operating system and storage. Netflix moved there to convert films into the formats different devices need.

Platform as a service

In platform as a service, or PaaS, customers run their own applications, built with the provider’s tools, with limited control beneath. The operating system, web server, database management system and tools arrive installed and updated, so no licences are bought for them. The example is Microsoft Azure.

Serverless computing goes further. On a platform such as AWS Lambda the customer supplies small functions that assemble into an application; the service manages and scales the platform, charging for the time those functions run. The servers have not gone anywhere — the customer never meets one.

Software as a service

In software as a service, or SaaS, the customer uses only applications delivered over a cloud infrastructure: no machine to choose, no operating system to patch, limited settings to configure.

You used it today: email such as Gmail, storage such as Dropbox, collaboration such as Slack and Zoom, suites such as Google Docs, business applications such as Salesforce. It deploys most easily, and the price is configurability.

Sort real arrangements into the three models.

Sort

Which service model is this?

Place each arrangement under the service model it describes, then read why it belongs there. Some are the chapter’s own examples; the ones marked as practice situations are hypothetical and no real organization is being described.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Infrastructure as a service — Processing, storage and networking are provided; the customer chooses the operating system and manages everything above it, licences included

  • A streaming company rents raw computing capacity, chooses the operating systems that run on it, and uses it to convert films into the many formats different devices need. — This is the chapter’s Netflix example. Only processing, storage and networking were bought; every layer above them, starting with the operating system, is still the company’s own responsibility.
  • A customer selects computing power, memory, operating system and storage from a provider’s control panel and builds most of its infrastructure there rather than in a room of its own. — Choosing the operating system is the giveaway. That choice exists in exactly one model, because in the other two the provider has already made it and will not let the customer change it.
  • A practice situation: a hypothetical architecture firm needs one licensed design package that runs on a specific older operating system, and needs control of the machine image it sits on. — A requirement about the operating system itself can be met only where the customer still chooses it, and the licence for the design package stays the firm’s to manage in this model.

Platform as a service — The operating system, web server, database engine and tools arrive running; the customer controls its own application and little else

  • A team deploys software its own developers wrote onto a rented platform built with the provider’s tools, and nobody on the team has ever installed or patched a database engine. — The customer controls the application and has limited or no control over the infrastructure underneath, and the provider manages the functioning and the updating of the platform. That is the definition.
  • Small, specific functions are run by the provider on demand, assembled into an application, and billed for the time they actually run, with no machine ever set up by the customer. — This is serverless computing, which the chapter presents as a current trend within the platform model: the platform is still provided, and the customer has simply stopped seeing even the machine.
  • A practice situation: a hypothetical charity has two developers who wrote a booking application, and wants the provider to keep the web server and database engine current while the booking rules stay the charity’s own. — The booking rules are the application, which the charity keeps; the web server and database management system are the platform, which the provider runs. The line falls exactly where the platform model draws it.

Software as a service — The customer uses only the finished application, with no control over the infrastructure and limited ability to configure it

  • Staff open a web-based email service through a browser, and nobody in the building has ever installed, patched or updated a mail server. — The chapter names web-based email as its first example of the model. The customer uses only the application and has no knowledge of or control over the infrastructure beneath it.
  • A firm keeps shared documents in a hosted storage service and sends large files through a hosted transfer service, having bought no equipment for either. — Document storage services are among the chapter’s own examples of the model, and nothing about the arrangement gives the firm a machine, an operating system or a platform to look after.
  • A practice situation: a hypothetical sales team logs in to a hosted customer-records application, can rename fields and add users, but cannot change how the application works. — Limited ability to control or configure application-specific settings is precisely what the chapter says distinguishes this model. The team manages its settings and its data, and nothing else.

The line that decides everything

Learners go wrong memorizing which brand belongs to which model; brands move, and providers sell all three. The durable test is what do my people still look after on Monday morning? Three things catch people out.

  • No rung takes away your data or decisions — which records exist, who may see them and what they mean is still your problem.
  • Higher is not better — less work and less control, and which matters depends on whether the thing is distinctive work or plumbing.
  • An organization sits on several rungs — finished applications for office work, a platform for developers, raw machines for one awkward package.

Handing over a layer hands over the labour of running it and the freedom to change it in one movement. You cannot take one half without the other.

Match

The responsibility ladder

Pair each arrangement with the honest description of what your own organization is still responsible for under it.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Owning the infrastructure outright
You look after every layer, from the electricity and the cooling up to the application your staff log in to With no provider anywhere in the picture, the facility, the hardware, the operating system, the platform, the application and the data are all in-house work, which is the arrangement objective 3.3 spent two sections describing the cost of.
Infrastructure as a service
You manage the operating system and everything above it, licences included, while the provider stops at the hardware Only the basic capabilities of processing, storage and networking are provided, so the customer has the most control over the resources — and managing software licences remains the customer’s responsibility.
Platform as a service
You manage your own application and nothing beneath it, because the operating system, web server and database engine are the provider’s to run and update The customer runs its own applications, typically designed with the provider’s tools, and has limited or no control over the underlying infrastructure; platform licences and platform updates both move to the provider.
Software as a service
You manage your settings and your data, and nothing else, because the application itself is maintained and updated for you The customer uses only the application, has no knowledge of or control over the infrastructure, and typically has only a limited ability to configure application-specific settings. It is the easiest model to deploy for exactly that reason.
Serverless computing
You supply individual functions and never set up a machine at all, and you are charged for the time those functions actually run The chapter presents this as a new trend designed to free users from having to set up virtual machines: the service takes care of all management of the underlying platform and enables continuous scaling, billed by usage time.

Are the three separate in your mind?

Check yourself

Telling the three service models apart

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical logistics firm rents computing capacity, installs an operating system of its own choosing on it, and runs its warehouse software on top. It is surprised to find it must still account for the operating system licences. Which model is this, and is the surprise justified?

  • A. Platform as a service, and the surprise is justified, because the provider supplies the platform and should therefore supply the licences that come with it — The platform model does remove platform licences, which is what makes this tempting, but the firm chose and installed its own operating system. That choice does not exist in the platform model, where the operating system arrives already running.
  • B. Infrastructure as a service, and the surprise is not justified, because only processing, storage and networking are provided and managing software licences remains the customer’s responsibility — correct. In infrastructure as a service only the basic capabilities of processing, storage and networking are provided, the customer therefore has the most control over the resources, and managing software licences is still the responsibility of the customer.
  • C. Software as a service, and the surprise is justified, because a rented application should arrive with everything it needs to run already paid for — Nothing here resembles software as a service. The firm is running its own warehouse software on an operating system it selected, which means it is managing layers that this model would have removed entirely.
  • D. Infrastructure as a service, and the surprise is justified, because renting hardware from a provider transfers the cost of anything installed on that hardware to the provider — The model is identified correctly, and this is the closest wrong answer for that reason. The reasoning fails: renting a machine buys you the machine, not permission to run licensed software on it, and the chapter says so explicitly.

2. A hypothetical insurer wants its own developers’ software running in production without anyone on staff installing or patching an operating system or a database engine, and without buying licences for either. Which model does the chapter describe for this?

  • A. Infrastructure as a service, because the insurer is running software it wrote itself and therefore needs the greatest possible control over the resources — This model gives the most control, but control is not what the insurer asked for. It asked to stop looking after operating systems and database engines, and that is exactly the work this model leaves with the customer.
  • B. Software as a service, because the insurer wants an application to run without maintaining anything, which is what this model exists to provide — The insurer does want to maintain nothing, which makes this look right, but the application is its own. Software as a service supplies the provider’s application, so there would be nowhere for the insurer’s code to run.
  • C. Platform as a service, because the provider supplies the operating system, web server, database management system and tools while the insurer controls only its own applications — correct. Customers run their own applications on tools the provider supplies, they have control over the applications but limited or no control over the underlying infrastructure, and they avoid buying licences for the web servers’ operating systems or the database management systems.
  • D. A private cloud, because software written in-house has to run on infrastructure the organization owns and controls itself — A private cloud is an answer to a different question, about whose machines these are rather than how much of the stack is provided. Software written in-house can run perfectly well on rented capacity, and often does.

3. Why does the chapter describe software as a service as typically the easiest model to deploy, and what does that ease cost the customer?

  • A. It is easiest because the customer maintains and updates nothing at all, and the cost is configurability, since what can be adjusted in the application is typically limited — correct. The customer does not have to worry about maintaining or updating the software, the underlying platform or the hardware infrastructure, and typically has only limited ability to control or configure application-specific settings.
  • B. It is easiest because it is the cheapest of the three models, and the cost is reliability, since a shared application is more likely to fail than one the customer runs itself — Cost is a separate question the chapter treats under evaluating providers, and it does not rank the models by price. Nor does it claim that a shared application fails more often; availability is a criterion to examine, not a property of the model.
  • C. It is easiest because the customer keeps control of the operating system, and the cost is the licences, which the customer must continue to purchase — This describes infrastructure as a service, where the customer does keep the operating system and its licences. In software as a service there is no operating system in the customer’s hands to keep.
  • D. It is easiest because it removes the need to keep any data at all, and the cost is that reports have to be requested from the provider each time — The data is emphatically still the customer’s, and the model changes nothing about which records exist or what they mean. Only settings and data remain the customer’s to manage, which is a small list but not an empty one.

Public, private, and the mixture most organizations reach

The second decision is whose cloud it is. One word underneath needs defining: scalability is the ability to adapt to increases or decreases in demand for processing or data storage — a promise to test, not to assume from the word “cloud”.

  • Public cloud — services any party can use pay-per-use, suiting work that must scale fast and firms without capital or staff.
  • Private cloud — internal to one organization, still self-service from a shared pool and billed to departments, but under its own control.
  • Hybrid cloud — some applications in-house and others public, where firms arrive once they stop seeking a single answer.

The private cloud is most often misunderstood. It balances supply and demand across departments and gives control, but does not free the organization from managing a cloud infrastructure: somebody still owns the building, power and machines, and it is you.

Private buys control and pays in money and effort; public buys speed and pays in standardization. Four signals say which an application belongs in.

  • Demand that swings hard without warning — points public, because capacity that grows and shrinks in minutes is what pooled rented equipment does.
  • A rule about where data may sit — points private, because policy or an industry duty may require records on your own machines.
  • No capital and no technical staff — points public, since a private cloud is equipment bought up front and then run.
  • Equipment already bought and idle — points private, because pooling what you own recovers value paid for.
Check yourself

Public, private, and what each one really buys

Four options, one best answer; every explanation is worth reading, because the wrong answers here are the ones people act on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical local charity has no capital to spend on equipment and no technical staff, but needs a service that can grow quickly if a campaign succeeds. Which kind of cloud does the chapter point to, and why?

  • A. A private cloud, because a charity handling donor details needs the control and privacy that only its own machines can provide — A private cloud does give a high degree of control and privacy, but it does not free an organization from managing an infrastructure — and this charity has neither the capital to build one nor the staff to run it.
  • B. Neither kind, because a charity of that size should buy a single server outright and avoid a recurring bill altogether — Buying a server outright is the arrangement with the largest capital cost and the least ability to grow, which is the opposite of what a campaign that may or may not succeed calls for.
  • C. A hybrid arrangement, because splitting the work between owned and rented capacity is the safest starting position for an organization with no experience — Hybrid is what many organizations settle on, which is why this sounds sensible, but it means running both arrangements at once. An organization with no technical staff has taken on the harder half rather than avoided it.
  • D. A public cloud, because its services can be used by any interested party on a pay-per-use basis and it suits applications that need rapid scalability — correct. Services in a public cloud can be used by any interested party on a pay-per-use basis, and the chapter recommends it for applications needing rapid scalability and for organizations with insufficient capital or other resources to build or expand an infrastructure.

2. A hypothetical manufacturer builds a private cloud so its departments can provision servers from a shared internal pool in minutes. Its finance director expects the infrastructure management work to disappear. What does the chapter say?

  • A. The expectation is wrong: a private cloud still leaves the organization managing the infrastructure, though it does give real customizability and control — correct. The chapter is explicit that a private cloud provides self-service access on a utility computing model but does not free the organization from the issues of managing the infrastructure; what it buys is customizability, flexibility and control over its data and applications.
  • B. The expectation is right, because self-service provisioning and a utility billing model are what define a cloud, and both remove the underlying management work — Self-service access and metered billing are genuinely present in a private cloud, which is what makes the reasoning attractive. They change who requests capacity and how it is charged internally, not who has to keep the equipment running.
  • C. The expectation is right for the machines but wrong for the network, since networking is the one layer a private cloud cannot pool across departments — Networking is not a special case here, and a private cloud can pool network resources like any other. The management work that remains covers every layer the organization still owns, not one of them.
  • D. The expectation is wrong, because a private cloud is simply a public cloud with a contract that restricts who else may use the same equipment — This confuses the two kinds. A private cloud is internal to the organization and owned by the client; the public cloud is owned by the service provider and open to any interested party on a pay-per-use basis.

3. What does the chapter mean by scalability, and what follows from that definition when choosing a provider?

  • A. The number of machines a provider owns, which follows directly from how large the provider is, so the largest provider is the appropriate choice — Provider size is not the definition, and it is a poor proxy for the thing that matters. What an organization needs to know is whether capacity moves with its own demand, which is a question about the service it is buying.
  • B. The speed at which data can be moved from one provider to another, so the organization should choose whichever provider transfers data fastest — That is closer to openness, which the chapter treats separately as a question about moving between providers and the cost of transferring large volumes out. It is a real criterion, but it is not this one.
  • C. The ability to adapt to increases or decreases in demand for processing or data storage, so it is a promise to test against your own demand rather than to assume — correct. The chapter defines scalability as the ability to adapt to increases or decreases in demand for processing or data storage, and because it is claimed rather than guaranteed it belongs on the list of things a customer examines about a provider.
  • D. The ability of an application to serve users in more than one country, so it matters to international organizations and not to local ones — Serving several countries is a matter of where resources are located and which rules apply to them, which the chapter treats under resource pooling and under compliance. Scalability is about volume of demand, not geography.

Two choices, taken together

A service model says how far up the stack somebody else is responsible; a kind of cloud says whose machines those are. They are independent, so a firm can rent applications publicly and still run a platform in its own building.

No single provider meets every need, so firms partner with several. Ask three questions of one application at a time: what must we still change, is this distinctive work or plumbing, and where may this data sit?

Decide

Choosing a model and a kind, one application at a time

Work the four decisions in order, and after each one read every outcome before moving on, including the ones you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Four hypothetical practice situations, invented for this exercise; no real organization is described in any of them. In each case ask the three questions from the section: what must we still be able to change, is this work distinctive or is it plumbing, and where is this data allowed to sit.

Decision 1. A hypothetical veterinary group with six clinics needs email, shared documents and video meetings for its staff. It employs nobody technical, and none of this work is what makes the group different from any other veterinary practice. What should it rent?

  • Software as a service: rent the finished applications and manage only accounts, settings and the records inside them. — the stronger call. Right. This is plumbing rather than distinctive work, so the group should hand over as much of it as possible. Web-based email, document storage and collaboration software are three of the chapter’s own examples of the model, and it is the easiest to deploy precisely because nothing has to be maintained or updated by the customer.
  • Infrastructure as a service: rent machines and install mail, file and meeting software on them. — This would work and it would be a poor use of the group’s money. Renting at this level leaves the operating system, the licences, the installation and the patching with a customer that has nobody to do any of it, in exchange for control over software that six veterinary clinics have no reason to customize.
  • Platform as a service: rent a platform and have someone build the group a mail and document system on it. — The platform model is for running an application you have and want to keep. Commissioning one that already exists in mature form, and then owning it forever, converts a solved problem into a permanent development project.
  • A private cloud: buy equipment and pool it across the six clinics so each one can provision what it needs. — A private cloud is the largest commitment on the table. It is capital expenditure, it is owned by the client, and the chapter is explicit that it does not free an organization from the work of managing the infrastructure — work this group has no one to do.

Decision 2. A hypothetical university research team has written its own analysis software and needs it available to collaborators. Nobody on the team wants to patch an operating system or a database engine, and the team has no licence budget. The software itself is ordinary code that any current platform can run.

  • Platform as a service, so the operating system, web server and database engine are provided and the team looks after only its own application. — the stronger call. Right. The team controls its application and has limited or no control over the infrastructure underneath, which is exactly what it asked for. Because the computing platform is provided, it also avoids buying licences for the web servers’ operating systems and for the database management system, and the provider manages the platform’s updates.
  • Infrastructure as a service, so the team can guarantee its software will run by choosing the machine and the operating system itself. — The guarantee is real, but it is being bought with the exact work the team said it would not do. Choosing the operating system means installing, configuring, patching and licensing it, which is why the chapter pairs this model’s flexibility with relatively high setup costs.
  • Software as a service, because a research team should use an existing analysis application rather than maintaining one of its own. — That may be sound advice about research, and it is not an answer to the question asked. The team has written the software; software as a service supplies the provider’s application, so there is nowhere in this model for the team’s own code to live.
  • Serverless computing, because it removes machines entirely and charges only for the time functions run. — Serverless is a real option within the platform model and would suit work that arrives in short bursts. It asks the team to restructure its software into small individual functions first, which is a rewrite nobody has asked for and which the situation gives no reason to want.

Decision 3. A hypothetical film archive digitises old reels using a specialised package that runs only on an older operating system, and its work arrives in unpredictable bursts: nothing for a month, then thousands of hours at once. It has the licence for the package already.

  • Infrastructure as a service in a public cloud: rent capacity as the bursts arrive, install the older operating system and the package on it. — the stronger call. Right. A requirement about the operating system itself can be met only in the model where the customer still chooses it, and the licence stays the archive’s to manage, which it already holds. Renting publicly means the idle month costs nothing, which is the whole answer to work that arrives in bursts.
  • Platform as a service, because the archive should let the provider handle the operating system and stop worrying about it. — That is usually good advice and here it is impossible. The platform model supplies the operating system already running and does not let the customer specify an older version, so the archive’s one indispensable package would have nowhere to run.
  • Buy a machine outright and run it in the archive’s own building, since the work is specialised and the software is already licensed. — Owning removes the rental bill and reintroduces every problem objective 3.3 described. Capacity would be sized for either the quiet month or the burst: idle equipment most of the year, or a queue when the reels arrive.
  • Software as a service, choosing whichever hosted digitisation application is closest to the package the archive uses today. — This throws away a licence the archive already owns and a workflow built around it, in exchange for an application it cannot configure beyond the provider’s settings. The chapter’s point about limited configurability is exactly the risk here.

Decision 4. A hypothetical city transit authority runs two things: a journey planner whose traffic multiplies whenever the weather turns, and a fare-card records system holding personal details that internal rules say must stay on machines the authority controls. A board member insists on one arrangement for both.

  • A hybrid arrangement: the journey planner on rented public capacity, the fare-card records on the authority’s own controlled infrastructure. — the stronger call. Right, and the chapter describes this as what organizations often choose — certain applications in-house while others move to the public cloud. There is typically no single provider that meets all of an organization’s needs, and the two applications here are asking for opposite things: elasticity for one, control for the other.
  • Everything in a public cloud, since a capable provider can secure the fare-card data as well as the authority can. — The provider may well be more capable, and that is not what the constraint says. An internal rule requiring the data to stay on controlled machines is a decision about control and location, and the chapter treats where data physically sits as a genuine limit rather than a technical detail.
  • Everything in a private cloud, so the authority controls both applications and can still provision capacity on demand internally. — This satisfies the fare-card rule and strands the journey planner. Internal pooling can only redistribute equipment the authority has already bought, so the weather-driven surge still has to be paid for in advance and sits idle the rest of the time.
  • Everything as rented finished applications, so neither system needs any infrastructure decision at all. — Neither system fits. The fare-card rule is about where data sits, which this model settles in the provider’s favour, and a journey planner built around one city’s network is distinctive work rather than something to buy off a shelf.

Section 3–4c

Deciding well: what to ask before you move

Renting an infrastructure takes an afternoon and a card. That speed is the appeal and the difficulty: a decision that once took months now takes minutes, so the thinking moves elsewhere.

The bill nobody was watching

A small software company ran a translation application. It sent text to another company’s service, reaching it with an interface key — a short secret string identifying the paying customer on every request.

Its usual spend was US$1,500 a month. Then one six-week bill came to US$450,000: somebody had apparently stolen the key and requested nineteen billion characters, all charged to the key holder, because that is what a key is for.

A quieter case sits beside it. A startup doubled its users and expanded its rented infrastructure without cost management. Resources were over-provisioned, nothing was monitored, and the cost went unnoticed until the bill came. Nothing was stolen; nobody was watching.

Read both against the five characteristics. Three did the damage, and all three were sold as benefits.

  • On-demand self-service — resources arrive without negotiation, and so without anybody inside the organization approving the spending.
  • Rapid elasticity — capacity scales instantly, so a runaway stream of requests meets no ceiling that owned machines would impose.
  • Measured service — the meter runs for whoever presents the credential, never asking whether the business wanted the work done.

The advice is vigilance, not avoidance, and the five defences are management, not technology: monitor cost as it is spent, review allocations, alert on anomalies, teach cost awareness, and read the fine print first.

Decide

Four moments in a runaway bill

Work the four decisions in order, and after each one read every outcome, including the ones for the options you did not pick.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

A hypothetical practice situation, built on the shape of the chapter’s own cautionary case rather than on any real company. You look after operations at a small analytics firm that has just started sending work to an outside provider’s metered service. Four moments arrive over the following year, and each one maps onto one of the chapter’s five prevention strategies.

Decision 1. Nothing is switched on yet. The engineering lead has an account ready and asks whether there is anything to do before the first request goes out. What matters most right now?

  • Read the terms first: how usage is charged, what happens when usage is not yours, and what the firm may be liable for. — the stronger call. Right. Reading the fine print is the one item on the chapter’s list that has to happen before the service is running, because it is the only moment when you can still decline the arrangement. It is also where you find out whether requests made on a stolen credential are billable to you, which is the question the chapter’s case turned on.
  • Switch it on and watch the first bill, since real numbers teach more than a contract does. — Real numbers do teach, but the first bill arrives only after a whole billing period of usage has already happened. That is exactly the interval in which the chapter’s company ran up a charge hundreds of times its normal size, and the interval it had no way of seeing into.
  • Ask the provider to cap the account so that overspending is impossible, and treat the matter as settled. — A spending cap is a useful control where a provider offers one, and it is worth having. Treating it as the whole answer skips four of the chapter’s five recommendations, and a cap set high enough not to interrupt normal work is still high enough to hurt.
  • Have the finance team approve every individual request the service receives. — This would defeat the arrangement entirely. On-demand self-service is what makes the service worth using, and a metered service may handle thousands of requests an hour; the chapter’s answer is oversight of the pattern, not approval of each event.

Decision 2. Three months in, a manager asks what the service has cost so far this quarter. Producing the answer takes two days, because somebody has to open the provider’s console, export the usage and add it up by hand. What is the missing practice?

  • Cost monitoring, so that spending is visible while it is happening rather than reconstructed afterwards. — the stronger call. Right. The chapter puts cost monitoring tools first for this reason: a figure that takes two days to assemble will be assembled rarely, and a cost nobody looks at is a cost nobody manages. This is the practice whose absence produced the chapter’s second case.
  • Nothing important. A monthly total is enough oversight for a service of this size. — That is precisely the reasoning behind the chapter’s second case, where a growing startup let costs escalate unnoticed until the monthly bill arrived. A monthly total tells you what already happened; it cannot tell you about it while you could still act.
  • Switch to a provider whose invoices are simpler to read. — Invoice formatting is not the problem here. The firm has no view of usage between invoices whatever their layout, and changing provider to solve a monitoring gap replaces a small piece of work with a migration.
  • Have the engineering lead estimate the monthly spend from memory at each management meeting. — An estimate from memory is the thing cost monitoring exists to replace. It will be roughly right while usage is steady, which is the only period in which nobody needed it, and roughly right is exactly the wrong answer during an anomaly.

Decision 3. Over a weekend, usage rises to many times its normal level and stays there. Nobody at the firm notices until the invoice appears eighteen days later. What should have been in place?

  • Budget alerts set to fire on an anomaly, so the pattern raises a flag on the day it starts. — the stronger call. Right. This is the third of the chapter’s five strategies, and it is the one that shortens the exposure. Cost monitoring makes spending visible to whoever looks; an alert removes the requirement that somebody happens to be looking on a Saturday.
  • A standing monthly review meeting where usage is examined alongside the other operating costs. — A monthly review is worth having and belongs to a different strategy, reviewing resource allocations. As a detector it is too slow: a monthly cycle can let an anomaly run for most of a billing period, which is roughly the interval that produced the chapter’s case.
  • A request to the provider to refund the unusual usage, since the firm did not authorise it. — The meter recorded real requests made with a valid credential, which is what a metered service bills for. The company in the chapter’s case was left pleading for help and leniency rather than exercising a right, which is the difference between a remedy and a favour.
  • A larger prepayment to the provider, so that a spike is absorbed without an unexpected invoice. — Prepaying changes when the money leaves rather than whether it is spent. The firm would still lose the same amount, and it would lose it without ever receiving the invoice that was the only signal anything had happened.

Decision 4. The investigation finishes. The credential had been readable in a place a departed contractor could still reach, and separately about half the capacity the firm was paying for had been provisioned for a product launch that never happened. What does the chapter’s list say the firm still owes itself?

  • Both a regular review of what is provisioned and cost awareness across the teams, because the two failures have different causes and different owners. — the stronger call. Right. One failure was a credential and the other was capacity nobody revisited, and the chapter’s five strategies cover both: regular review of resource allocations catches the idle capacity, and educating teams on cost awareness with a culture of accountability addresses the gap between whoever provisions a resource and whoever pays for it.
  • A security review only. The unused capacity is a finance matter and belongs on a different agenda. — Splitting them is how the second one survives. The chapter’s own second case involved no attacker at all, only over-provisioned resources and no monitoring, and it produced the same result: money leaving the business without anybody deciding that it should.
  • A move back to machines the firm owns, since a metered service has proved too dangerous to use. — The chapter draws no such conclusion. Owned machines would replace a visible metered bill with the fixed costs and idle capacity of objective 3.3, and the firm would still have had a credential where a contractor could read it.
  • A stricter approval process for new services, so that no team can start using a provider without sign-off. — Sign-off before the first use is worth having and overlaps with reading the fine print. It does nothing about either failure here, though: both happened long after the service was approved, and neither would have been prevented by an extra signature at the start.

Ten questions to put to a provider

A prior decision comes first: which applications, services or data should move at all. No single provider meets every need.

For each candidate the chapter lists ten criteria: availability, reliability, scalability, viability, security, privacy, compliance, diversity of offerings, openness and cost. Treat them as questions — one you cannot phrase as a question you will not ask.

Sort

Which criterion is this question testing?

Each question below is one a manager might put to a provider. Place it under the criterion it is really testing; the organizations described are hypothetical.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Availability and reliability — will it be running, what is backed up, and how do we keep trading on the day it is not

  • What uptime is promised for this service, and what will we be doing during the hours that promise is not met? — Availability is the primary concern for most organizations, and the chapter notes that not even the largest public providers are immune from hardware failures, programming errors or network outages. Because of that it expects the customer to plan ahead and replicate its cloud-based infrastructure in different locations.
  • What backups are taken of the servers and storage, and will there be enough bandwidth for us to reach large amounts of our data quickly? — These are two of the three questions the chapter tells organizations to examine when judging whether an application can be moved: the promised uptime, the backups made to servers and storage, and whether sufficient bandwidth will be provided for large amounts of data.

Scalability and viability — can the provider grow with us, and will the provider still be there in a few years

  • Our transaction volume triples every December. Can this provider absorb that, and the volumes we expect to reach in three years? — Scalability is one of the biggest promises of cloud computing, yet the chapter warns that not every provider will meet every organization’s demands, so the evaluation has to cover both current and future needs in storage and transaction volume.
  • If this provider were to stop trading, what would it cost us in money and time to set up somewhere else and move everything across? — That is viability: the stability of the provider in the long run. The chapter lists the repercussions precisely as the costs and efforts of setting up a new infrastructure, migrating applications and transferring the data to it.

Security, privacy and compliance — who can reach the data, whose duties apply to it, and where may it physically sit

  • How is our data protected from outside intruders, and how would we ever establish who had access to a particular record? — The first half is the chapter’s security question. The second half is its structural warning: because a public cloud is shared among different companies on the same hardware, auditing who has access to the data is extremely difficult, if not impossible.
  • May the records of the people we serve be held on machines outside this country, given the duties our sector works under? — This is privacy and compliance together. The chapter treats compliance duties as applying in particular industries and jurisdictions, and notes that some providers allow a customer to specify geographic areas for exactly this kind of requirement.

Diversity of offerings and openness — how many providers must we manage, and how hard would it be to leave one

  • Will one provider cover the services we need now and the ones we will need next, or are we about to manage several separate relationships? — Diversity of offerings is about the management burden: a larger number and diversity of providers is more difficult to manage, so many organizations prefer to deal with fewer providers that can meet all their needs.
  • How would we get several terabytes back out again if a better offer arrived, how long would that take, and what would the transfer be charged at? — That is openness. Providers use different infrastructures and different ways to store data, which makes migration extremely difficult and produces lock-in, and bandwidth plus the charges providers levy for moving data into or out of their infrastructure make it slow and expensive as well.

Cost — what the meter shows, set against what the same work truly costs us

  • The rented figure is on the invoice. What does the same machine truly cost us once licences, electricity, the facility and the staff are counted? — This is the cost comparison the chapter calls hard. Calculating the monthly cost of a rented server is easy, while many organizations do not know what a comparable server of their own costs once the machine, the licence fees, the electricity, the data center and the staff are all included.
  • If we rent capacity only for our few peak weeks each year, who actually operates that arrangement and what does the extra complexity cost us? — The chapter raises exactly this balance: using a cloud infrastructure only for periods of peak demand is sensible, and, needless to say, it adds another layer of complexity to the IT operations, which is a cost like any other.

What an agreement actually promises

Not even the largest providers escape hardware failures, programming errors or outages, so the question is not whether one happens but what was arranged for the day it does.

The service-level agreement is meant to answer that: a contract specifying service levels such as uptime, with warranties and disaster recovery. It reads like a guarantee and is not one.

  • It does not guarantee availability — it promises levels and refunds when missed, settling disputes after the fact.
  • A refund is not compensation — refunds cover fees paid, never business lost while the service was down.
  • Self-service cuts both ways — doing it yourself is an advantage until something breaks, because help is not guaranteed.
  • The customer still has to plan — organizations take precautions, including replicating the infrastructure in more than one location.

Sharing a building you cannot see

Security, privacy and compliance follow from one fact: a public cloud is shared, with different companies running different applications on the same hardware.

  • You cannot say where the data physically are — resources are pooled and assigned dynamically, so you never know which machine holds the records.
  • Auditing who touched the data is very hard — possibly impossible, and knowing who reached a record is often the substance of an obligation.

Control is the other half. In a rented infrastructure control over data is reduced, legal rights fewer, and providers may be required to hand records to law enforcement. Firms holding medical records often keep those in their own building.

Getting out again

Openness, or interoperability, is noticed last and felt hardest. Providers store data differently, which makes moving between them extremely difficult and can lock a company in. Their tools make moving easier — inward.

The second force is physical. Moving terabytes takes real time on the bandwidth available, and providers charge for transfers in or out. A weekend of copying becomes months, with an invoice attached.

Ask the exit question at the beginning, while you still have leverage. Once the data are large and the applications built around one provider, the cost of leaving stops being a choice and becomes a fact.

Check yourself

Agreements, exposure, and getting out again

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not choose. Any organization described is hypothetical.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A provider’s agreement promises a very high uptime figure and pays a discount whenever that figure is missed. What has the customer actually obtained?

  • A. A guarantee that the resources will be available, which can be enforced if they are not — The chapter is explicit that such agreements do not guarantee the availability of resources. A commitment with a penalty attached is a different instrument from a guarantee, and confusing the two is what leaves an organization with no plan.
  • B. A promise of certain service levels together with refunds or discounts when they are missed, which works mostly as a way of resolving disputes — correct. The chapter describes service-level agreements as promising certain service levels and providing refunds or discounts if the promises are not met, which makes them mostly a vehicle for resolving conflicts in case of problems.
  • C. Protection against the business lost during an outage, since the discount is calculated from the revenue affected — Refunds and discounts normally cover only the fees paid for the service. They can never offset the opportunity costs arising from lost business, which is usually the larger figure by a wide margin.
  • D. A reason to stop planning for outages, because responsibility for uptime has now moved to the provider — This is the conclusion the chapter warns against. Because being affected by a negative event is often too costly in lost business or goodwill, organizations are expected to plan ahead and replicate their cloud-based infrastructure in different locations.

2. In the chapter’s cautionary case, an enormous volume of work was requested using a credential that did not belong to the requester. Which feature of the arrangement turned that into a financial event of that size?

  • A. Broad network access, because the account could be reached from anywhere and from almost any web-enabled device, which is what put it within reach of somebody it did not belong to — Broad network access explains how the service was reachable, which is true of every cloud service and of the ones that never produce a surprise bill. Reachability alone does not decide what anything costs.
  • B. Resource pooling, because the customer’s work was running on hardware shared with other companies — Resource pooling explains where the work physically ran and why the customer could not say which machine held it. Nothing about sharing hardware makes a request more expensive than it would otherwise be.
  • C. Measured service together with rapid elasticity: the meter runs for whoever presents the credential, and capacity rose to meet every request without a ceiling — correct. Metering is what makes usage billable to whoever holds the credential, and elasticity is what let the requested volume actually be served rather than refused, so the two together convert a stolen key into a bill hundreds of times the usual size.
  • D. On-demand self-service by itself, because the account could be opened without negotiating with the provider — Self-service explains how quickly the arrangement could be set up in the first place, and it is genuinely part of why nobody had to approve the spending. It does not explain why nineteen billion characters of work were served and charged.

3. A hypothetical research institute holds several terabytes with one provider and is offered better terms by another. Its analysts budget a weekend for the move. Which criterion is about to correct them, and why?

  • A. Viability, because the real question is whether the new provider will still be trading in three years — Viability is a real criterion and worth asking about before signing anything, but it concerns whether the provider survives rather than what makes this particular migration difficult.
  • B. Openness, because providers store data differently, and bandwidth limits plus transfer charges make moving very large volumes slow and expensive — correct. Most providers use different infrastructures and different ways to store data, which makes migrating between them extremely difficult, and the chapter adds that bandwidth and data transmission costs limit it further because providers often charge for moving data into or out of their infrastructure.
  • C. Scalability, because the new provider may not be able to hold the volume the institute expects to accumulate over the next few years, and a second migration would cost more than this one — Scalability concerns whether a provider can meet current and future demands for storage and transaction volume. It says nothing about the cost or the duration of the move itself.
  • D. Availability, because the institute cannot work while its data are in transit between the two providers — Working around a transition is a genuine operational problem, but it is a consequence of the migration rather than the criterion that predicts how long and how expensive the migration will be.

4. A hypothetical clinic is told by a provider that its patient records will be completely secure and fully compliant in the provider’s public cloud. What does the chapter say the clinic still cannot obtain there?

  • A. Encryption of the records, which is unavailable on any shared infrastructure — Nothing in the chapter says protective measures are unavailable in a shared infrastructure. The difficulty it identifies is about location and auditing, not about whether the data can be protected in transit or at rest.
  • B. Knowledge of exactly where the data physically sit, together with a workable way to audit who has reached them — correct. Because a public cloud is shared among different companies with different applications on the same hardware, it is impossible for organizations to know exactly where the data are physically located, and auditing who has access is extremely difficult if not impossible.
  • C. Any protection at all from outside intruders, because the hardware is shared with other companies — This overstates the chapter considerably. It treats security as a question to put to the provider, not as something that cannot exist in a public cloud, and providers are described as being well aware of these concerns.
  • D. The freedom to keep some records in its own building, because a provider agreement has to cover all of an organization’s data — The chapter recommends the opposite. Organizations are expected to weigh which applications and data to move and which to keep in-house, and it names medical and legal work as fields where that judgment matters most.

Five new organizations, none of them real, ask you to use this vocabulary cold.

Apply it

Five decisions you have not seen before

Each question drops you into a different, invented organization mid-decision. Any organization described is hypothetical.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A four-person architecture firm wants shared project boards, file storage and e-signature for contracts, with no interest in writing or customizing any software themselves. Which service model fits what they are actually asking for?

  • A. Software as a service, since they want finished applications to use, not infrastructure or a platform to build on — correct. Project boards, storage and e-signature are complete applications delivered over the internet; the firm wants to use them, not to manage the machines or the platform underneath them.
  • B. Infrastructure as a service, since it gives them the most control over how the applications run — Control over how applications run is exactly what this firm has no interest in. Infrastructure as a service would hand them a set of virtual machines to administer, which is more responsibility than four people asked for.
  • C. Platform as a service, since it lets them build exactly the workflow they want — Nothing here asks to build a custom workflow. A platform to develop on solves a problem this firm does not have; they want to sign in and use existing software.
  • D. None of the three; a firm this size should keep everything on its own office server — Size is not the deciding factor. Even a very small firm can reasonably run entirely on finished cloud applications rather than maintaining a server at all.

2. A mobile game studio's servers sit mostly idle, then strain under ten times the normal traffic for the first week after every major update, then fall quiet again. Which pressure on their infrastructure is this, most precisely?

  • A. Rising energy costs, since more players means more electricity drawn by the servers — Energy cost would rise during the spike, but that is a consequence of the real pressure, not the pressure itself, and it says nothing about why capacity is hard to plan for.
  • B. Obsolescence, since the hardware clearly cannot keep up with a growing player base — Obsolescence is hardware falling behind over time regardless of traffic. This studio's problem repeats on a predictable weekly pattern around each release, which is a sizing problem, not an aging one.
  • C. Demand fluctuation, since capacity has to be sized for a spike that does not last — correct. The studio faces short, sharp spikes it has to be ready for without paying to keep that much capacity running the other fifty weeks of the year, which is exactly the fluctuating-demand pressure the chapter describes.
  • D. Growing storage needs, since more players generate more data to keep — Storage would grow steadily as data accumulates. A spike that rises and falls within a week is about processing and network capacity in the moment, not about how much has been saved up.

3. A regional accounting firm plans to move several years of client records to a new provider over a single weekend, and has budgeted for the new provider's fees but nothing else. What is most likely to go wrong?

  • A. The new provider is likely to be less reliable, since switching providers tends to increase the chance of downtime — Reliability is a property of the provider chosen, not a consequence of switching itself; nothing here suggests the new provider is less dependable.
  • B. The volume of data will make the transfer itself slow and possibly costly, a fact the weekend budget does not account for — correct. Providers store and structure data differently, and bandwidth limits plus transfer charges make moving a large volume slow and often expensive — a cost this budget never priced in.
  • C. Client records cannot legally be moved between providers without a court order — No such requirement exists in general; moving business records between commercial providers is a contractual and technical matter, not one that needs judicial approval.
  • D. Nothing is likely to go wrong, since fees are the only real cost a migration of this kind involves — This ignores exactly the cost the scenario is testing. Fees are one line item; the data transfer itself is frequently the larger and less visible one.

4. A boutique hotel-booking platform owns its own servers, sized to handle the single weekend each year when a local festival triples normal traffic. The rest of the year, most of that capacity sits unused. What does this tell you about the fit between the cost model and the workload?

  • A. It fits well, since owning hardware is generally the cheaper option once a company can afford the upfront cost — Ownership is not cheaper by default; a fixed asset sized for one weekend a year is paid for in full whether it is used or idle, which is precisely the mismatch here.
  • B. It fits poorly; a metered, elastic arrangement would charge mostly for the one busy weekend, not for capacity idle all year — correct. Rapid elasticity and a measured, pay-for-what-you-use model exist for exactly this kind of workload: capacity that is needed briefly and would otherwise sit idle almost all year.
  • C. It fits poorly, but only because the servers should be replaced on a faster schedule than this company follows — Replacement frequency is a separate question from utilization. A brand-new server sized this way would sit idle just as often as an old one.
  • D. It fits well, since owning the hardware means the company fully controls every machine during the busy weekend — Control during the festival is not what is being asked. The company already controls its own hardware today; the problem is what that control costs the other fifty-one weeks of the year.

5. An environmental testing lab has written its own image-analysis software for soil samples and runs it in intense bursts a few times a month. It wants to stop maintaining physical servers, but still needs to install and configure its own software stack. Which service model matches that?

  • A. Software as a service, since the lab wants to stop managing hardware of any kind entirely — Wanting to stop managing hardware is necessary but not sufficient here: software as a service would hand the lab someone else's finished application, and this lab has already written its own.
  • B. Platform as a service, since the lab would be handed a ready-made analysis application to run — The lab already has its analysis software; it is not looking for one to be provided. A platform to develop on also usually constrains how software is built, which is not what a bursty, already-written workload needs.
  • C. None of the three fit well, since custom-written software cannot run in a rented arrangement — Custom software runs routinely on rented infrastructure; this is one of the most common uses of the cloud in fields with bursty, specialized computing needs.
  • D. Infrastructure as a service, since it removes the hardware while leaving the software up to the lab — correct. Infrastructure as a service supplies the computing, storage and networking while leaving the operating system and everything installed on it to the customer, which is exactly the fit for software the lab already wrote and wants to keep running its own way.

What it actually costs

Metered billing shows what each part costs. Owned equipment tells you nothing comparable: a server in a cupboard costs the same busy or idle.

The chapter will not claim the metered bill is smaller; there is considerable disagreement over whether the cloud is ultimately cheaper. The comparison is unfair one way: the rented figure is exact, the in-house figure is not.

  • The machine itself — the element every quick comparison includes, its price divided by the years it should last.
  • Software licences — for the operating system and database engine, which under an infrastructure service stay yours.
  • Electricity — counted twice: the machine draws power, and the cooling draws power to remove the heat.
  • The facility — this machine’s share of floor space, power distribution, cooling and physical security.
  • The staff — the fraction who install, patch, monitor, back up and replace it, usually the largest figure and least written down.

One game developer moved back out of a public cloud into equipment it owned. Build the in-house figure on the hypothetical sheet below; every number is invented.

Spreadsheet

Build the in-house figure before you compare it

Type one formula for row 2 in each column, then run it; the formula is applied down every row the way a filled-down formula behaves in a real sheet.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Columns: Cost element · Cost per year · In the quick comparison? · Cost per month · Counted per month · Full cost so far, per month

1. Column D: put every element on the same footing as a monthly rented bill by turning the yearly figure into a monthly one.

=B2/12

Comparisons are only possible between figures covering the same period. A rented bill arrives monthly, so the owned costs have to be expressed monthly before either number means anything next to the other.

2. Column E: show only what a quick comparison would have counted. Where column C says yes, show that element’s monthly figure; otherwise show zero.

=IF(C2="yes", B2/12, 0)

Only the first row survives, which is the whole problem. A comparison built on the purchase price of the machine alone is being made against a rented bill that already includes the licences, the power, the building and the people.

3. Column F: accumulate the full monthly cost as you go down the list, so the last row shows what this one machine truly costs each month.

=SUM($B$2:B2)/12

The final row is several times the figure the quick comparison produced. That gap is the chapter’s point exactly: the rented number is known precisely and the owned number usually is not, so the two are rarely being compared on equal terms.

Nobody signs up for a runaway bill, an unaffordable migration or an outage with no plan. They sign up for something quick and cheap, postponing the questions that would have surfaced all three.
