  • I can list the five things the chapter recommends to prevent a runaway bill, and say which one has to happen before anything is switched on. The numbered defences immediately after the two cases; the last of the five is the one that has to come first in time.

  • I can state the chapter’s counterpoint about in-house uptime without it sounding like an argument against ever renting anything. The paragraph after that list, where the chapter compares a missed promise against a poorly managed operation of your own.
  • I can say why an organization cannot know exactly where its data physically sit in a public cloud, and what that makes difficult. The section on sharing a building you cannot see, where pooling and auditing are set side by side.

Section 3–4d

What the cloud made possible

Once capacity could be summoned in minutes and dropped again, impractical arrangements became ordinary: software assembled from blocks, many machines aimed at one problem, content kept near its readers, and a push to use less power.

One program that does everything

The traditional way to build business software was one large program holding every feature: a monolithic application, built as a single unit with the entire code in one base.

  • Everything ships together — one build, one test and one installation cover the whole application, simpler than coordinating a dozen pieces.
  • Everything changes together — altering one feature means rebuilding the whole program, so a small change carries the risk of the entire system.

The second is why a monolith is hard to adapt: the part you want to change is bolted to every part you do not.

Building out of blocks instead

The alternative is to assemble a program rather than write one. A modular architecture means choosing the building blocks best suited to a need and connecting them through APIs, like a model made of Lego.

A packaged business capability, or PBC, is one such block performing a well-specified function such as processing payments, itself made of smaller microservices. Vendors offer competing blocks, so a firm picks best of breed.

Why you do not care how the oil gets changed. Somebody else changes your car’s oil. All that matters is the expected quality and cost, not the tools. An interface is that agreement written down for software.

Uber built driver management, trip management, billing and payments as separate components joined by APIs, so each could change when its process did. But modularity demands expertise to plan the architecture, select components from thousands, and orchestrate them.

Modularity moves the difficulty rather than removing it: less code to write, far more to choose and connect.

Check yourself

Monoliths, blocks, and what an interface promises

Four options, one best answer; every organization described here is a hypothetical example written for practice, and every company named is one the chapter names, so read all four explanations including the ones you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical distributor runs its whole ordering system as one large program containing every feature it needs. Which pair of consequences does the chapter attach to that design?

  • A. It is difficult to develop, test and deploy, which is precisely why organizations began assembling software from separate blocks — The chapter says the opposite about building it: because the entire application code sits in a single code base, a monolithic application is relatively easy to develop, test and deploy. The difficulty arrives later, when the thing has to change.
  • B. It is relatively easy to develop, test and deploy, and correspondingly inflexible and very difficult to adapt to changing business or user needs — correct. The chapter grants the monolith its advantage and then names the price. The same single code base that makes the application easy to build and ship makes it inflexible and very difficult to adapt to changing business or user needs.
  • C. It cannot be hosted on rented infrastructure, because providers run applications that have been split into separate components — Nothing about a single code base prevents it from running on rented infrastructure. The infrastructure service model described earlier in this objective rents an operating system upward and lets the customer run whatever it likes on top.
  • D. It costs less to run than a modular equivalent, because a single code base consumes less storage and network capacity than many blocks would — Storage and network capacity are not the comparison the chapter draws, and it says nothing about a monolith being cheaper to run. The trade-off it names is ease of building set against the ability to change.

2. A hypothetical clinic buys a component that handles patient billing and connects it to the rest of its systems through an interface. In the chapter’s vocabulary, what has it bought, and what is that component built from?

  • A. A packaged business capability, which on a technical level is composed of smaller blocks called microservices — correct. A packaged business capability is an individual building block designed to perform a well-specified business function, such as processing payments or managing orders, and the chapter says such capabilities are composed on a technical level of smaller building blocks referred to as microservices.
  • B. A microservice, which is composed of several packaged business capabilities working together — The relationship runs the other way around. Microservices are the smaller parts that a packaged business capability is assembled from, not the larger thing assembled out of capabilities.
  • C. A monolithic application, because billing is a complete piece of software in its own right — A monolithic application contains every feature the system needs inside one code base. A component bought to perform one well-specified function and connected through an interface is the opposite arrangement.
  • D. A grid, because the work of producing each bill is distributed across many networked machines — Grid computing combines many small computers to attack a single large computation. Producing a bill is ordinary business work, not a calculation that has to be divided across machines.

3. The chapter explains interfaces by comparing them to having someone else change your car’s oil. What is that comparison actually teaching?

  • A. That the cheapest supplier is usually adequate, since the same task produces the same result wherever it is carried out — Price is not what the comparison turns on. The chapter lists a dealership, an independent garage, an oil-change service and a friend as equally acceptable, which is a statement about the agreed result rather than about cost alone.
  • B. That what matters is the service arriving at the expected quality and cost, while how the provider does the work is not the customer’s concern — correct. The chapter says all that matters is that the service will be provided at the expected level of quality and cost, and that you typically do not care if different providers do things differently or use different tools. That is exactly what an interface promises between two pieces of software.
  • C. That specialist work belongs in-house, because a customer cannot judge whether an outside provider did the job properly — The chapter argues the reverse. Its starting sentence is that you cannot be an expert in everything, so it is probably more effective to have the work done by someone who is.
  • D. That a modular approach removes the need for planning, since each provider takes responsibility for its own block — Planning is precisely what a modular approach demands. The chapter warns that it takes tremendous effort and expertise to plan the architecture, select the right components from hundreds or thousands available, and orchestrate and deploy them.

Many small machines, one enormous problem

Some organizations need more performance than an ordinary arrangement supplies, usually to simulate events that are expensive, dangerous or impossible to stage.

  • Crash and design simulation — manufacturers simulate crashes and test designs for vibration and wind noise before metal is bent.
  • Research modelling — laboratories model neutron transport inside nuclear reactors and study climate scenarios.
  • Earth science — earthquake simulation, where the alternative is waiting for the real event.

The obvious answer is a supercomputer, and it fails twice. Some simulations take a year even on one, and the fastest cost more than US$200 million — a purchase price that is not the total cost of ownership, which also carries staff and facilities.

Grid computing is the third answer: combining many smaller, independent, networked computers, often ordinary desktops, into one system solving problems only supercomputers could. Large tasks break into chunks that individual machines complete.

The line to remember. Grid and cloud both use distributed resources, which is why they get confused. In a grid they go to a single large problem; a cloud serves many customers doing many things.

Reassemble the argument in order; a grid is a last answer, not a first one.

Sequence

Why a grid, and how the work gets divided

Put the six stages into the order the chapter’s own argument runs, then read why each one sits where it does.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

A hypothetical materials research group needs a simulation that would take far longer than it can wait on any machine it already owns. Two answers get ruled out before the chapter reaches grid computing, and the ruling out is the part worth following, because it explains what a grid is actually for.

  1. The work is stated: one simulation, far too large for the machines the organization already owns to finish in a useful time. — Grid computing answers a particular shape of problem, so the shape has to be named first. The chapter’s own cases are crash simulation, reactor and climate modelling, and earthquake simulation, each of them a single large calculation rather than many small unrelated ones.
  2. A supercomputer is considered, and speed alone turns out not to settle the question, because some complex simulations take a year or longer to calculate even on a supercomputer. — This is the step most people skip. Buying the fastest available machine does not automatically make the problem tractable, so the organization cannot treat raw performance as the whole answer before it has looked at the size of its own task.
  3. Cost rules the purchase out. The fastest supercomputers can cost more than US$200 million, and the purchase price does not represent the total cost of ownership, which also carries personnel, facilities, storage and software. — The chapter separates the sticker price from the running commitment on purpose. A machine also needs people who can operate it, somewhere to put it, storage to feed it and software to run on it, and an organization needing it only occasionally cannot justify any of that.
  4. The historical fallback is named and found wanting: rent time on somebody else’s supercomputer, or simply decide not to solve the problem. — This is the state of affairs grid computing improved on, and the second half of it is the honest one. The chapter says organizations sometimes decided not to solve the problem at all, which is what an unaffordable capability actually costs a research programme.
  5. The large computing task is broken into small chunks, each of which can be completed on its own. — Divisibility is the precondition, not an afterthought. If the pieces cannot be worked on independently then handing them to separate machines gains nothing, which is why not every heavy calculation is a candidate for this treatment.
  6. The chunks are distributed to a large number of smaller, independent, networked computers, often ordinary desktop machines, and the completed pieces are combined into the finished result. — This is the definition itself: combining the computing power of many smaller networked computers into a cohesive system able to solve problems that only supercomputers could previously solve. Note that the resources are all aimed at one problem, which is what separates a grid from a cloud.

When the computers are inside a moving object

Car hacking. A modern vehicle holds many control units — small computers running engine, airbags, steering and braking — coupled through a maze of networks, plus Bluetooth and Wi-Fi.

Researchers have repeatedly broken in. The reason is not clever attackers: a vehicle holds a tremendous amount of code, most from many vendors, so no manufacturer understands every vulnerability it ships.

Keeping the content near the people who want it

Distance costs time: the further a user is from the server holding the content, the longer it takes. A content delivery network answers that with servers in many geographical locations storing copies of particular websites, so the closest one answers each request.

These became edge computing, where storage and processing move to the edges of the network to minimize latency, with less traffic and lower cost.

  1. Annoying — latency spoils a home assistant, because a pause before every answer turns a conversation into a wait.
  2. Impractical — automated stock trading becomes impossible, since the point is acting before somebody slower does.
  3. Dangerous — autonomous vehicles become impossible, because a car cannot wait for a round trip across a continent.
  4. Fatal — a patient in an internet-connected EKG vest, where the delay can result in life or death.

Pair each arrangement with the problem it answers.

Match

Which arrangement answers which problem

Pair each arrangement from this section with the problem it exists to solve; the explanations name the chapter’s own reasoning for each pairing.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Modular architecture
An application that has to change often is built as one unit, so every small change carries the whole system with it The chapter presents modular architectures as the answer to the monolith’s inflexibility: choose the blocks best suited to a particular need and connect them, rather than holding every feature in one code base.
Packaged business capability
A well-specified business function such as processing payments would otherwise have to be written from scratch inside your own application That is the definition: an individual building block designed to perform a well-specified business function, with processing payments and managing orders as the chapter’s two examples.
Microservices
Even a single business capability is too large to replace in one piece, so it is assembled from smaller parts each doing one narrow job The chapter says a packaged business capability is composed on a technical level of smaller building blocks referred to as microservices, which is what makes a capability adjustable from the inside.
Best-of-breed selection
Several vendors offer a block for the same function, and their strengths and prices differ The chapter notes that you can typically find capabilities offered by different vendors, allowing you to choose the one that best meets current or future needs.
Connecting blocks through APIs
Software written by different people, often at different companies, has to work together without either side knowing how the other is built This is the oil-change comparison in software form: what matters is the service arriving at the expected quality and cost, not whether the provider does things differently or uses different tools.
Grid computing
A single large problem needs more computing power than the organization can justify buying, and would take too long on the machines it owns The chapter reaches grid computing only after ruling out a supercomputer on cost and on total cost of ownership, and it stresses that the pooled resources are aimed at one problem.
Content delivery network
Users far from the one server holding the content wait noticeably longer for it to arrive The chapter names distance itself as the cause, and answers it with servers in various geographical locations holding copies, the closest one delivering the content.
Edge computing
A round trip to a distant central location is too slow for work that has to react immediately Edge computing is what content delivery networks evolved into: not only storage but also processing moves to the edges of the network in order to minimize latency, which is what a vehicle or a monitoring device needs.
Virtualization
A room full of servers each uses a small fraction of its capacity while drawing power and needing cooling The chapter gives virtualization as its first green computing tactic, consolidating many underutilized machines onto far fewer and cutting both the energy bill and the carbon footprint.
IT asset disposition
Retired equipment cannot simply go to a landfill, and may still hold user data when it leaves the building The chapter says drives must be wiped, and describes third-party vendors that wipe them and then either refurbish and resell the equipment or dismantle it to recycle materials and dispose of hazardous waste.

Using less power to do the same work

Organizations act on energy for two reasons: scrutiny over their contribution to climate change, and savings on energy, water, waste and carbon taxes. Green computing covers both — using computing resources more efficiently, and using information systems to cut environmental impacts elsewhere.

  • Virtualization — several computing environments on one machine, consolidating barely used servers onto a few well-used ones, cutting power and cooling.
  • Shared provider infrastructure — the cloud is argued to cut consumption, because one provider’s infrastructure is shared rather than idling everywhere.
  • Power management — software recovering the energy wasted by desktops idling overnight, invisible until measured.
  • Printing less — discouraging staff from printing emails and documents cuts paper waste.

Retiring equipment is the forgotten part. Old machines cannot go to landfill and must be wiped of user data; specialist firms resell them or dismantle them to recycle materials and handle hazardous waste.

The cards set all four trends side by side, with what each asks in return.

Explore

The four trends, and what each one asks for in return

Open each card and read all four panels; the third panel is the one worth lingering over, because it names what the arrangement costs rather than what it saves.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Modular architectures · Assembling software rather than writing it

  • The idea in one line: Building software by choosing individual blocks best suited to a particular need and connecting them through interfaces, in place of one large program holding every feature in a single code base.
  • What it looks like in practice: A system whose ordering, inventory, customer and payment functions are separate packaged business capabilities, each chosen from whichever vendor suits it best, and each replaceable without disturbing the others.
  • What it demands in return: Tremendous effort and expertise to plan the architecture, to select the right components from hundreds or thousands of available blocks, and to orchestrate and deploy them so they work as one thing.
  • The limit worth knowing: The chapter says the integration can be extremely complex and time-consuming, and well beyond the means of small enterprises, so modularity is not automatically the cheaper road for a small organization.

Grid computing · Many small machines, one large problem

  • The idea in one line: Combining the computing power of a large number of smaller, independent, networked computers into a cohesive system able to solve problems that previously needed a supercomputer.
  • What it looks like in practice: A crash, reactor or earthquake simulation broken into small chunks, each completed by an ordinary machine somewhere on the network and returned to be combined with the rest.
  • What it demands in return: A problem that genuinely divides into independent chunks, and a population of machines whose spare capacity can be borrowed without disrupting whatever else those machines are doing.
  • The limit worth knowing: It is not a general substitute for renting infrastructure. The resources in a grid are typically applied to a single large problem, whereas cloud resources serve many separate customers doing many separate things.

Content delivery and edge computing · Moving the work closer to the person

  • The idea in one line: Keeping copies of content on servers in several geographical locations so the nearest one answers a request, and then moving processing as well as storage out towards the edges of the network.
  • What it looks like in practice: A page or a video that arrives promptly for viewers on three continents because each of them is served from a machine a few hundred miles away, a process normally unnoticed by the viewer.
  • What it demands in return: Somewhere to hold the copies and a way to keep them current, plus the judgement to decide which work has to happen near the user and which can afford a round trip to the centre.
  • The limit worth knowing: Distance is the constraint it removes, not capacity. An application that is slow because of its own design, or because its origin is overloaded, is not repaired by holding copies nearer to anybody.

Green computing · Doing the same work with less power

  • The idea in one line: Using computing resources more efficiently in order to reduce environmental impacts, and using information systems to reduce negative environmental impacts elsewhere in the organization.
  • What it looks like in practice: Consolidating underused servers through virtualization, shifting work to a shared provider, managing power on idle desktops, printing less, and routing retired equipment through a specialist rather than a skip.
  • What it demands in return: A decision about when equipment is retired, and a process that wipes user data from every machine before it leaves the building, whether it is resold, refurbished or dismantled.
  • The limit worth knowing: The chapter credits shared cloud infrastructure with lower energy use while describing an enormous new demand for computing power to train models, and it does not reconcile the two claims.

One last check across the four trends and the security box.

Check yourself

Grids, distance, vehicles, and watts

Four questions across the whole section; every organization described is a hypothetical example written for practice, and each explanation says what the option you did not pick would actually describe.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical university research group splits one very large simulation into thousands of small pieces and has hundreds of ordinary networked desktop machines complete them. How does the chapter separate this from cloud computing?

  • A. Both use distributed resources, but the resources in a grid are typically applied to a single large problem, whereas a cloud serves many separate customers and purposes — correct. The chapter says that similar to cloud computing, grid computing makes use of distributed resources, but that in contrast to cloud computing the resources in a grid are typically applied to a single large problem.
  • B. A grid uses machines the organization owns itself, whereas a cloud uses machines belonging to somebody else — Ownership is not the line the chapter draws, and a grid can be assembled from machines belonging to several organizations or contributed by volunteers. What the machines are aimed at is the distinguishing feature.
  • C. A grid is a way of storing data across many machines, whereas a cloud is a way of processing it — Grid computing is defined as combining computing power to solve problems that previously required a supercomputer, which is processing rather than a way of storing data across machines.
  • D. There is no real difference between them, because grid computing is simply the earlier name for what is now sold as cloud computing, and the change of word marked a change of marketing — The chapter sets the two side by side precisely in order to separate them, and it defines cloud computing separately as renting configurable resources on demand with minimal management effort.

2. The chapter’s security box argues that vehicle manufacturers cannot know every vulnerability in their own vehicles. What reason does it give?

  • A. Because attackers work faster than manufacturers can test, so any list of known vulnerabilities is out of date before it is finished — The chapter says the opposite about speed. A successful break-in typically is not easy and often requires several researchers several months, which is why some observers regard the danger as more hype than reality.
  • B. Because a modern vehicle contains a tremendous amount of programming code, most of it supplied by a broad range of outside vendors — correct. The chapter states that there is a tremendous amount of programming code in modern vehicles and that most of this code comes from a broad range of vendors, making it virtually impossible for manufacturers to understand all potential vulnerabilities.
  • C. Because the control units in a vehicle are not connected to one another, so a fault in one cannot be traced from another — The box describes the control units as coupled together through a maze of networks, alongside Bluetooth for hands-free calling and sometimes a passenger hotspot, so connection is part of the problem rather than absent from it.
  • D. Because vehicles are tested for safety rather than for security, and that testing is carried out by regulators rather than by manufacturers — Testing regimes are not what the box discusses. Its recommendation is that component vendors standardize approaches, share information and secure supply chains against tampering and counterfeit parts.

3. A hypothetical museum streams video to visitors on three continents from a single server in one country, and distant viewers wait noticeably longer for it to start. Which arrangement does the chapter offer, and why does it work?

  • A. A content delivery network, because copies held on servers in several geographical locations let the nearest one answer, which removes the delay caused by distance — correct. The chapter says the larger the geographical distance between a user and the web server hosting the content, the longer transmission takes, and that a content delivery network reduces this latency with servers in various geographical locations holding copies, the closest one delivering the content.
  • B. A private cloud, because owning the infrastructure gives the museum direct control over how quickly the video is delivered — A private cloud changes who owns and controls the machines, and the chapter values it for customizability and control. It does nothing about the distance between one location and a viewer on another continent.
  • C. Grid computing, because dividing the video among many small machines lets them deliver the pieces in parallel — Grid computing applies many machines to a single large computation. Delivering a video to a distant viewer is a transmission problem, not a calculation that can be divided into chunks.
  • D. A faster connection at the museum’s own server, because the delay comes from the capacity of that connection rather than from distance — Capacity at the origin can matter, and the chapter treats bandwidth as a real constraint elsewhere. The cause it names for this particular delay is the distance itself, which is why the remedy is to move copies closer rather than to widen one connection.

4. A hypothetical charity runs forty servers in its own building, each using a small fraction of its capacity, and wants to cut both its power bill and its environmental impact. Which tactic does the chapter name first, and what does it do?

  • A. Power management software, which stops individual machines idling overnight and so reduces the load on every server in the room — Power management software is one of the chapter’s tactics and does recover energy wasted by machines left idling or on standby overnight. It is aimed at individual desktops rather than at a room of servers each running well below capacity.
  • B. Virtualization, which runs several separate computing environments on one physical machine so underused servers can be consolidated onto a few well-used ones — correct. The chapter says organizations can save large amounts of money on power and cooling by using virtualization to replace many individual servers with far fewer machines, and notes that computing resources in organizations are often very much underutilized.
  • C. Printing less, since paper waste is the largest environmental cost that an organization of this kind carries — Printing less is a genuine tactic on the chapter’s list, but it addresses paper waste rather than the power and cooling drawn by underused servers, and the chapter makes no claim that paper is the largest cost.
  • D. Disposing of the least used servers immediately, since equipment that is doing almost nothing still draws power and still has to be cooled, and costs more to keep than it would cost to replace — Retirement is a decision the chapter treats carefully rather than quickly. Companies cannot just send retired equipment to a landfill, drives must be wiped of user data, and usable machines are refurbished or dismantled for recycling and safe disposal.

Application supplement · 3–5

Where the data itself lives: databases and SQLite

Everything so far has been the container: machines, software, wire. None of it says what all of it exists to hold. An organization’s records are the part that cannot be bought again after a bad day. This supplement prepares for the course’s separate SQLite work rather than replacing it.

Why a pile of files eventually fails

A file is a block of content whose meaning lives in the head of whoever made it. That works for documents and fails once several people record the same kind of fact — say a hypothetical music school where three staff each keep a loans spreadsheet.

  • The same fact is stored twice — an address typed into whichever file was open, so corrections never reach the others.
  • Nothing decides which copy is authoritative — two files disagree, and whoever sounds surer settles it.
  • The shape of a record becomes habit — one file dates in words, another in digits, and headings change meaning.
  • Questions spanning the files cannot be asked — a year of loans means opening each file and adding by hand.

A database answers that: one stored, shared set of records everyone reads and writes, held in a declared shape and asked questions of instead of copied. The program keeping it is a database management system, which enforces the shape, lets many people work at once, and answers questions.

That shape is the difference. A table has named columns, each holding one kind of value, and one row per thing it is about, so the system can refuse a loan with no borrower.

Check yourself

Files, records, and what a database actually changes

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. Two of the hypothetical music school’s spreadsheets disagree about how many instruments are out on loan. A volunteer proposes settling it by declaring one of the three files the master copy. What is the strongest objection?

  • A. Nothing is wrong with the idea, because declaring a master copy is exactly what a database does, only without needing any software — A database does something stronger than nominate a favourite copy: it removes the other copies, so there is nowhere else for a loan to be recorded. A nominated file is a convention, and a convention only holds while everybody remembers it.
  • B. The other two files still exist and are still being edited, so the totals part again the first time somebody records a loan in the wrong one — correct. The problem is not which file is trusted but that three places can accept a record. As long as the other two remain open on somebody’s screen, the school is one distracted afternoon away from the same disagreement.
  • C. Spreadsheets cannot store dates reliably, so the same disagreement would return in a different form within a term or two — Spreadsheets handle dates perfectly well. The inconsistency in the files came from three people typing them differently, which is a question of who may write where rather than of what the software can store.
  • D. A single master file would be too large for one person to keep up to date, so the work has to stay divided across the three files — Size is not the difficulty here; a year of instrument loans would be a small file by any measure. The cost of the arrangement is inconsistency between copies, and dividing the work is what created it.

2. In the school’s loan records, every loan carries a member identifier rather than the member’s name. Why is it arranged that way?

  • A. An identifier occupies less storage space than a name, and storage is the constraint that shapes how tables are designed — The space saved is trivial and would not justify the extra table. Facts are separated for correctness, and the join you pay for afterwards is the price of that correctness rather than a saving.
  • B. A query cannot compare text, so a numbered identifier is required before two tables can be matched at all — Queries compare text quite happily, and plenty of tables are matched on text columns. The trouble with matching on a name is that two members may share one, not that the language cannot do it.
  • C. The name is a fact about the member, so it is stored once on the member’s row and every loan simply refers to it — correct. One fact, one home. Correcting a spelling on the member’s row makes every loan correct at once, because no loan ever contained a copy that could fall out of step with it.
  • D. Typing a name onto every loan would take longer, and saving that typing is the reason the tables were split — It does save typing, but that is a side effect rather than the reason. Even with perfect typists, copying the name onto every loan creates as many chances to disagree as there are loans.

3. The chapter says web servers often assemble a page by retrieving data from a database as the request arrives. What follows from that for someone managing the site?

  • A. The finished page already sits on the server’s disk in the form the visitor sees, and the database holds only a spare copy of it — For a page assembled on request there is no such stored copy: the layout is stored, but the prices, the availability and the names are fetched and dropped in as the page is built for that visitor.
  • B. What the visitor sees is produced from stored records at the moment of asking, so a slow or unavailable database is a slow or unavailable site — correct. The page is a view of the records, made on demand, so the quality of the records is the quality of the page and the availability of the store is the availability of the site.
  • C. The site cannot be copied to servers nearer the visitor, because the records behind it can exist in one location only — Copies of content can certainly be pushed closer to visitors, which is what the earlier section on content delivery networks described. What travels is usually the parts that do not change per visitor.
  • D. The database matters for internal reporting, while the public site is a separate system fed by an overnight export — This describes one possible arrangement rather than the one the chapter names. When the page is assembled from a query at request time, the public site and the store are the same system by definition.

How to read a stored table

A table has two directions, and both are ordinary.

  • A row is one thing the table is about — one loan, learner or payment, with a value in each column.
  • A column is one kind of fact — every value means the same thing, so you can filter, sort or total on it.
  • A key identifies the row — a value no two rows share, so a record is named without ambiguity.
  • A relationship names a row in another table — a loan carries a learner identifier, not a name, stored once.

The language for asking is SQL, the structured query language, much the same in any system. Six words carry most of it.

  • FROM names the table the rows come from, deciding what is counted at all.
  • WHERE keeps only rows meeting a condition, and running first, decides every number that follows.
  • SELECT names the columns returned; a calculation such as booked minus attended can be one.
  • GROUP BY and HAVING collapse rows into one per distinct value, then filter those totals, which WHERE cannot do.
  • ORDER BY and LIMIT sort and keep the first rows — the busiest, the longest, the worst three.

One whole query: SELECT Learner, Fee FROM signups WHERE Term = 'Spring' ORDER BY Fee DESC. Rows come from sign-ups, only spring survives, two columns return, dearest first — and it names no learner, so it still works after another hundred.

Sequence

From a business question to a query you can trust

Put the five steps into the order that produces an answer to the question actually asked, then read why each one sits where it does.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The hardest part of querying is not the words. It is resisting the urge to start typing before the question has been stated precisely enough to be answered. These five steps are the same discipline the earlier modules asked for when turning evidence into a claim.

  1. State the question in ordinary business words, and name the decision the answer feeds. “Which instruments are out right now, and who has them?” is a question; “have a look at the loans” is not. — A query can only be as precise as the sentence behind it. Naming the decision the answer serves is what stops you producing a screen of rows that is technically correct and useless, because nobody can act on it.
  2. Find where the fact is stored: which table has one row for each thing the question is about, and which other table holds the extra detail the question also mentions. — The question mentions instruments and people, and those are two different kinds of thing. The table you count from is the one whose rows are the units being asked about, which here is loans rather than members.
  3. Decide which rows. Every condition in the question — still out, this term, longer than a month — has to be written down as a filter before anything is counted. — The filter runs before any total exists, so whatever it excludes is missing from every number that follows. Most confidently wrong answers were produced by a filter that nobody went back and read.
  4. Decide what comes back: the rows themselves with the columns the question mentions, or one summary value for each group when the question asks how many, how much, or how long on average. — Choosing rows and choosing columns are separate decisions, and summarising is a third. A question about loans per town does not want the loans at all; it wants one line per town, which is a different result rather than a different layout.
  5. Run it, then read the result back against the original question and satisfy yourself that it answers that question rather than a neighbouring one. — A query that runs is not a query that is right. The commonest failure is a clean answer to a slightly different question — every loan rather than every loan still out — and only rereading the question catches it.

Asking one table a question

The table below records sign-ups at that hypothetical school; every person is invented. Each row carries learner, instrument, level, term, sessions booked and attended, and fee. Any query returning the right answer is accepted.

Database

Question one table

Write a SELECT for each question and run it. Any query that returns the right answer is accepted, so there is more than one correct way through.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

signups — RecordID, Learner, Instrument, Level, Term, Sessions, Attended, Fee (10 rows)

1. List the learner and the instrument for every sign-up at the beginner level.

SELECT Learner, Instrument FROM signups WHERE Level = 'beginner'

SELECT chooses the columns and WHERE chooses the rows. They are two independent decisions, and confusing them is the most common early mistake: asking for fewer columns never removes a row.

2. Show every sign-up with the learner, the instrument, and the number of sessions missed, with the worst attendance first.

SELECT Learner, Instrument, Sessions - Attended AS Missed FROM signups ORDER BY Missed DESC

Missed sessions are nowhere in the table; they are worked out as the query runs. Naming the calculation with AS is what lets ORDER BY refer to it, and it also gives the reader a heading that says what the number means.

3. Which instruments does the school actually teach? List each one once.

SELECT DISTINCT Instrument FROM signups

DISTINCT answers a question about the set of values rather than about the records. It is the smallest example of the difference between listing rows and describing them, which is what grouping does at greater scale.

4. Name the three most expensive sign-ups, showing the learner, the instrument and the fee.

SELECT Learner, Instrument, Fee FROM signups ORDER BY Fee DESC LIMIT 3

Questions phrased as the worst three or the busiest five are a sort followed by a cut, not a filter. Nobody could have written a WHERE for this, because the threshold depends on the data rather than on the question.

Missed sessions are stored nowhere; they are worked out from two columns as you ask. Storing the number too would create a third value that can disagree — the files again.

Questions no single row can answer

Everything so far returned rows that already existed. Two kinds of question do not.

  • Summaries ask about groups — loans per instrument, or average length, give one line per group.
  • Joins ask about facts kept apart — borrower and item live in two tables, matched on the value they share.
  • Filters apply before or after grouping — loans still out tests rows; instruments borrowed twice tests a total.

The two invented tables below belong to that school: one row per member with town and join date, one row per loan carrying a member identifier.

Database

Two tables, and questions about groups

Each question needs either a join, a grouping, or both; run each query and compare the result with what the question actually asked for.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

members — MemberID, Name, Town, JoinedOn (6 rows)

loans — LoanID, MemberID, Instrument, Status, Weeks (10 rows)

1. Which instruments are out at the moment, and who has them? Show the member’s name and the instrument.

SELECT m.Name, l.Instrument FROM loans l JOIN members m ON l.MemberID = m.MemberID WHERE l.Status = 'out'

A join puts related rows from two tables side by side on a matching value. Notice that the name is stored once and borrowed by the query, which is precisely why correcting it in one place corrects every answer.

2. How many times has each instrument been loaned? Show the most borrowed first.

SELECT Instrument, COUNT(*) AS Loans FROM loans GROUP BY Instrument ORDER BY Loans DESC

Grouping turns a list of events into a description of them. The result has one row per instrument and none of the original loans, which is the clearest illustration that a summary is a different answer rather than a tidier one.

3. Which instruments have been borrowed more than once? Show the instrument and the number of loans, busiest first.

SELECT Instrument, COUNT(*) AS Loans FROM loans GROUP BY Instrument HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY Loans DESC

WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups. Putting the count condition in WHERE fails because at that stage nothing has been counted yet, and the distinction becomes intuitive once you read a query in execution order rather than in writing order.

4. How many loans has each town produced? Show the busiest town first.

SELECT m.Town, COUNT(*) AS Loans FROM loans l JOIN members m ON l.MemberID = m.MemberID GROUP BY m.Town ORDER BY Loans DESC

This answer exists in neither table. Nobody recorded a town against a loan, yet the question is answerable because the two facts were stored in a way that lets them be brought together on demand.

5. For loans that have already come back, how long did they run on average?

SELECT AVG(Weeks) AS AvgWeeks FROM loans WHERE Status = 'returned'

The filter decides the answer here as much as the function does: including loans that are still out would average an unfinished length against finished ones. An average is only as honest as the set of rows underneath it.

Neither of the last answers exists in any row: the count per town is assembled as you ask, from records never entered with towns in mind. Files answer what they were built for; a database answers questions nobody thought of.

What renting takes off your hands

The service models decide who installs and patches the database software.

  1. Infrastructure as a service — you get processing, storage and networking; the operating system, database software and backups are yours.
  2. Platform as a service — the provider supplies and updates the platform, database system included, so licensing and patching are not yours.
  3. Software as a service — you use a finished application, choose settings and own the records; nothing beneath is visible.

None takes away the design. Which records exist, how they relate and what must be unique are decisions about the organization. A rented platform holds whatever shape you give it, including a poor one.

Check yourself

Who is responsible for the data

Each question is about where responsibility sits rather than about syntax; read every explanation before moving on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical town archive moves its catalogue onto a rented platform, where the provider supplies and updates the database software. Which statement is accurate?

  • A. The archive no longer has to decide what counts as a catalogue record or which questions the catalogue must be able to answer, because a rented platform arrives with both of those already settled — A platform supplies a general-purpose place to keep records. It has no view about what an archive record ought to contain, and it will accept an incoherent design as readily as a good one.
  • B. The archive keeps paying the database licence but gives up control of how the catalogue is designed — This has the trade-off backwards. The platform model is defined by the licence and the platform maintenance moving to the provider, and design was never something the provider held.
  • C. The archive stops buying and patching the database software, and still decides which records exist, how they relate, what must be unique, and which questions the catalogue has to answer — correct. The licence, the patching and the underlying machines move to the provider; the meaning of the data does not move anywhere, because it was never a technical question in the first place.
  • D. A rented platform cannot host a catalogue, because a catalogue needs database software the archive installs on its own machines — Hosting a catalogue is ordinary platform work. Nothing about a catalogue requires locally installed software, which is why so many organizations run this kind of store on rented platforms.

2. A hypothetical youth theatre runs its booking system on the infrastructure service model. Who is responsible for the database software it depends on?

  • A. The theatre, because that model supplies processing, storage and networking, and everything from the operating system upward is the customer’s to install, licence and patch — correct. The chapter describes that model as providing only the basic capabilities of processing, storage and networking, which is also why it says the customer keeps the most control and keeps responsibility for managing software licences.
  • B. The provider, because supplying storage necessarily includes supplying the software that organizes what is stored — Storage in this sense means space and the machines that hold it. Organizing what goes into that space is exactly the work the customer takes on in exchange for the extra control.
  • C. Neither, because on that model the database runs as a shared service used by every customer on the same machines — That describes a shared service somebody else operates, which is a different model. Here the customer receives raw capacity and decides what runs on it.
  • D. The theatre for the software and the provider for the data held inside it, which is the division of responsibility that this service model was designed around and the reason it costs less than the alternative — The split is the other way round in one half and wrong in the other: the customer runs the software, and the data inside it is the customer’s responsibility on every one of the three models.

3. A hypothetical dental practice proposes recording far more detail about every appointment so that it can analyse patterns later. Which cost picture matches what the chapter says?

  • A. A single one-off cost, since the records are captured by staff who are already there and stored on machines the practice already owns — The capture is close to free and the keeping is not. Data recorded once has to be stored, backed up, moved and eventually archived for as long as the practice keeps it, which is a commitment rather than a purchase.
  • B. A rise in storage only, because processing and software costs are fixed regardless of how much data is kept — Storage is the visible cost and rarely the only one. Analysing a much larger set of records needs hardware that can work through it, which is why the chapter names the two together.
  • C. A rise in bandwidth only, because the extra detail has to travel between the practice and wherever it is stored — Bandwidth does grow with richer content, and the chapter makes that point about video. It is one strand of the story rather than the whole of it, and the practice would still be paying to keep and process everything it sent.
  • D. More storage space, more capable hardware to process the data, and database software to manage and analyse it — three running costs from one decision — correct. The chapter states it plainly: capturing more data requires ever more storage space, ever more powerful computing hardware, and database management systems to manage and analyse it. Deciding to record something is deciding to pay for it repeatedly.

The hand-off to SQLite

SQLite keeps a whole database in one ordinary file and runs inside the program using it, with no server to install and nothing hidden behind an administrator. The queries here are the same language; there you also decide what the tables are.

The container can be rented; the meaning cannot. Somebody still has to know what a record is, which is why tables belong in a module about machines.

Application supplement · 3–6

The internet as a business tool

Every part of this section has appeared already. What the chapter never does is set them side by side and ask what a company uses all of it for. The answer is three things, told apart by one decision a person takes.

Three jobs, one set of parts

A browser asking for a page behaves identically whether the reader is a shopper, a member of staff or a supplier’s dispatcher. The technology has no opinion about who is at the other end. What differs is who is authorized — a decision somebody takes before any system enforces it.

  • Selling to customers — general, public content anyone connected may read, which the chapter calls the internet.
  • Communicating with employees — specific, proprietary content restricted to authorized employees, which the chapter calls an intranet.
  • Working with business partners — communications between firms doing business together, restricted to authorized partners: an extranet.

Selling to customers: almost any business is an e-business

The chapter says almost any business today can be considered an e-business. That is stronger than it looks: not that almost any business sells online, but that it runs on its data being reachable.

A hypothetical veterinary practice publishing only its address, hours and a booking form has put its bookings on the internet. When that page fails on Monday morning, appointments are not made and money is not taken.

  • Answering while the customer is there — operational data belongs on fast disk, or flash where speed is crucial, because a late page loses the sale.
  • Surviving the busiest fortnight — consumer commerce spikes before December, and the capacity that felt generous in March decides how it goes.
  • Closing the distance — the further a user is from the server, the longer content takes; copies held in several locations remove it.
  • Being available at all — firms trading electronically strive for the highest availability, and five-nines leaves five minutes of downtime a year.

None of those is a marketing decision, and none can be taken after the campaign is booked. For a business selling online, the shopfront is the infrastructure.

Check yourself

Selling over the internet, and what it demands underneath

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for the options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A hypothetical veterinary practice takes no payments on its website and sells nothing there. Its owner says the practice is therefore not an e-business and does not need to think about availability. Which reading matches the chapter?

  • A. Almost any business can be considered an e-business, so the real question is what happens to the practice on a morning when its data are not reachable — correct. The chapter says that today almost any business can be considered an e-business, and that because data are the lifeblood of almost all organizations, reliably accessing those data is a key concern rather than an optional refinement.
  • B. The owner is right, because being an e-business means selling goods or services over the internet and the practice does neither — This reads e-business as a synonym for online retailing, which is narrower than the chapter’s claim. The practice’s bookings, records and opening information already depend on the same infrastructure a retailer’s orders depend on.
  • C. The practice becomes an e-business only once it accepts card payment on the site, since a completed transaction is what makes trading electronic — Payment is one thing a site can do, not the thing that makes a business dependent on the internet. A booking form that stops working costs the practice appointments long before any card is presented.
  • D. The distinction does not matter, because availability targets apply to organizations large enough to run a data center of their own — Availability is about whether the organization can reach and be reached, and the chapter attaches it to being data-intensive rather than to owning a facility. A small practice renting everything still loses the morning when the pages do not load.

2. A hypothetical ticket seller’s pages take several seconds to appear while a customer sits waiting, and the delay is in reading the records the page is built from. Which of the chapter’s storage decisions is at stake?

  • A. Archival storage, since these records are being kept for the long term and it is the archive the customer is really waiting on while the assistant apologizes for the delay — Archival data are long-term copies held for compliance and reporting, typically on tape, where data sit sequentially so access is slow and not quickly searchable. That is the wrong medium for anything a person is waiting on.
  • B. Backup storage, since the recovery copy is what would be read if the main records were slow to answer — Backup data are short-term copies for recovering from a disaster, and the chapter’s reason for keeping them on hard drives is quick recovery. They are not the copy a page is built from during normal trading.
  • C. Operational data belongs on fast disk-based storage where response time is of the essence, and on flash-based storage where access speed is of crucial importance — correct. The chapter puts operational data on disk-based media precisely because hard drives offer high access speeds where response time matters, and names an e-commerce site as its example, with flash used where speed is crucial.
  • D. None of these, because the delay a customer experiences is decided by bandwidth rather than by where the records are kept — Bandwidth is the capacity of the pathway, and widening it does not help when the time is being spent reading a record before anything is sent. The two delays have different causes and different remedies.

3. A hypothetical gift retailer’s site is slow for two separate reasons: everybody arrives at once in the fortnight before the holidays, and customers on another continent wait noticeably longer than customers at home. Which pairing matches the chapter’s account?

  • A. Both are capacity problems at heart, so one larger server at the retailer’s own site answers the seasonal slowness and the overseas delay together, and no second arrangement is needed — A larger server does nothing about distance. The overseas customer is waiting on transmission across a long path, and that wait is unchanged by how quickly the far end could have replied.
  • B. Both are distance problems, since a network carrying more traffic behaves like a longer one — Congestion and distance both add delay, but the chapter treats them separately: one is demand exceeding capacity in a fortnight, the other is the geographical gap between a user and the server holding the content.
  • C. The seasonal slowness is a bandwidth shortage and the overseas delay is a storage shortage — Neither label fits. The December problem is a fluctuation in demand rather than a fixed shortage, and the overseas delay is caused by the length of the path, not by where the records are stored.
  • D. The seasonal slowness is a demand fluctuation answered by capacity that can grow and shrink; the overseas delay is distance, answered by copies of the content held near those users — correct. The chapter treats the pre-holiday spike as a demand fluctuation, and treats distance as its own cause of latency answered by a network of servers in various geographical locations holding copies, the nearest one delivering the content.

Communicating with employees

The second audience is the organization’s own staff, served by the intranet: the same web technologies, secured with authentication, firewalls or both. What is worth adding is what each internal use replaced.

Disseminating corporate information replaces a notice kept in whichever copy each person saved. Training replaces scheduling everybody into a room. Project management replaces status reported upward and redistributed down. Collaboration replaces documents mailed between buildings. Self-service replaces a form completed by staff and keyed in by an office.

Only the last saves money you could point at. Nothing was automated: a step was deleted, because the person holding the information could record it directly.

An intranet reachable only from a desk fails a workforce increasingly elsewhere, so employees use a virtual private network to connect securely while travelling. The audience has not changed; only the road.

Working with partners: the second keystroke

The third audience is the companies the organization depends on. Not employees, so the intranet is shut; not the public, so the public site is useless. The answer is the extranet: a private part of the internet reachable by authorized partners after logging on.

Follow one hypothetical order through two companies that share nothing.

  1. The buyer records the order — a clerk enters quantities into the buyer’s system, creating an authoritative record, then emails a copy.
  2. The supplier records it again — somebody types the same quantities into another system, creating a second record that merely resembles the first.
  3. The buyer changes something — a quantity is revised, a second email goes out, and the supplier is a version behind, with nothing saying which counts.
  4. The goods arrive — the disagreement surfaces in the receiving bay, the most expensive place to find it, costing a credit note and sometimes a second lorry.

Nobody was careless. Step two manufactured the error, and exists only because two firms keep separate copies of one fact. The chapter’s name for removing it is a single point of data entry, from which data updates across disparate platforms without being reentered.

There is a version with the people removed. An interface lets one firm’s system use a service another provides by passing agreed values and receiving an answer. A shared area lets two firms read one record; an interface lets their systems do it unattended.

Every situation below is hypothetical. Sort each by the audience it really serves.

Sort

Which audience is this really serving?

Place each situation with the use it serves. Every organization below is a hypothetical practice situation, and each one states the conditions you need in order to decide.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Selling to customers — general, public content that anyone with an internet connection may read, with access public and not restricted

  • A hypothetical bakery publishes its product range, its opening hours and an order form that anybody who finds the site can use — General, public content readable by anyone with an internet connection, with access public and not restricted — the chapter’s own description of the internet, and the reason nothing goes here that the bakery would not tell a stranger.
  • A hypothetical bus operator publishes its timetable for any passenger to check, and the pages are copied to servers in several regions so they load quickly wherever the passenger is — Public content plus a content delivery network, which the chapter describes as the way to reduce the delay caused by geographical distance. The copies change how fast the public is served, not who is served.
  • A hypothetical museum lets a visitor reserve a timed entry from home at eleven at night, weeks before arriving — The museum sells nothing on the page beyond a place in a queue, and it is still trading electronically: almost any business can be considered an e-business, and the booking is taken from a member of the public with no account and no prior relationship.

Communicating with employees — specific, corporate and proprietary content, restricted to authorized employees or members, with access private and restricted

  • Staff at a hypothetical building society open a page from their own desks and enrol in this year’s health cover without sending a form to anybody — Employee self-service through a portal is one of the five internal uses the chapter names for an intranet, and the content is proprietary and restricted to authorized employees.
  • Shift supervisors at a hypothetical parcel depot read the week’s safety notices and finish a required training module from any depot in the country — Two of the chapter’s named intranet uses at once, disseminating corporate information and employee training, both restricted to the organization’s own staff wherever in the country they are working.
  • Site surveyors at a hypothetical engineering firm open the internal drawing archive from a hotel, through a secured tunnel, rather than from the office — A virtual private network changes where the employee is standing, not who the audience is. The chapter treats the tunnel as the way an intranet reaches a mobile workforce, and the content remains internal.

Working with partners — communications between two or more firms doing business together, restricted to authorized business partners

  • A hypothetical dairy cooperative gives each of its two haulage contractors a login to see tomorrow’s collection schedule and confirm the volumes lifted today — Two firms using the internet to do business together, reachable only by authorized business partners after logging on. The confirmation is also the single point of data entry that spares both sides from keying the same volume twice.
  • A hypothetical seed laboratory posts every test result it produces into an area that its two client growers can read the moment the result exists — Content whose focus is communication between business partners, private and restricted to authorized partners, and an example of the real-time visibility the chapter lists among the benefits of working this way.
  • A hypothetical grain merchant’s system asks a haulier’s system directly for a delivery slot and receives an answer, with nobody at either firm involved — This is the machine-to-machine version of the same partner relationship: a service consumer uses a provider’s service without knowing how it is produced, by passing agreed values. The browser and the clerk are gone; the audience is not.

Getting the audience wrong

The wrong answer here is almost never a technology. It is publishing to the wrong audience, and there are three familiar ways.

  • Internal material on the public site — done to avoid managing accounts, and it works until proprietary content is public and cannot be recalled.
  • Obscurity mistaken for restriction — an unindexed page is still reachable by anyone with the address, which is why authentication makes content private.
  • Partners handed employee access — the quickest way to show an outside firm one schedule grants it everything an employee can reach.

Work the four decisions below in order, reading every outcome, including those you rejected.

Decide

Four requests in one week

Work the four decisions in order, and after each one compare every outcome before moving on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

A hypothetical practice situation. You have taken over systems and communications at an invented regional food cooperative that sells produce boxes to the public, employs about forty people across three sites, and works with two haulage contractors. Four requests land in your first week. Each one looks like a technology question and is really a question about which audience is being served.

Decision 1. The membership secretary wants the annual report, the monthly member notices and the compulsory food-handling training module put on the public website, so that members can always find them and nobody has to manage accounts.

  • Put them behind authentication as an intranet for authorized members, and leave the public site to the catalogue. — the stronger call. Right. Same web technologies, different audience, different access rule: internal communications, specific and proprietary content, authorized users, private and restricted. Notice that you decided this by naming the reader, not by comparing products — which is what makes it a management decision rather than a technical one.
  • Publish them on the public site as asked, since nobody outside the cooperative would go looking for member notices. — The chapter treats authentication and firewalls, not the unlikelihood of being found, as what makes content private. Member notices and a training module are proprietary content, and once they are public they are readable by any competitor, any journalist and any search engine, permanently and without your knowing.
  • Publish them on the public site but leave them unlinked from the menu, so only members who were sent the address can reach them. — An unlinked page is exactly the third kind of content the chapter puts in the deep web: invisible to a search engine and reachable by anyone holding the address. It is one forwarded email away from being fully public, and nothing in the arrangement will tell you when that happens.
  • Issue every member an account on the extranet the cooperative already runs with its two haulage contractors. — It would work on the day, and it dissolves the boundary you will later be asked to audit. The chapter defines an extranet’s users as authorized business partners; putting several hundred members inside it gives them the partner content too, and leaves you unable to say who may see the collection schedules.

Decision 2. The public produce-box shop runs at a steady level for most of the year. In the fortnight before the December holidays orders run several times higher, and last year the site was slow enough that customers abandoned their baskets. The equipment currently sits in a room at the main site.

  • Move the public shop onto rented capacity that grows and shrinks with demand, and serve the pages and images from copies held near customers. — the stronger call. Right, and note that it is two answers to two different problems. Capacity that can grow and shrink answers the seasonal fluctuation the chapter describes for December electronic commerce; copies held in several geographical locations answer the delay caused by distance. Neither one fixes the other.
  • Buy a second server sized for the December fortnight and keep it in the room with the first. — This is the demand-fluctuation problem the chapter describes, met in the most expensive way available. Capacity bought in whole units leaves idle resources for most of the year, and what you have actually purchased, permanently, is a fortnight. It may be the only option if you must own the equipment, but it should be chosen knowingly.
  • Ask customers to place their holiday orders earlier in the season so the load is spread out. — This asks the customer to solve the cooperative’s capacity problem, and most of them will simply buy elsewhere in the fortnight when they were going to buy anyway. For a business selling over the internet the site is the shop, and telling shoppers to come at a quieter time is closing the door at the busiest hour.
  • Reduce the size of the product photographs so that each page is smaller. — It genuinely helps, and it is not enough. Smaller pages reduce the bytes each visitor pulls but not the number of visitors arriving at once, so the peak still exceeds what the room can serve. It is also a poor trade for a business whose product is food that people buy by looking at it.

Decision 3. The two haulage contractors currently receive collection schedules by email and retype them into their own systems. Twice this year a lorry arrived for a volume that had been revised after the email went out, and both times the cooperative and the contractor each produced a document proving they were right.

  • Give both contractors access to the schedule where it is maintained, and let them confirm the lifted volume in the same place. — the stronger call. Right. This is the chapter’s single point of data entry, from which data can be updated on disparate corporate computing platforms without being reentered. One record exists, so there is nothing left for the two firms to disagree about, and management gets real-time data on what was actually lifted rather than a reconciliation after the fact.
  • Send the schedule twice, once as an email and once as an attached spreadsheet, so each contractor can check one against the other. — Two copies do not settle a disagreement; they create a third version and a new question about which one is authoritative. The chapter’s benefit is the removal of the reentry, not better documentation of it, and every extra copy is another thing that can be a version behind.
  • Publish the collection schedule on the public site so the contractors can always see the current version. — It does make the schedule current, and it also tells every competitor what this cooperative moves, from where, and on which days. The content’s focus is communication between business partners, and the chapter makes that category private and restricted for exactly this reason.
  • Require both contractors to telephone the depot each morning to confirm the day’s volumes before loading. — A call is simply a third place for the number to be transcribed, and it adds a person to a process that is failing because of people copying figures. It also produces nothing management can track or analyze, since the confirmation exists only in somebody’s memory of the conversation.

Decision 4. Six delivery drivers and two field buyers are almost never at a desk. They need the week’s notices, the compulsory training module, and a way to file expense claims from wherever they happen to be.

  • Let them reach the same internal pages the office staff use, over a secured tunnel from whatever device they carry. — the stronger call. Right. Increases in employee mobility are the chapter’s own reason for virtual private networks: staff connect securely to the intranet while travelling or working away from the office. The audience did not change, so the arrangement should not either — only the road into it is different.
  • Email the notices out weekly and have the drivers post paper expense forms back to the office. — This is precisely the arrangement the intranet replaced. Notices sit in eight separate mailboxes with no way to tell who is reading a superseded one, and every posted form is a keystroke for somebody in an office — the work that employee self-service was named for removing.
  • Publish the notices and the training module on the public site and accept expense claims by email, since these people are outside the building anyway. — Being outside the building is a location, not an audience. The chapter separates these arrangements by who is authorized, and a driver in a lay-by is still an employee, so putting internal material in front of the general public to reach eight of them is a large exposure for a small convenience.
  • Give each of them a laptop with a copy of the internal pages stored on it, so no connection is needed at all. — A copy taken on Monday is wrong by Tuesday. The chapter’s observation that very little information in business is static is the whole reason internal communication moved onto web technologies in the first place, and eight stored copies recreate exactly the problem one current copy was there to solve.

One set of web technologies, three audiences, separated by who is authorized — and the separation is drawn by a manager naming the reader, not by a product being purchased.

One last pass over the three uses before the module closes.

Check yourself

Three uses, one technology

Four options, one best answer; the explanations are where the distinctions live, so read all four.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. According to the chapter, what actually separates the internet, an intranet and an extranet from one another?

  • A. The software and networking technologies each is built from, since the three arrangements use different products — The chapter says the opposite: an intranet uses the same software, hardware and networking technologies as a publicly accessible website. Nothing in the comparison table mentions a product at all.
  • B. Whether the traffic crosses the public internet, since intranet traffic stays inside the organization and extranet traffic does not — This is nearly true and still unreliable. The simplest form of an intranet does stay within organizational boundaries, but most companies let employees reach the intranet over a tunnel across the public internet, so the route cannot be the divider.
  • C. Who is authorized to see the content, since the three carry different content for different audiences under different access rules — correct. The chapter’s table separates the three by focus, type of content, users and access: public content for anyone with a connection, corporate and proprietary content for authorized employees, and partner communications for authorized business partners.
  • D. Which department owns the pages, since internal pages belong with human resources and partner pages belong with purchasing — Ownership inside the organization is a question of who maintains the pages, not of who may read them. Two arrangements owned by the same department can still face entirely different audiences.

2. A hypothetical cannery gives its two ingredient suppliers a shared area in which to confirm each shipment as it leaves. Its operations manager notices she no longer waits for a monthly summary to know what is in transit. Which of the chapter’s stated benefits is she describing?

  • A. Central management of documents, which reduces the number of versions in circulation and the amount of out-of-date information stored around the organization — That benefit is about which copy of a document is the current one. It is real and it is not what changed here: the manager’s complaint was about when she learned something, not about which version she was reading.
  • B. Management can obtain real-time data with which to track and analyze business activities — correct. The chapter lists exactly this among the benefits of working with partners this way, and it follows from the transactions arriving as they happen rather than being gathered up and reported afterwards.
  • C. Automating business transactions, which reduces processing costs and cycle times — Automation lowers what each transaction costs and how long it takes to complete. That is a benefit of the same arrangement, but the manager described visibility of activity rather than cheaper or faster processing.
  • D. The internet can be used as a relatively secure medium over which to do business with another firm — Security is the chapter’s judgment that the public internet can carry this traffic acceptably, which is a precondition for the arrangement existing at all rather than the improvement the manager noticed.

3. A hypothetical wholesaler’s system asks a courier’s system for a delivery slot and receives one back, with nobody at either firm involved. How is this best described, and how does it relate to the shared partner area the two firms already use?

  • A. It is a content delivery arrangement, since the courier is supplying content to the wholesaler across a distance — A content delivery network holds copies of a site closer to its users to reduce the delay caused by distance. Nothing here is about distance, and the courier is answering a question rather than serving a stored page.
  • B. It is a form of intranet, because the two systems are communicating privately rather than publicly — An intranet serves an organization’s own authorized employees. These are two separate firms, which is what makes the relationship a partner arrangement no matter how private the exchange is.
  • C.
