It replaces the shared partner area entirely, since once two machines exchange the figures directly there is nothing left for a person to log in and read, and the web area can be switched off — The two do different jobs. A shared area lets people at both firms read and confirm records; an interface lets their systems exchange a specific answer unattended, and most partnerships end up using both.
  • D. It is an interface between applications: one program uses another’s service by passing agreed values, without knowing how the result is produced — correct. The chapter defines an interface between applications as letting a service consumer use a service provider’s service without having to know how the underlying service is created, by passing pre-specified values and receiving the requested service back.

Reference

Chapter vocabulary

Every term the chapter defines, in one place, written so it makes sense on its own with an example beside it. Search by word, or filter by the objective the term belongs to. This chapter has more vocabulary than the two before it, and a good deal of the difficulty is pairs of terms that sound almost the same and mean genuinely different things — the deep web and the dark web, an intranet and an extranet, grid computing and cloud computing, a client and a server. Use this while you read rather than after.

3.3AI infrastructure
The hardware and software systems used to support artificial intelligence work. It has special requirements: specialized processors rather than ordinary ones, storage that is both larger and faster than usual, and particular machine learning libraries and frameworks for the people building the models.For example: A company that wants to train its own model discovers it cannot simply run it on the servers it already owns, and has to budget for a different class of machine entirely.
3.2application programming interface (API)
An arrangement that lets one piece of software use a service provided by another without knowing how that service works inside. The consumer passes agreed-on values across and gets a result back, which is why software can be assembled out of parts built by different companies.For example: A ride-hailing app sends a pickup point and a destination to a mapping service and receives the best route, without its developers ever having written a map.
3.2archival data
Long-term copies of organizational data, kept mainly for compliance and reporting rather than for daily use. Because it is rarely read, it can live on slow, cheap, removable media, and it needs a life span measured in years rather than days.For example: Internal email from several years ago that nobody expects to open, but that the organization must be able to produce if it is ever asked to.
3.2assembly language
A very low-level programming language that lets a computer operate quickly and efficiently, and the language operating systems are often written in. Part of an operating system’s job is to insulate everyone else from it.For example: Dragging a file from a flash drive to a hard drive is one gesture for you and a long sequence of low-level instructions underneath, which you never have to see.
3.2backup data
Short-term copies of organizational data, made so the organization can recover from a failure or disaster. Backups are frequently overwritten by newer ones, so their value is in being recent and quick to restore rather than in lasting.For example: Last night’s copy of the order system, held on fast storage so that if this morning’s server fails the business is running again in minutes rather than days.
3.2bandwidth
The transmission capacity of a computer or communications channel, measured in bits per second or multiples of it. It is how much data can reliably be carried in one second, and it is what decides whether a file takes eight seconds or a day and a half to arrive.For example: The same video downloads in seconds over a fiber connection and takes hours over an old telephone modem, because only the capacity of the path changed.
3.2bit
The smallest unit of data used by computers. Human communication is made of words; computer communication is made of bits, and everything sent over a network — a document, a song, a film — is bits, differing only in how many of them there are.For example: A page of text runs to roughly fourteen thousand bytes while a print-quality photograph can be more than two hundred million, which is why one arrives instantly and the other does not.
3.4broad network access
One of the five characteristics of cloud computing: because the services are reached over the internet, they are available from almost anywhere and from almost any web-enabled device. It is what lets a manager act on something without going back to an office.For example: Approving an urgent order from a phone in an airport, using the same system that sits on the desktop back at work.
3.2campus area network
A wide area network that spans several buildings belonging to one organization. It is a middle case between a network inside a single building and one that crosses a city or the world.For example: A hospital group whose clinic, laboratory and administration buildings sit on one site and share one network across all three.
3.4capital expenditure and operational expenditure
Two ways of paying for the same computing. A capital expenditure is money spent up front to own equipment; an operational expenditure is money spent continuously to use a service. Cloud computing converts one into the other, which changes the budget it comes out of and who has to approve it.For example: Buying servers is a large purchase in one year; renting the same capacity is a monthly bill that rises and falls with how much the business actually used.
3.2cascading style sheets (CSS)
The standard used to specify the formatting and layout of the elements on a web page. It separates how a page looks from what the page says, so the wording and the appearance can be changed independently.For example: Changing one style rule makes every heading on a thousand-page site larger, without anyone editing a thousand pages.
3.2central processing unit (CPU)
The general-purpose processor that performs a computer’s calculations. It is built to handle instructions one after another very quickly, which suits ordinary software where each step depends on the result of the last one.For example: Recalculating a spreadsheet, where each formula may need the answer from the formula above it before it can run.
3.2client
Any computer or software application on a network that uses the services a server provides. Clients only request; they do not serve. A client usually has one user, whereas many users share the server it talks to.For example: The mail program on a laptop asks a mail server for new messages; it never answers requests from anyone else.
3.2client-server network
A network in which servers and clients have defined roles, some machines providing services and others only requesting them. It is the normal business arrangement, and nearly everyone at work is using one whether they know it or not.For example: Every desk in an office opening files kept on a shared server rather than on each other’s machines.
3.4cloud computing
A model for enabling convenient, on-demand access over a network to a shared pool of configurable computing resources — networks, servers, storage, applications and services — that can be provisioned and released quickly with minimal management effort or interaction with the provider. In plainer words: computing rented by the hour from somebody else’s building.For example: A company that needs two hundred servers for a week gets them the same afternoon with a payment card and a web page, and stops paying when it stops using them.
3.2collocation facility
A data center managed by a third party that rents space to several organizational customers. The tenant still owns and manages its own servers; what it stops paying for is the building, the power, the cooling and the physical security.For example: A regional firm that puts its own machines in a rented, professionally run room instead of building a server room and a generator of its own.
3.2computer networking
The sharing of data or services between machines. It needs three things and no fewer: a sender and a receiver with something to share, a pathway between them, and rules both sides follow.For example: Two people can only have a conversation if there is something to say, a room to say it in, and a language they both speak; a network is the same three requirements in equipment.
3.3consumerization of IT
The trend in which the devices people choose for themselves arrive at work and have to be integrated into the organization’s infrastructure. It shifts part of the equipment decision away from the technology department and toward the individual.For example: Employees expecting to read work email on their own phones, which the organization must then decide how to secure and support.
3.4content delivery network
A network of servers in different geographical locations that store copies of the same content, so a request is answered by the copy nearest the user. It reduces the delay caused by distance, saves bandwidth, and is invisible to the person browsing.For example: A video that plays instantly for viewers on three continents because each of them is actually being served from a machine a few hundred miles away.
3.2cyber-physical system
A system that integrates computing with physical processes, coordinating software, sensors and mechanical components closely enough to monitor and control something in the real world with a high degree of autonomy. The consequences of a fault are physical, which is what makes securing them different.For example: A factory where sensors, controllers and machines run most of the production line between them and reorganize the work without a person intervening.
3.2dark web
Those areas of the web used for various criminal purposes, typically reachable only with specialized browsers that anonymize the user and hide their traces. It is deliberately hidden, and it is not the same thing as the deep web.For example: A marketplace trading stolen payment card numbers, which no ordinary browser or search engine will take you to.
3.2database
An organized collection of related data held so that it can be stored and retrieved reliably. The chapter treats databases as the thing hardware exists to run and storage exists to hold, which is why a storage decision is really a decision about how well questions can be answered later.For example: A shop’s record of every product, every supplier and every sale, kept once so that a price change is made in one place rather than in four spreadsheets.
3.3database management system
The software that stores data, keeps it consistent, and answers questions about it. The chapter counts it as a third cost of capturing more data, alongside the storage space and the processing power, because somebody has to license, configure and run it.For example: Two clerks record a sale at the same moment and the totals still agree afterwards, which is the software doing work nobody sees.
3.2data center
Dedicated space set aside for an organization’s infrastructure, ranging from a single server room to a building the size of a warehouse. Keeping the equipment in one place makes it easier to manage, repair, upgrade, power, cool and secure.For example: A parcel carrier’s facilities that can run for days on their own generated power, with cooling capacity comparable to that of a whole neighbourhood of houses.
3.2digital density
The rising proportion of an organization’s activity that exists as data and is carried out through connected devices. The chapter names it as the reason a well-functioning infrastructure has become essential rather than merely useful.For example: A delivery that once left only a signed paper docket now leaves a scan at every handover, a location trace and a photograph, so the same journey produces a hundred times the record it used to.
3.2deep web
Those parts of the web that conventional search engines cannot index: pages behind a login, pages generated from a database when somebody asks for them, and pages nothing links to. Most of the web is like this, and none of it is necessarily sinister.For example: Your own course pages, your bank statements and an online store’s product listings are all invisible to a search engine, for three different reasons.
3.2desktop virtualization
Providing workers with a desktop environment that actually runs on a server rather than on the machine in front of them. It reduces the cost of licensing and maintaining software and helps with strict privacy and data protection duties, because the data never leaves the data center.For example: A hospital where every screen shows the same working environment, and nothing is stored on the terminal itself if it is stolen.
3.2device driver
Software that allows a computer to communicate with a particular piece of hardware. It is the translation layer between one general operating system and the specific behaviour of one make and model of device.For example: Plugging in an unfamiliar printer and having the computer fetch the small piece of software that teaches it how to talk to that printer.
3.2domain name
The part of a web address that helps a person recognize the company or individual it belongs to. Names exist because the numeric addresses machines actually use are hard to remember and can change.For example: Seeing a familiar name in the address bar tells you whose server you have reached, which a string of numbers would not.
3.2e-business
A business whose ordinary operations depend on internet technology rather than merely using it at the edges. The chapter’s position is that almost any business today can be considered one, which is what makes infrastructure everyone’s problem rather than the technology department’s.For example: A family bakery that takes orders on a website, buys flour through a supplier portal and rosters staff in a shared calendar is running on the internet even though nobody there would call it a technology company.
3.4edge computing
What content delivery networks grew into: moving not only stored data but also the processing away from one central location out to the edges of the network, close to where the data is produced. The point is to cut the delay, and secondarily to cut traffic and cost.For example: A monitoring device that decides for itself that a reading is dangerous, instead of sending every reading across the country and waiting for an answer.
3.2embedded system
A computer designed to perform one specific set of tasks well, built into something that is not thought of as a computer. It has no general-purpose life; it does the one job.For example: The computer that manages a car engine, a traffic light or a media player, which nobody ever installs software on.
3.2extranet
A private part of the internet, cordoned off from ordinary users, that lets two or more firms do business together. The content is on the web, but only authorized partners can reach it after logging in, and it usually travels through a secured tunnel because the path itself is public.For example: A supplier logging in to a manufacturer’s system to see current orders, confirm shipments and update prices without anyone rekeying the data.
3.2field-programmable gate array (FPGA)
A processor whose circuitry can be reconfigured after it is built, offering customizable hardware acceleration. It sits between a general-purpose processor and a chip designed for a single task.For example: A team that needs one unusual calculation run very fast reshapes the hardware around that calculation instead of buying a chip that will never exist.
3.2file
A block of data that stores specific content, such as a document, an image or a spreadsheet. It is the unit people name, move, share and delete, and it is the reason ordinary users never have to think about where anything physically sits.For example: The report you saved yesterday, which you can find by its name without knowing anything about the disk it is on.
3.2five-nines availability
Availability of 99.999 percent, which works out at just over five minutes of downtime in a year. It is the target data-intensive organizations aim for, and reaching it constrains everything from component design to the choice of site.For example: A payment system that is expected to be unavailable for less time in a whole year than an average lunch break.
3.2folder
A grouping of related files, shown as a folder in a graphical interface and called a directory underneath. Folders nest inside folders, which is how a large amount of digital content stays findable.For example: Keeping coursework in one folder, then a folder per term inside it, then a folder per course inside that.
3.2frameworks and libraries
Collections of prewritten code that developers assemble rather than write. They shorten development time, help one program run on several platforms, and supply the building blocks for specialized work such as machine learning.For example: A small team shipping a working application in weeks because most of what it does was already written by somebody else and is being reused.
3.3generation of computing
Each fundamental change in the way computing technologies work. The usual account runs from vacuum tubes through transistors and integrated circuits to low-cost multimedia machines, widespread internet access, ubiquitous mobile connectivity, and now artificial intelligence and quantum computing.For example: The move from a room-sized machine that a few specialists operated to a phone in everyone’s pocket is several such changes stacked on top of one another.
3.2graphical user interface (GUI)
An interface that lets you instruct a computer by selecting or manipulating pictures, icons and menus rather than by typing commands. It is the reason using a computer no longer requires learning its language first.For example: Dragging a file onto a disk icon instead of typing a copy instruction with the exact path of both places.
3.2graphics processing unit (GPU)
A processor optimized for doing the same operation on very many pieces of data at once, using thousands of small cores. It was built for rendering images, where every pixel can be worked out independently, and turned out to suit machine learning for the same reason.For example: Training a model, where enormous numbers of similar calculations have no need to wait for one another and can all run side by side.
3.4green computing
Using computing resources more efficiently to reduce environmental impact, and using information systems to reduce environmental impact elsewhere. The chapter’s tactics are consolidating underused machines, shifting work to shared providers, managing power on idle desktops, and printing less.For example: Replacing a room of servers that each ran at a fraction of capacity with a few machines doing the same work, and paying less for power and cooling as a result.
3.4grid computing
Combining the computing power of many smaller, independent, networked computers into one system in order to solve a problem that previously needed a supercomputer. Like cloud computing it uses distributed resources, but unlike cloud computing those resources are all applied to a single large problem.For example: A simulation broken into thousands of small pieces, each finished by an ordinary desktop machine somewhere and sent back to be reassembled.
3.2hardware
The physical machines that run the applications and databases an organization needs in order to process transactions and analyze business data. Because organizations perform many different kinds of activity, they need several different kinds of computer to support them.For example: The register at the front of a shop, the server in the back room and the phone in the manager’s pocket are all hardware doing three different jobs.
3.2host name
The part of a web address naming the particular server, or group of servers, that will answer the request. The prefix www usually means the default site, and larger organizations use other host names for their separate services.For example: One organization’s mail service, map service and document storage each answer on a different host name in front of the same domain.
3.2HTML tag
A code set apart with angle brackets that tells a browser how part of a document should be presented, or what that part means. Most tags come in pairs, one to start an element and one to end it.For example: A pair of tags around a phrase can make it bold, mark it as a heading, or turn it into a link to another document.
3.2HTML5
The chapter’s name for the current version of the web’s markup language, which added ways of structuring a page and of presenting modern multimedia without extra software. Treat it as a label for the modern language rather than as a version number still being counted up, because the markup is now revised continuously rather than released in numbered editions.For example: Video that plays in the browser itself, with no separate plug-in to install, because the page can simply say that this is a video.
3.2HTTPS
The secure version of the web’s transfer protocol, now used routinely for anything sensitive because data travelling between a server and a browser can otherwise be intercepted and read. The padlock in the address bar is the browser reporting that it is in use.For example: Entering a card number on a page without the padlock means the number crosses several unknown networks in a form anyone along the way could read.
3.4hybrid cloud
An arrangement in which an organization keeps some applications and data in-house and moves others to a public cloud. The chapter presents it as what organizations usually settle on, because no single provider meets every need and some data is not worth moving.For example: A firm running its public website on rented capacity while its patient records stay on machines it owns and controls.
3.2hyperlink
A reference from one document to another, which the reader can follow. Links are what turn a collection of separate pages into a web rather than a library of unconnected documents.For example: Clicking a word in an article and arriving at the source it was quoting, on a completely different organization’s server.
3.2hypertext
The key feature of the web: documents that contain links to other documents, so a reader can move between them in any order rather than front to back. Everything else about the web is built on top of this one idea.For example: Reading three paragraphs of one page, following a link, and finishing on a page written by somebody who has never heard of the first author.
3.2Hypertext Markup Language (HTML)
The standard method of specifying the structure and content of web pages. It is a text-based format that uses codes called tags to tell the browser what each part of the document is and how it should be presented.For example: Choosing to view the source of any page shows the same words you were reading, wrapped in codes that gave them their headings, links and emphasis.
3.2Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
The protocol web servers use to process requests for pages. It is the agreed set of rules by which a browser asks for a document and a server answers, and it is the reason a browser made by one company can read a page served by another.For example: Typing an address and pressing return is a request in this protocol, whether the server at the other end runs the same software as your machine or not.
3.4infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
The cloud service model in which only the basic capabilities of processing, storage and networking are provided. The customer has the most control and the most responsibility: it still chooses the operating system, manages its software licences, and bears relatively high setup costs.For example: A streaming company renting raw computing capacity to convert films into different formats and to run its own website on top of it.
3.2information systems infrastructure
The hardware, system software, storage, networking and data centers an organization needs in order to operate fully and to meet its goals. It is the foundation everything else in the organization is built on, and the chapter’s point is that it creates value by enabling efficiency, effectiveness and increasingly agility.For example: Nobody buys a bank because of its servers, and every service the bank sells stops the moment those servers do.
3.2input device
Hardware that supplies data to a computer. Keyboards, mice, touch screens and cameras are the familiar ones, and sensors have widened the category enormously.For example: A scanner at a receiving dock, which is doing nothing more than getting a number into a system without anybody typing it.
3.2internet
A large worldwide collection of networks that use a common protocol to communicate with one another. It is not one network but an agreement that lets many separately owned networks behave as though they were one.For example: A message from a home connection to an office server crosses several companies’ equipment on the way, and nobody involved had to arrange it in advance.
3.2Internet of Things (IoT)
A vast network of interconnected physical devices that collect and share data, often producing very large amounts of information that can be gathered and analyzed centrally. It extends the reach of information systems to objects that were never previously connected to anything.For example: Refrigerated containers reporting their temperature continuously across a supply chain, so a spoiled shipment is known about before it is opened.
3.2internetworking
Connecting host computers and their networks together to form larger networks. The word internet is a contraction of it, and it describes exactly what the internet does.For example: A company network, a university network and a home network all reaching each other without any of them merging into a single owner’s system.
3.2intranet
An internal site that looks and behaves like a public website and uses the same technologies, but uses authentication or firewalls so that only authorized employees can see it. In its simplest form the traffic never leaves the organization at all.For example: The internal pages where staff read announcements, take required training and change their own benefit elections without contacting anyone.
3.2IP address
The address of a computer or device that enables a network to route messages to the right destination. The older form is four numbers between 0 and 255 separated by dots; the newer, much larger form exists because the world ran short of the older kind.For example: Every device on a home network has one, which is how the router knows which machine asked for the page that just came back.
3.3lean startup methodology
An approach built on rapid cycles of devising a solution, building the smallest version of it that can be tested, and finding out quickly whether it has the effect it was supposed to have. It matters for infrastructure because it means committing to equipment before the answer is known makes no sense.For example: Putting a rough version of a new service in front of real customers for a month before deciding whether it deserves a permanent system.
3.2local area network (LAN)
A network for sharing data, applications and other resources between several users, typically within one building. It is the ordinary office or home network, and its capacity is usually far higher than the connection leaving the building.For example: Everyone in an office printing to the same printer and opening the same shared drive, all without anything crossing the internet.
3.2mainframe
A large computer used as the main central computing system of a major organization, optimized for high availability, heavy use and security. It is the machine of choice for mission-critical work such as processing very large volumes of transactions.For example: A bank whose account balances all live on one heavily protected system that thousands of tellers and cash machines use at the same time.
3.4measured service
One of the five characteristics of cloud computing: the provider monitors usage and the customer pays only for what it uses. Fixed costs become variable costs that are easy to track — and easy to run up if nobody is tracking them.For example: A bill that is small in a quiet month, large in a busy one, and catastrophic in a month when somebody else was using your account.
3.2metropolitan area network
A wide area network covering the area of a city. It is larger than a network in one building or on one site, and smaller than a network spanning a country or the world.For example: A city transit authority connecting stations, depots and its control room across the whole urban area.
3.4microservices
The small building blocks that packaged business capabilities are made of on a technical level. Each does one narrow job and communicates with the others across defined interfaces, so one can be replaced without rebuilding the rest.For example: Changing how a company calculates delivery charges without touching the part of the system that takes payment.
3.3minimum viable product (MVP)
The smallest version of a solution that can be put in front of real users to find out whether it has the desired effect. It exists to produce an answer cheaply, not to be the finished thing.For example: A single page and a form, launched to see whether anybody signs up, before a system is built behind it.
3.2mobile device
Tablets and smartphones, which have become part of an organization’s information systems infrastructure rather than a personal convenience beside it. They have one user, travel everywhere, and are increasingly where work is actually done.For example: A field technician who receives the day’s jobs, records what was done and takes payment on the same handheld device.
3.4modular architecture
Building software by choosing individual blocks best suited to a particular need and connecting them through interfaces, rather than writing one large program that contains everything. It buys flexibility at the cost of having to plan, select and orchestrate the pieces.For example: Assembling a service out of separate components for orders, inventory, customers and payments, each of which can be swapped later.
3.4monolithic application
An application built as a single unit that includes all the features it needs, with the whole thing in one code base. That makes it relatively easy to develop, test and deploy, and correspondingly hard to change one part of without disturbing the rest.For example: A long-serving system where adding one field to a form means retesting and redeploying the entire program.
3.3Moore’s law
The prediction, made in 1965 by one of Intel’s cofounders, that the number of transistors on a chip would keep doubling at regular intervals. It is an observation and an industry roadmap rather than a law of nature, and its pace has slowed, with recent gains coming increasingly from adding more cores that work in parallel.For example: The first processors held a few thousand transistors and current ones hold billions, which is why a phone outperforms the machines that once filled a room.
3.2neuromorphic chip
A processor whose design is inspired by the architecture of the brain, aiming to improve energy efficiency and speed for artificial intelligence work. It is one of several attempts to escape the power cost of doing this work on general-purpose hardware.For example: Research hardware that tries to do recognition tasks at a small fraction of the electricity a conventional processor would need.
3.4on-demand self-service
One of the five characteristics of cloud computing: a customer can obtain resources as needed, without lengthy negotiation and in many cases without speaking to anyone at the provider at all. It is what makes an experiment possible this afternoon rather than next quarter.For example: Setting up new servers through a web control panel with a payment card, and having them running before the meeting that requested them has ended.
3.2operating system
The most prominent kind of system software. It coordinates the interaction between hardware components, attached devices, application software and users, and it provides a common layer so that programs can be written for the operating system rather than for every individual model of machine.For example: The reason a word processor ships in one version for one operating system rather than a separate version for every laptop ever made.
3.2operational data
Data used to manage business processes as they happen, such as processing transactions, or to analyze the business. It needs to be current and fast to reach, which is why it lives on the quickest storage an organization has.For example: The stock level a shopping site checks the instant you add something to a basket, which would be worthless if it took a minute to read.
3.2output device
Hardware that presents results to a person. Monitors, printers and speakers are the familiar examples, and the category matters because a system nobody can read the results of has not finished its job.For example: A picking list printed in a warehouse, which is where the computer’s decision finally becomes something a person can act on.
3.4packaged business capability (PBC)
A building block designed to perform one well-specified business function, such as processing payments or managing orders. Different vendors offer competing blocks for the same function, so an organization can choose the one that best fits and connect it to the others.For example: Using a specialist payments component inside your own ordering system instead of writing payment handling yourself.
3.2packet
One of the small chunks a request or a file is broken into for transmission. Breaking data up allows it to be routed and moved efficiently, and the pieces are reassembled at the far end before anyone sees them.For example: A photograph you send arrives as thousands of fragments that may take different paths and are put back in order at the other end.
3.2peer
Any computer that may both request and provide services, rather than being only a client or only a server. Peer arrangements are common in small offices and homes, where no machine is dedicated to serving the others.For example: Two laptops sharing a folder directly with each other, with neither of them being the office server.
3.2peer-to-peer network (P2P)
A network that lets any computer or device on it both provide and request services. It needs no dedicated server, which makes it cheap and simple, and correspondingly harder to control centrally.For example: A household where any machine can reach the shared printer and the shared drive without a server sitting between them.
3.2peripheral
A device attached to a computer, such as a printer, whose interaction with everything else is coordinated by the operating system. From the software’s point of view a peripheral is something the operating system knows how to reach.For example: Any application can print, because the operating system rather than each program deals with the printer.
3.2personal area network (PAN)
Wireless communication between devices over a very short range, under about ten meters, using technologies such as Bluetooth. It is the smallest of the network types and the one most people use without noticing.For example: Headphones connected to a phone, or a laptop connected to a wireless keyboard on the same desk.
3.2personal computer
A computer used for personal computing and small business computing, serving one user at a time. It is the reference point against which the other classes of computer are usually described.For example: The machine on an office desk, which does one person’s work and would be overwhelmed if a thousand people asked it questions at once.
3.3planned obsolescence
Designing a product to last only for a certain life span. In hardware it appears as components that cannot be serviced, so the device is replaced when one fails; in software it appears as older versions that cannot open newer files, or support that is simply withdrawn.For example: A vendor announcing an end-of-support date, which turns a working fleet of machines into an upgrade decision whether the organization wanted one or not.
3.4platform as a service (PaaS)
The cloud service model in which the provider supplies the computing platform — operating system, web server, database management system and development tools — and the customer runs its own applications on it. The customer controls the application and little else, and stops buying platform licences.For example: A team deploying software it wrote onto a rented platform, without anyone on that team ever installing or patching a database engine.
3.4private cloud
A cloud internal to one organization, which still provides self-service access to pooled resources on a pay-for-use basis but keeps everything inside the organization’s own control. It does not remove the work of running an infrastructure; it buys customizability, control and privacy instead.For example: A large firm letting its own departments provision servers from a shared internal pool in minutes, rather than from an outside provider.
3.2programmable logic controller (PLC)
A specialized computing device used to automate machines and processes, from a factory line to a ski lift. It is built to run one control task reliably for years in conditions no office machine would survive.For example: The device that decides when a conveyor starts and stops, which has no screen, no keyboard and no user.
3.2protocol
A definition of the procedures computers follow when they transmit and receive data. It is the agreed language of a network, and without it a message can arrive perfectly and still mean nothing to the receiver.For example: An email that reaches you in a language you cannot read has travelled the whole way successfully and still failed to communicate.
3.4public cloud
Cloud services that any interested party can use on a pay-per-use basis. It suits work that needs to scale rapidly, and organizations that do not have the capital or the people to build capacity of their own.For example: A new company launching a service worldwide on rented capacity, having bought no equipment at all.
3.2QR code
A two-dimensional bar code with a high storage capacity, usually holding a web address so that scanning it with a camera opens a page. It can also trigger an action, such as starting a call, sending a message, or making a payment.For example: A code on a table in a restaurant that opens the menu on your phone, with no address to type and no application to install.
3.2radio frequency identification (RFID)
A technology that uses electromagnetic fields to transmit data between a reader and a small tag attached to an object. Unlike a bar code it does not need line of sight or hand scanning, can hold more data, and can be read at a distance.For example: A pallet passing through a doorway and being counted automatically, without anyone pointing a scanner at each carton.
3.4rapid elasticity
One of the five characteristics of cloud computing: resources can be scaled up or down almost instantly, often automatically, in step with demand. Equipment ordinarily takes weeks to arrive and days to configure, which is why owning means guessing in advance.For example: A retailer whose capacity grows through a holiday rush and shrinks again in January, without a single purchase order.
3.4resource pooling
One of the five characteristics of cloud computing: the provider manages distributed resources that are assigned dynamically to many customers, so a customer rents capacity without knowing which machine or which building it came from. Providers often do allow a region to be specified.For example: A European company insisting its storage stay on servers in Europe, which is a data protection decision rather than a technical one.
3.2RFID tag
The small transponder attached to an object so it can be identified by a reader. Passive tags cost a few cents and are read from a few feet away; active tags contain a battery, cost several dollars, and can be read from hundreds of feet.For example: A tag under an animal’s skin carrying an owner’s details, and a tag on a shipping container carrying a manufacturing history, are the same technology at two sizes.
3.2root directory
The top of a file hierarchy, typically the drive itself, from which every subdirectory branches out. It is the reason a location can be described as a path from a known starting point.For example: Following a chain of folders from the drive down to one document is walking the tree from the root to a leaf.
3.4scalability
The ability to adapt to increases or decreases in demand for processing or data storage. It is one of the main promises of cloud computing, and not every provider can meet every organization’s idea of it, so it is something to test rather than assume.For example: A ticket site that stays up when a popular event goes on sale, because capacity grew in the minutes when it was needed.
3.2sensor
An input technology that collects data about the physical environment — temperature, pressure, vibration, proximity — and supplies it in real time. Sensors are what let information systems observe the world rather than only record what people type.For example: A vibration sensor on a motor that reports a change in behaviour days before the motor fails.
3.2server
Any computer on a network that makes files, printing, communications and other services available to other users of the network. Servers are optimized for many simultaneous users, so they carry more processing power, memory, storage and network capacity than a single-user machine.For example: One machine answering thousands of visitors at once, some of them getting the identical page and others getting a page assembled for them individually.
3.4serverless computing
A newer platform arrangement that frees the customer from setting up machines at all: small, specific functions are run by the provider on demand, scaled automatically, and billed by the time they actually run. The servers still exist; the customer just never meets them.For example: A function that resizes an uploaded photograph, which costs nothing on a day when nobody uploads anything.
3.4service-level agreement (SLA)
A contract specifying the level of service to be provided in terms of performance, warranties and disaster recovery. It does not guarantee that resources will be available; it promises service levels and provides refunds or discounts when they are missed, which makes it mainly a way of settling disputes.For example: A refund covering the fee for the hours a service was down, which does not cover the orders the business lost while it was down.
3.4software as a service (SaaS)
The cloud service model in which the customer uses only the application, with no knowledge of or control over the infrastructure beneath it and usually limited ability to configure it. It is the easiest model to adopt because nothing has to be maintained or updated by the customer.For example: Company email, shared documents, meetings and customer records that staff simply log in to, with nobody in the building patching anything.
3.2supercomputer
The most expensive and most powerful class of computer, used mainly for massive scientific problems rather than by business organizations. Even at the top of the range some problems take a year to compute, which is what motivated spreading work across many ordinary machines instead.For example: Modelling a climate scenario or a nuclear reaction, work that no ordinary machine could finish in a useful amount of time.
3.2system software
The collection of programs that control the basic operations of computer hardware. Application software does not talk to hardware directly; it talks to the system software, which talks to the machine.For example: A spreadsheet asks to save a file and never has to know what kind of drive is fitted or how it is wired.
3.2tensor processing unit (TPU)
A processor custom-designed to optimize the kind of matrix calculations that dominate deep learning. It is more specialized than a graphics processor and correspondingly faster on the work it was built for.For example: Hardware built by a large provider specifically to run its own language models, and then rented out to customers doing similar work.
3.2thin client
A machine with minimal memory, storage and processing capability, used as a window onto software that actually runs elsewhere. It is cheap, replaceable, and holds nothing worth stealing.For example: A terminal in a public area that has no data on it at all, so losing it costs the price of the box and nothing else.
3.2top-level domain
The suffix at the end of a domain name. Some indicate a kind of organization, such as commercial, educational, non-profit or government; more than two hundred are two-letter country codes; and a growing number of generic ones name particular industries or uses.For example: The last part of an address tells you something about who registered it, which is why an unexpected suffix on a familiar-looking name is worth a second look.
3.2transmission control protocol/internet protocol (TCP/IP)
The protocol suite the internet uses to move web pages and other information. It breaks a request into packets, routes them, reassembles them at the destination, and does the same in reverse with the reply.For example: Every page you open is this cycle running twice: a request out in pieces, a page back in pieces, reassembled before you see anything.
3.2transmission media
The physical pathway — cables and wireless — used to carry data. It is the second of the three requirements of a network, and the one that most directly limits how much can be sent and how quickly.For example: The difference between a fiber line and an old copper connection is nothing but the pathway, and it changes a download from seconds to hours.
3.2uniform resource locator (URL)
The address people actually use to identify and locate a web page. It names the host, the domain and the top-level domain, and usually a path to the particular resource wanted within that site.For example: A long address ending in a series of words after a slash is naming a specific page inside a site, not just the site itself.
3.4utility computing
The model cloud computing uses: renting processing, storage or networking from an outside provider as needed and paying only for what is actually used, the way a household pays for electricity. It is where the shift from buying capacity to buying service comes from.For example: Paying for computing by the hour that it ran, rather than paying once for a machine that then sits idle most nights.
3.2virtual private network (VPN)
A technology that lets someone outside the office connect securely to the organization’s internal network across the public internet. It is what makes an intranet reachable from home or on the road without putting it on the open web.For example: Working from home and reaching the same internal systems as a colleague at a desk, over a connection that is encrypted the whole way.
3.4virtualization
Running several separate computing environments on one physical machine, so that many underused servers can be consolidated onto a few well-used ones. It is the technique underneath both desktop virtualization and most of what cloud providers sell.For example: Twenty servers that each ran at a fraction of capacity replaced by three that run properly loaded, with a large fall in power and cooling cost.
3.2Voice over IP (VoIP)
Technologies that use internet infrastructure to place telephone or video calls. Their existence is the clearest sign that computing and telecommunications have converged: the call and the web page now travel the same way.For example: A team meeting held over an internet application rather than a conference call, with the organization’s telephone system quietly becoming software.
3.2web browser
A software application used to locate and display web pages, including their text, graphics and multimedia. It requests documents, interprets the markup it receives, and decides how the result looks on your screen.For example: The same page looks slightly different on two machines because the browser, not the server, does the final drawing.
3.2web page
A hypertext document containing both content and links to other documents. It is the unit the web is made of, and the thing a web server actually sends when it is asked for something.For example: An article you are reading, together with the links inside it that would take you somewhere else entirely.
3.2web server
A computer that stores web pages and processes requests for them. Many of them do not store finished pages at all: they run a program that assembles the page when it is asked for, often by querying a database.For example: A product page that did not exist a second before you asked for it, because it was built from stored rows about that product.
3.2website
A collection of interlinked web pages owned by the same organization or individual, usually hosted on a web server. The site is the unit an organization publishes; the page is the unit a visitor reads.For example: One organization’s address covering thousands of pages, all reachable from each other and all under the same name.
3.2Wi-Fi network
The everyday name for a wireless local area network, which connects devices using high-frequency radio waves instead of cables. Ease of installation made it the default in offices, homes and public places.For example: A cafe where a dozen strangers are all on one network that took an afternoon and one box to install.
3.2wide area network (WAN)
A network connecting multiple local area networks over a large distance, often with ownership and management distributed among several parties. It ranges from a few buildings to a city to the whole world, and the internet is the largest example of one.For example: A retailer whose stores, warehouses and head office are all on one network although no single organization owns every link between them.
3.2wireless local area network (WLAN)
A local area network that uses high-frequency radio waves rather than cables, installed to connect mobile devices or where running cable is impractical. It is the same idea as a wired local network with the pathway changed.For example: A warehouse where handheld scanners work anywhere in the building because no cable could reach a moving person.
3.2workstation
A computer built for medical, engineering, architectural, animation or graphics work, optimized for visualizing and rendering three-dimensional models. It typically serves one user, but with far more processing power, memory and graphics capability than an ordinary desktop.For example: The machine an architect uses to walk a client through a building that has not been built, which would defeat an ordinary office computer.
3.2World Wide Web
A system of interlinked documents on the internet, and in effect a graphical interface to it. The web is not the internet: the internet is the network of networks, and the web is one very successful thing running on top of it.For example: Email, video calls and file transfers all use the internet without being the web at all, which is why the two words are not interchangeable.
Put it together

Final challenge

Situations rather than definitions. Each one describes something happening in an organization and asks what is actually going on, which is the form this material takes once you are the person being asked. Every company described is invented. Answer all of them, then score: the result breaks out by objective, so a weak area points at the section to reread instead of disappearing into a single number.

Final challenge

Final challenge

Answer key — the interactive, self-scoring version loads when scripting is available.

1. 3.2 A hypothetical national insurer processes millions of policy transactions a day against one central system that ten thousand staff and a public website all use at once. It is being replaced, and four options are on the table. Which class of computer does the chapter describe for this work, and why that one?

  • A. A supercomputer, because the volume is enormous and this is the most powerful class of machine available — Supercomputers are the most expensive and most powerful class, but the chapter says they are used primarily to assist in solving massive scientific problems and are typically not used by business organizations. Raw speed is not what this workload needs.
  • B. A mainframe, because it is optimized for high availability, heavy shared use and security, and is the chapter’s machine for mission-critical transaction processing — correct. The chapter defines a mainframe as a large computer used as the main central computing system for major corporations, optimized for high availability, resource utilization and security, and typically used for mission-critical applications such as transaction processing.
  • C. A rack of workstations, because workstations carry fast processors and large memory and several of them together would cover the load — Workstations are optimized for visualization and rendering of three-dimensional models for medical, engineering, architectural and graphics work, and typically serve one user each. Their strengths are the wrong strengths for shared transaction processing.
  • D. A larger personal computer, because the difference between the classes is mostly physical size, and a desktop machine can be ordered with as much memory and as fast a processor as the nightly run needs — The classes differ by what they are optimized for, not by size alone. A personal computer serves one user; the chapter’s comparison has mainframes serving ten thousand or more at once, which is a difference in kind.

2. 3.2 A hypothetical architecture practice buys two machines in the same month. One will let a designer walk clients through unbuilt buildings in three dimensions. The other will hold the practice’s drawings and be reachable by everyone in the office. How does the chapter classify them?

  • A. Both are servers, because both are more powerful than an ordinary desktop and both are shared resources of the practice — Cost and power do not decide the class. The chapter separates them by what they are optimized for: one machine visualizes and renders for the person sitting at it, the other answers many people at once.
  • B. The first is a server because rendering is a service, and the second is a workstation because it stores the working files people work on — This reverses both definitions. The word service in the chapter means making files, printing and communications available to users of a network, not the professional service the practice sells to its clients.
  • C. Both are workstations, because a workstation is any professional machine used for architectural or engineering work and both were bought for the practice — The intended use of the practice does not classify the machine. The second one has no single user sitting at it and exists to answer requests, which is the chapter’s definition of a server rather than a workstation.
  • D. The first is a workstation and the second is a server, because one is optimized for rendering for a single user and the other for access by many concurrent users — correct. A workstation is optimized for visualization and rendering of three-dimensional models and typically has one user; a server makes files, printing and other services available to users of the network and is optimized for many concurrent users, with more memory, storage and network capability.

3. 3.2 On a hypothetical bottling line, small dedicated controllers start and stop conveyors, sensors report temperature and vibration continuously, and the whole line reorganizes itself when a batch changes without an operator intervening. Which description matches the chapter?

  • A. The controllers are embedded systems and the sensors are output devices, and because they exchange readings continuously over the factory network the arrangement is best described as an intranet on the production floor — The controllers are indeed a kind of purpose-built computer, but sensors supply data rather than present results, which makes them input devices. An intranet is a private internal website, not a factory network.
  • B. This is a peer-to-peer network, because the machines request and provide services from one another with no central server involved — Peer-to-peer describes machines that both request and provide services on a general-purpose network, and the chapter places it in small offices and homes. It says nothing about coordinating physical processes.
  • C. The controllers are programmable logic controllers, the sensors are input devices supplying environmental data in real time, and the whole arrangement is a cyber-physical system — correct. Programmable logic controllers are the chapter’s specialized devices for automating machines and processes, sensors are input technologies collecting environmental data such as temperature and vibration in real time, and a cyber-physical system integrates computing with physical processes through tight coordination of software, sensors and mechanical components.
  • D. This is grid computing, because many small independent machines are combining their computing power to complete one large task — Grid computing combines many independent computers, often ordinary desktops, on a single large computational problem. Nothing here is being computed collectively; the machines are running a physical process.

4. 3.2 A hypothetical equipment hire firm wants to identify returned items automatically as they come through a doorway, without anyone pointing a scanner at each one. Items are low in value and arrive in bulk. Which reading of the chapter’s material is accurate?

  • A. Passive tags are the obvious fit, because they cost a few cents and are read from a few feet, and the doorway can be the reader — correct. The chapter describes passive tags as small and inexpensive, starting from a few cents, with a typical range of up to several feet, and lists eliminating line-of-sight reading and reading at greater distances among the advantages over bar codes.
  • B. Active tags are required, because only a tag with its own battery can be read without the item being pointed at a scanner — Active tags include a battery and can transmit hundreds of feet, but they cost several dollars each. Paying that for a low-value item is the trade-off the chapter is asking you to notice, not a requirement.
  • C. Bar codes are the better answer, because the chapter says radio-frequency identification cannot be read unless the tag is plainly visible — This inverts the chapter. Not needing line of sight is precisely the advantage it lists first: the data is readable regardless of the item’s position or whether the tag is plainly visible, which is what bar codes cannot do.
  • D. Neither technology applies, because identification at a distance requires a network connection on each item — A tag is not a networked computer. It is a small transponder that answers a reader’s electromagnetic field, which is why a passive one needs no battery and no connection of its own.

5. 3.2 A hypothetical software company sells one product that runs on two different operating systems. A new manager asks why the company does not instead ship a version for each of the several hundred computer models its customers own. What does the chapter’s account of system software say?

  • A. Each model would need its own build, and testing every combination of processor, graphics card and disk on the market would be far too expensive, so the company ships two versions and accepts that some machines will run them badly — Cost is not the reason, because the per-model builds are not needed in the first place. The chapter’s point is structural: the operating system removes the need for them entirely.
  • B. Applications talk to hardware directly, so the company writes one version and relies on device drivers supplied by customers to make up the difference — The chapter states the opposite. Application software cannot interact directly with hardware; it interacts with the system software, which in turn interacts with the hardware, and drivers are part of that layer rather than a customer responsibility.
  • C. Modern hardware is standardized enough that any program will run on any machine, so the two versions exist only for commercial reasons — Hardware is not uniform, which is why drivers exist at all. Two versions are needed because the two operating systems present different layers, not because of marketing.
  • D. The operating system provides a common layer over different underlying devices, so applications only have to be built for the operating system rather than for each computer model — correct. The chapter says the operating system provides a common layer for different underlying devices so that applications only have to be developed for different operating systems rather than for each different computer model, which is exactly why a product ships in two versions and not two hundred.

6. 3.2 A hypothetical veterinary group must keep three kinds of data: today’s appointments and charges, a nightly copy in case a server fails, and years of old internal correspondence it must be able to produce if asked. Which arrangement matches what the chapter says about matching data to media?

  • A. All three belong on the fastest available storage, because data that cannot be reached instantly has no value to the practice — The chapter separates the three types precisely because their requirements differ along timeliness, access speed, searchability and life span. Paying for instant access to correspondence nobody reads is the waste the distinction exists to prevent.
  • B. Operational data on fast disk or flash storage, backups on hard drives so recovery is quick, and archival data on low-cost removable media such as magnetic tape — correct. The chapter puts operational data on disk-based or flash storage for speed, notes that storing backups on hard drives enables quick recovery without slowing operations, and archives data that is no longer used operationally on magnetic tape, which is slow and not quickly searchable but very low cost and removable.
  • C. Operational data on tape because it is written continuously, backups on flash storage, and archival data on hard drives so it stays searchable — This reverses the media. Tape stores data sequentially, so access can be very slow and the contents are not quickly searchable, which is why the chapter reserves it for archives rather than for live transactions.
  • D. Operational and backup data together on one drive, and archival data deleted once the retention period is over, since old email has no operational use — Keeping the backup on the same drive as the live data defeats its purpose, since one failure takes both. Whether old correspondence may be deleted is a compliance question, and archival data exists precisely because the answer is often no.

7. 3.2 Two hypothetical laboratories agree to exchange results automatically. The cable is installed, the files leave one system and arrive intact at the other, and the receiving system rejects every one of them. Which of the chapter’s three requirements of a network has not been met?

  • A. The pathway, because a cable that delivers unusable files has not really transmitted the data — The pathway is the physical medium, cable or wireless, used to transmit data, and here it did its job: the files arrived intact. Arrival is a separate question from comprehension.
  • B. The sender and receiver, because a system that rejects a file is not genuinely a receiver for that message — Both ends exist and one of them has something to share, which is what the first requirement asks for. Rejecting a message you cannot interpret is what a receiver without a shared protocol does.
  • C. The protocol, because the two sides have not agreed on the procedures they will follow when transmitting and receiving — correct. The chapter’s third requirement is rules or protocols governing communication between sender and receiver, and its own illustration is an email that arrives perfectly in a language the reader cannot decode: if the message is not understood by the receiver, there is no communication.
  • D. None of them, because all three are present and the problem is simply a software defect at the receiving laboratory — Calling it a defect skips the diagnosis. The chapter’s framework says a message can travel the whole way successfully and still fail, and the missing element in that case is the agreed procedure, not the code.

8. 3.2 A hypothetical training department must move a one gigabyte video file to a site that has an old low-speed connection. Someone proposes buying a much faster connection for the site instead. Which statement follows from the chapter’s own comparison of connection speeds?

  • A. Transfer time falls roughly in proportion to the increase in capacity, so a connection a thousand times faster turns a transfer of well over a day into seconds — correct. Bandwidth is the transmission capacity measured in bits per second, so time is size divided by rate: the chapter’s own table takes the same one gigabyte video from more than a day and a half on an old modem down to a few seconds on gigabit fiber.
  • B. Transfer time depends mainly on the size of the file, so a faster connection will make only a marginal difference to a file this large — Size is only half of the calculation. Holding the file constant and changing the rate is exactly the comparison the chapter’s table makes, and it changes the answer by orders of magnitude.
  • C. Transfer time is set by the slower of the two connections only when both ends are wireless, and by the faster one otherwise — The slower link limits the transfer regardless of whether either end is wireless. Nothing in the chapter makes the medium decide which end governs.
  • D. Transfer time cannot be estimated in advance, because bandwidth describes capacity rather than speed and the two are unrelated — Bandwidth is defined as how much binary data can reliably be transmitted over the medium in one second, which is precisely what makes an estimate possible.

9. 3.2 A hypothetical clinic replaces the computers in its examination rooms with cheap terminals that hold no data and run everything from a server in the basement. What has it done, in the chapter’s terms, and what does it gain?

  • A. It has built a peer-to-peer network, gaining resilience because any terminal can serve any other if the basement server fails — Peer-to-peer means any device can both request and provide services. These terminals only request, and if the server fails none of them can serve anything, so no resilience has been gained.
  • B. It has installed embedded systems, because each terminal now performs one specific set of tasks rather than being a general-purpose computer — An embedded system is built into a device to perform a specific set of tasks, such as controlling an engine. A thin client is still a general-purpose window onto general-purpose software running elsewhere.
  • C. It has moved to a public cloud, because the applications now run somewhere other than where the user is sitting — A public cloud is a service any interested party can rent on a pay-per-use basis. The clinic still owns the server in its own basement, so the resources were never pooled with anyone else’s.
  • D. It has adopted thin clients with desktop virtualization, reducing software licensing and maintenance costs and helping with strict privacy and data protection duties — correct. Thin clients are microcomputers with minimal memory, storage and processing capability, and the chapter says they use desktop virtualization to provide workers with a virtual desktop environment, helping reduce costs for software licensing or maintenance and comply with stringent privacy and data protection laws.

10. 3.2 A hypothetical university librarian is asked why a search engine cannot find the library’s catalogue records, its subscription journals, or the student portal, and whether that means they are on the dark web. What is the accurate answer?

  • A. They are on the dark web, which is the chapter’s name for everything a conventional search engine cannot index — The chapter is explicit that the dark web is not to be confused with the deep web. The dark web is the part used for nefarious purposes and reachable only with specialized anonymizing browsers.
  • B. They are on the deep web because somebody hid them deliberately, and material reaches the surface web only when an organization pays a search company to index it, which is why public bodies with no advertising budget stay invisible — Nothing here is hidden in the sense the dark web is hidden, and indexing is not something an organization purchases. A catalogue is unindexable because its pages are generated from a database when somebody asks.
  • C. They are on the deep web: pages behind authentication, pages generated from databases on demand, and pages nothing links to are not indexable, and that is unrelated to the dark web — correct. The chapter enumerates the deep web as private areas requiring authentication such as a learning management system, dynamic pages created from connected databases, and static pages not connected to others by hyperlinks — and separately warns that the dark web is something else entirely.
  • D. They are on the surface web but rank too low to appear, so better search terms would eventually reach them — Search terms cannot reach a page that was never indexed. A search engine cannot traverse content that only exists once a database query is run for a specific request.

11. 3.2 A hypothetical charity is told that its address, its mail service and its donation service can share one domain while behaving as separate systems. Which explanation of a web address matches the chapter?

  • A. The three parts of an address are the protocol, the domain and the file path, and only the file path can vary between one service and another, so the two names must be reaching the same machine and the same software — The chapter’s dissection names the host name, the domain and the top-level domain. A path to a particular resource may follow, but it is not one of the three parts of the address itself.
  • B. An address is one indivisible name registered as a whole, so a separate service requires a separately registered domain name — Registrars register domains, and the organization is then free to use as many host names in front of that domain as it needs. The chapter’s own example lists several services on one domain.
  • C. The address names a host, a domain and a top-level domain, and different host names in front of the same domain reach different servers or groups of servers — correct. The chapter says a URL has three distinct parts — the host name, the domain and the top-level domain — and gives examples of one organization’s mail, photo and mapping services each answering on a different host name in front of the same domain.
  • D. Host names are decorative, since the numeric address underneath is what actually identifies the organization to a browser — The host name is what tells the network which server or group of servers should answer, so it is doing real routing work rather than decoration.

12. 3.2 A hypothetical manufacturer wants three things: a public site, a private site where employees enrol in benefits, and a site where its suppliers see live order status. It asks whether these are three technologies or one. What does the chapter say?

  • A. One set of technologies used three ways: an internet site, an intranet restricted to authorized employees, and an extranet restricted to authorized partners — correct. The chapter says an intranet looks and acts just like a publicly accessible website and uses the same software, hardware and networking technologies, but adds authentication or firewalls; an extranet is a private part of the internet enabling two or more firms to do business together. Its summary table separates them by focus, content, users and access, not by technology.
  • B. Three different technologies, because an internet site is built with web standards while an intranet and an extranet run on proprietary software that the organization buys separately for each audience — The chapter explicitly says the same technologies are used. What differs is who is authorized and whether the content ever crosses the public internet.
  • C. One technology used twice, since an extranet is simply the name for an intranet once suppliers are given accounts on it — The chapter’s table gives them different users, different content and different focus: internal communications with corporate content for employees, versus external communications between business partners. Adding supplier accounts to an internal site is not the same design.
  • D. Three different networks, because internal communication cannot travel over the same infrastructure as public content — Internal communication in the simplest intranet stays inside organizational boundaries, but an extranet deliberately uses the public internet infrastructure and protects the traffic with a secured tunnel.

13. 3.2 A hypothetical logistics company is choosing where to build a facility that will hold its servers. Two candidate sites are equally priced: one is far from any customers but very safe from severe weather, the other is close to its largest customer base but on a more exposed coast. What does the chapter say the decision involves?

  • A. Proximity is irrelevant once a connection is fast enough, so the safer site wins automatically — Distance still costs time, which is why the chapter says organizations weigh proximity to customers to reduce latency rather than treating location as settled by the network.
  • B. The exposed site wins automatically, because reducing delay for users is the only thing customers ever notice — Latency matters, but a facility that floods is unavailable, and the chapter’s availability discussion makes downtime the more expensive failure. Both considerations are live.
  • C. Neither site should be built on, because reliability of this order is obtainable only by renting space in a facility a third party already operates, and a company of this size has no business running a data center at all — Renting space in a collocation facility is a real option the chapter names, but it is an alternative to be weighed rather than the only way to reach high availability.
  • D. A genuine trade-off between protection from the elements and proximity to users for lower latency, decided alongside power, cooling, connectivity, expandability and security — correct. The chapter says organizations go to great lengths selecting locations that strike the optimal balance between protection from the elements and proximity to customers or users to reduce latency, and separately lists connectivity, floor space, energy, cooling, security and modular expandability as requirements of the facility overall.

14. 3.3 A hypothetical municipal utility is told that its five-year-old server fleet is fine because nothing has broken. Its technology manager disagrees and points to the chapter’s account of obsolescence, in which the planning horizon of five years managers once worked to has given way to new versions of devices every six to twelve months. Which argument is the chapter’s?

  • A. Capability keeps advancing underneath a fleet that is standing still, so the question to put to the machines is not whether they still work but what the utility can no longer do with them — correct. The chapter says rapid advances continuously force organizations to upgrade to gain or maintain competitive advantage, and that whereas managers once thought in terms of five years, new versions of devices are now released every six to twelve months.
  • B. Equipment that has not failed has not yet been used up, so replacement should wait until something actually stops working and the money already committed to these machines has been earned back in full — Whether a machine still runs is not the chapter’s test. It frames obsolescence as the gap between what current technology enables and what the installed base can do, which opens long before a failure.
  • C. Machines become unreliable at a known age, so a fixed replacement interval removes the need to make a judgment — The chapter gives no such interval, and a fixed schedule would replace machines that are still capable while leaving others in place after they have become a constraint.
  • D. Obsolescence is a hardware problem only, so a fleet that runs current software is by definition current — The chapter devotes a whole subsection to software obsolescence: new operating systems often require new hardware, and older applications may not be compatible with the new operating system.

15. 3.3 A hypothetical school district hears that its operating system will stop receiving mainstream support, with paid extended updates available for a limited period afterwards. The new version has strict hardware requirements. What is the managerial shape of this situation, in the chapter’s terms?

  • A. A software licensing question, since paying for the extended updates converts a fleet-wide upgrade into an ordinary recurring subscription the district can carry in its operating budget for as long as it likes — Extended updates buy time rather than removing the decision, and they are a bridge with an end date rather than a permanent arrangement.
  • B. Planned obsolescence, in which a vendor’s end-of-support decision forces a fleet-wide upgrade whose real cost is the hardware and the labour of upgrading every machine — correct. The chapter defines planned obsolescence as designing a product to last only a certain life span, notes that a company may cease support for a product and effectively force users to switch, and says the cost lies both in hardware and software and in the time and resources needed to upgrade tens, hundreds or thousands of computers.
  • C. A security question only, because support and updates concern vulnerabilities rather than capability — Security is part of it, but the chapter’s emphasis is the compulsory upgrade: a new operating system that requires new hardware and may not run the organization’s older applications.
  • D. A negotiation, because vendors routinely extend support indefinitely for large institutional customers who ask — Nothing in the chapter suggests support dates are individually negotiable, and building a plan on that assumption would leave the district without a path when the date arrives.

16. 3.3 A hypothetical publisher notices a pattern: each hardware refresh is justified by software that will not run on the old machines, and each new software release is justified by capabilities the new hardware made possible. A director asks whether someone is being manipulated. What does the chapter’s figure describe?

  • A. A loop in which more powerful hardware enables more powerful software, and the more powerful software then requires hardware more powerful still — correct. The chapter draws exactly this two-arrow loop: powerful hardware enables powerful software, which requires powerful hardware. It names the same pattern a vicious circle when describing how enhanced capabilities enable new applications that then demand more data and communications capacity.
  • B.
